Folio II

An abridgment of the capitular recesses of the fathers of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, celebrated from the time of the Council of Constance down to the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1493; and also the method for visiting monasteries of both sexes, together with a summary of the privileges of the aforesaid province, diocese, and order, happily begin.

On the visitations of monks, the preface begins. Chapter 1.

“You shall visit your brothers, to see whether they are acting rightly.” 1 Kings 17. In these words it is briefly indicated what sort of visitation of monasteries there ought to be. For the visitation itself ought to be charitable, not hateful: 10, q. 3, Cavendum. And this is marked in that phrase, “your brothers.” For the visitor, in order to produce a worthy fruit of his visitation, should show himself brotherly and charitable to those who are to be visited, and should know that he is the brother of those to be visited, not their lord; he should hate vices, but love the brothers: dist. 86, Odio; 23, q. 4, Duo. And in the Rule of the holy father Benedict, chapter 2, What sort of man the abbot ought to be. For if visitation is to be fruitful, it must be charitable; for charity is the proper gift of Catholic unity and peace: 1, q. 1, Multae autem. And where charity is not, justice cannot exist: 24, q. 1, Ubi. Therefore visitation must be carried out from charity, without hatred and cruelty: 10, q. 3, Cavendum.

Secondly, visitation ought to be examining, that is, investigative concerning the life and morals of those to be visited: 10, q. 1, Episcopum; Extra, De statu monachorum, Ea quae. And this is indicated in the word “you shall visit,” that is, “you shall examine.” Thirdly, visitation should be discreetly deliberative; and this is indicated when it says, “whether they are acting rightly.” But these matters will be spoken of at the appropriate places. Therefore let visitation be such as was instituted by the holy fathers, and it will bring much fruit. For if it is done duly,

it is the reform of order, the preservation of discipline, the restoration of peace and concord, and the consummation of all honor and beauty. For it raises up what has collapsed, gathers what is scattered, reforms what is dissolved, reintegrates what is broken, brings back what wanders, joins together what is torn apart, and suitably preserves the things that are holy and just. It restores unity and peace between head and members, abbot and brothers, and reconciles inferiors to superiors. If visitation is carried out zealously, charitably, and discreetly, it compels due obedience to be shown by subjects to chapters. Let it cease, and the discipline of religion will quickly expire. Finally, if it is neglected [unclear]. For it is what preserves the obedience of the good and humbles the insolence of the contumacious. For it makes offenders fear, and embraces those who are advancing in the bosom of charity. Few are those who obey from love; servile fear restrains many from evils. And happy is the necessity that compels one toward better things. For as the bristle introduces the thread, so initial fear introduces charity. De pe. dis. 2, § hec que, before the end. And woe is there where fear has perished from the earth. Micah 7; 16, q. 7. And we have said these things, after me. Since therefore visitation was instituted for this, that gains of souls may be sought through it, 10, q. 3, it is to be guarded against; all visitors must carefully weigh what is required of them. And lest they deviate from the statutes of the ancients, they should always strive to imitate their forms and examples. For the sake of this matter the present formula of visitation, drawn from the constitutions of the fathers, has been brought together in the following manner, so that new visitors, seeing before their eyes the due order of their office, may avoid various and dangerous errors.

Who has authority to appoint visitors of monks. Visitors of our monks. Chapter 2.

Visitors are to be appointed by the presidents of the provincial chapter, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, c. In singulis, where it is said as follows: [unclear]

Let religious and circumspect persons also be appointed in the same chapter, who should strive, in our place, to visit each abbey of that kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, according to the form prescribed for them, etc. And in the constitutions of Benedict XII, chapter 2, it says as follows: Let them also provide which abbots, and which and how many cathedral churches, monastic monasteries, and other places of the same order or religion, and how often, they ought to visit up to the provincial chapter itself. Long custom also, since it is not contrary to the constitutions, is to be held as law, 11, distinction, In his. Hence it is clear that the authority of the presidents has the power to appoint visitors; yet if at any time it should seem necessary and useful, they can apply the counsel of the chapter in choosing visitors.

What sort the visitors ought to be. Chapter 3.

Furthermore, in order that the visitors may be able fruitfully to visit others, religious men of the same order are to be chosen, having zeal for God and for souls according to knowledge, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, In singulis. And in the constitution of Benedict XII, chapter 3, it says: Let the visitors be suitable, careful, and discreet in carrying out the office of visitation; and let them observe all the things that are known to have been established in the aforesaid constitution of the same council and in the other constitutions of the said Honorius, our predecessor. Thus there. And they ought to be diligent, De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in Clementines, De censibus, c. Romana, book 6. In the constitution of lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, which begins Cum pridem, it says as follows:

First of all, therefore, we wish and, under the solemn attestation of the strict examination of the last judgment, enjoin upon you, namely the visitors, that at every time, and especially during your visitation, in all conduct, life, morals, and discipline, you strive to bear and conduct yourselves so religiously, holily, and honorably that to the others to be visited by you, not so much by word as by example, you may offer the form of all perfection; proceeding during the time of visitation in fitting habit, with a suitable household and mounts, and

honorable, not superfluous: that each should be content with a chaplain and a servant, with three horses; let moderate refreshment suffice for you without murmuring. Thus he.

Moreover, they must be gentle, not cruel. 10, q. 3, Cavendum. For this office men are to be chosen who are mature and experienced in many matters, not neophytes, masters before they have been disciples. 16, q. 1, Si clericatus; 61 dist., Miserum. Yet I do not say that mature young men are not to be preferred to dissolute old men, since they are deservedly called presbyters, that is, elders, by wisdom and not by age. 84 dist., Porro. But those gray-haired in morals should be appointed as visitors. What this grayness is is stated in Job 28: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding.” 26, q. 2, Qui sine. And prelates are also called elders because of their honor. 21 dist., Cleros post me.

Let the visitor be a companion to the good through humility; but toward the insolent and those who despise discipline, let him show the severity of his authority, because governance is diminished if too much humility is shown by prelates toward subjects. 86 dist., Quando. And yet this severity must be tempered with kindness. 45 dist., Disciplina, and c. Sunt. Therefore, from among the fathers, if it can be done, let the better men always be appointed to this office, men who know and are able to take counsel for the needs and cases of individuals; men who first do in their own affairs what they try to do in those of others. For thus in c. 6 our provincial fathers said, c. 5: “Visitors appointed by the sacred provincial chapter shall first and before all things visit and reform themselves and their monasteries, with those subject to them everywhere, lest, when they direct their eyes to the reform of others, the weak mutter under their breath and say, ‘Physician, heal thyself.’” Luke 4. Therefore let them first begin with themselves; then let them visit and reform the other monasteries committed to them, both of monks and of nuns, with such diligence as they can. To this pertains De censibus, Romana, book 6, and 2, q. 7, Iudicet and the two following chapters; 25 dist., Primum; 61 dist., In sacerdotibus. 83 dist.: “No one rightly assumes the office of a monitor unless he condemns errors by his own actions and shows love of innocence by his manner of life.” Thus there.

Therefore let visitors strive first to visit themselves, and so proceed to the correction of others. For it is written in Job 5: “Visiting your appearance, you will not sin.” For he who neglects himself cannot amend another, as the Lord says in Luke 6: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.”

III

Lastly, That Visitors Should Have Zeal for God and for Souls. Chapter 4.

Finally, the visitors themselves must, according to knowledge, be zealous for the salvation of those to be visited, so that they do not conduct their office negligently and in passing, lest, with the lazy servant, they be judged useless by the sentence of condemnation. And let them have zeal for regular discipline and for the constitutions of the fathers, knowing beyond doubt that they will be richly rewarded for their labors by the giver of all good things. Let them carry out the office of visitation committed to them as if the care of all whom they visit belonged to them alone. Yet let their zeal be discreet, lest, if, which God forbid, they correct sinners indiscreetly, they themselves incur a graver fault. 24, q. 3, Non imperpetuum. And where they find things worthy of some correction, let them correct not from love of vengeance nor from hatred, but from zeal for justice. 23, q. 4, final section. And the just and holy are indignant at sinners not through hatred but through zeal for discipline. 45 dist., Vera iusticia. Nor should they be remiss where fault has deserved discipline, because if they leave the faults of offenders unpunished, they sin gravely. 11, q. 3, Si is; 23, q. 5, Qui viciis. And a prelate who does not correct crimes is called not a prelate but a shameless dog. 83 dist., Nemo. He has the guilt of the doer who, when he is able to correct, neglects to amend. 86 dist., Culpam; 83 dist., Error. And not to correct the wicked but to foster them is to kill them. 23, q. 5, Qui viciis; 45 dist., Sed illud. And it is not charity but weakness if evil morals are not corrected. 23, q. 5, Non putes. [Correction?] ought not to be indiscriminate, but, according to blessed Gregory in the Moralia, judging justly, holding the balance in its hand, it should carry justice and mercy in either scale-pan. Dist. 45, Omnis. For the harshness of excessive rebuke receives neither correction nor salvation. Ibid., Cum beatus, and c. Disciplina. Therefore, lest zeal be deemed indiscreet, let it be tempered with mercy and gentleness.

That visitors should be discreet in their inquiries. Chapter 5.

Those also who are appointed as visitors should be wisely discreet, imbued with the divine Scriptures, and experienced in this business either in themselves or in others, lest they rashly believe things that ought not to be believed, or impudently conceal things that ought to be believed. For either is an evil. For he who believes quickly is light of heart. Ecclesiasticus 19. And we ought not quickly to believe evil things about others. Dist. 86, Si quid. And evil things concerning one’s neighbor must first be proved before they are believed. 2, q. 1, Deus. And 3, q. 8, Iudicet. 11, q. 3, In cunctis, and c. Quamvis. For it is written, Ecclesiasticus 19: Do not believe every word. 11, q. 3, Non solum per [unclear]. But to wish to believe no one is the mark of an impudent man. And indeed the innocent man always believes well and judges well of others. Proverbs 14. 22, q. 4, Innocens. Therefore visitors should be discreet and prudent, so that, considering the zeal, life, and merit of those making depositions, they may be able to know whom they ought to believe. For witnesses are to be weighed according to worthiness of faith and seriousness of conduct. 4, q. 3, § Item in testibus. And there throughout. Therefore, insofar as it can be done, visitors ought diligently to examine the intentions, motives, and causes of those making depositions, lest perhaps they be moved by no just reason. Finally, our fathers decreed thus on this matter: Visitors ought especially to be zealous for religion, mature and discreet in character, and also very solicitous and circumspect in carrying out the act of their visitation. And a little later it is added: But visitors should not readily believe every [unclear].

the spirit. 1 John 4. Nor should they condemn anyone on mere suspicion or on the deposition of a single witness. But manifest matters do not need accusation. 2, q. 1, [unclear], § In manifestis, etc. and following. I judge him, too, to be not a lover of charity but a deceitful man, who for the sake of defamation or revenge reveals a brother's hidden crime. 5, q. 5, Qui ambulat; 6, q. 1, Summa. By crime one can understand not only a mortal offense, but also every venial one. 25, dist., Unum orarium, § Nunc autem. In serious matters, however, and those concerning reputation, diligent inquiry should be made; but before just proof, except in manifest cases, no one should be judged or condemned. 30, q. 5, Nullum ante veram, etc. and following. And in such matters two or three witnesses must be brought forward. 2, q. 5, c. 1, etc.; Placuit.

Therefore visitors should be cautious in judging such secret matters, in order to avoid scandal, unless the person has been convicted or has confessed of his own accord. 2, q. 1, Nos vero quemquam, and following; Nomen presbyteri, and following. But if the accuser fails in proof, he ought to be punished with the penalty of retaliation. Extra, De calumniatoribus, c. 1; 2, q. 3, Calumniator, and following; q. 8, Qui crimen; 3, q. 10, Eos, and following. It must also be guarded against that matters which have been corrected and punished be taken up again anew. Extra, De accusationibus, c. De his; and 2, q. 1, Prohibentur; 23, q. 4, Si illic. Thus also the holy fathers established.

Let everyone beware, moreover, lest by [unclear] he disturb the minds of his brothers or of his fathers. Furthermore, if any secrets have been revealed to the visitors themselves, they should beware of bringing them into public. 2, q. 1, Si peccaverit; 6, q. 2, Episcopus si clerico; c. Placuit. And concerning hidden matters one must not inquire too curiously. Extra, De accusationibus, Qualiter, iii. Yet concerning manifest matters, as I said above, the outcry of an accuser is not necessary. Same title, c. Evidentia.

If at any time they perceive that some matters have not been properly proposed, let them act as prudent men; and, so far as can be done while preserving the truth, let them not readily believe them. And if they must be believed, nevertheless those things of which it is not known with what intention they are done should be interpreted in the better part, because we ought rather to presume good than evil. De regulis iuris, c. Estote. And in such matters the intention of the deponent is to be weighed rather than his words. For if someone sets forth true things from an evil intention, the intention makes a good work evil. 23, q. 5, Cum minister.

Let visitors be cautious and especially discreet in examining the excesses of prelates; since they have to correct the sins of others, they frequently incur the hatred of many and suffer snares. Extra, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, ii. In all things let them always act in such a way that they do not lose the form of charity. For correction ought to be made according to each person's rank and with the peace of the Church preserved. 23, q. 4, Ecce, and c. Quisquis; c. Quidam; c. Cum quisque; c. Ipsa pietas; c. Quid faciet circa me. Likewise correction ought to be made with the intention of healing, not of raging. 86, dist., Odio; 23, q. 4, Ita plane circa me. And not from hatred, but from charity. Extra, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, ii; 24, q. 3, Corripiantur. And sometimes it should have more gentleness than severity. 45, dist., Qui sincera, and c. Licet; because one gently chastised shows reverence to the one chastising. c. Cum beatus Paulus; 12, q. 2, Fraternitas; 24, q. 3, Corripiantur. These and other testimonies of discretion, the mother of virtues, visitors ought not to omit, so that they may proceed worthily and justly.

The form of the oath which visitors once used to present to presidents. Chapter 6. Once the presidents, not only in Mainz but also in other provinces, used to require from visitors an oath concerning the diligent fulfillment of their office. This, however, is not done in our times, nor do I judge that it would be useful or necessary; because one whom the spur of his own conscience does not drive to exercise diligence is scarcely or rarely compelled by another's command. Nevertheless I have wished to insert the form of the oath here, so that, when [they have sworn?]

[unclear] is read, let it be considered what is to be done. It follows thus, namely the form of such an oath as I found in ancient books.

I, brother N., abbot of such-and-such a monastery, appointed by the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents of the provincial chapter recently held in the monastery of N., as visitor of the diocese of N. with respect to the monasteries of our order, swear by these holy Gospels of God that I will carry out faithfully and diligently, to the best of my powers, the office of visitation enjoined upon me, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the decrees of the holy fathers, setting aside love, hatred, favor, and any other disordered affection whatsoever. So may God help me and these holy Gospels. Those who were absent used to give this oath; those present, however, swore in chapter before the lord presidents. But neither now seems necessary.

On the Power and Authority of Visitors. Chapter 7.

They have it from the Apostolic See, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, where it is said: “Let religious and circumspect persons also be appointed in the same chapter, who, in our stead, shall take care to visit the several abbeys of that kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, according to the form prescribed to them.” “In our stead,” he says, so that, while authority is weighed in the visitor, none of those being visited may dare to rebel. Their authority is more fully noted by the abbot above, in the same chapter, and in the final chapter of De statu monachorum. Nevertheless their power is limited, as in the chapter In singulis, because they cannot depose the rector of a place from his office without a special mandate.

For if they see that he must be removed altogether, let them denounce him to his own bishop, so that he may see to removing him; but if he does not do so, let the visitors refer this to the judgment of the Apostolic See. Exempt persons, however, are to be denounced immediately to the lord pope. Visitors should also have monks corrected by the abbot of the place, as in the same place, chapter Ea quae. But those whom they find contumacious and rebellious, according to the measure of the fault, let them strike with regular censure in the stead of the lord pope, without respect of persons, not sparing rebels on account of their obstinacy or the power of their friends, but rather casting the diseased sheep out of the sheepfold lest it infect the healthy sheep. Nor is there to be appeal from correction: De officio ordinarii, chapter Licet; and De appellatione, Ad nostram; and chapter Reprehensibilis; and chapter Cum speciali. Understand this unless the one correcting should exceed the measure: 23, question 4, Qui peccat.

Visitors, therefore, according to the decree of Honorius III in chapter Ea quae, if they find monks offending, should command the abbots of the places to correct them, as in the aforesaid constitution it says in these words: “But if abbots, in correcting according to the command of the visitors and the regular institutes, are found negligent in themselves or in their monks, let them be proclaimed and corrected, and let them be punished publicly in the general chapter in such a way that their penalty may be an example to others.” And note according to what is said there: a visitation of this sort ought to be made plainly and without the noise of judgments: De accusationibus, Olim. For regulars are easily removed from their administrations: De simonia, chapter Per tuas. And therefore the judicial order is not in every respect to be observed in inquiries of this sort. Let them inquire diligently, and let them correct and reform, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, the things which they see must be corrected.

But it is asked whether the bishop of the place can visit the monasteries of his diocese. It is answered that he can, as in the chapter [unclear], In singulis, section Porro.

He can visit them, but he ought not to bring secular persons in with him, as Hostiensis notes there in the gloss. For the visitation which the visitors make does not take away the bishop’s own jurisdiction, as is noted in the same chapter In singulis. Custom, however, has otherwise; for bishops also very often commit their own turns to abbots.

Likewise, concerning the authority of visitors, the fathers in provincial chapters also enacted several things. Whence chapter 1 says: Visitors can make statutes imposing penalties heavier than those in the constitution. [unclear]

Ad hāc scrupulositatem decidendā ꝯsiderari oportet: ꝙ motus ep̄orū ad visi tandū monasteria cū visitatoribus ordinis/ duas ex quibus orit̓ habet ratōes.Aut hoc faciūt zelo discipline: aut machinatōe malicie.Si pͥma ratōe si notus est zelus eoꝝ et tāta fuerit necessitas monasterij visitādi possūt admitti: sed nō nisi in ꝓpria ꝑsona: qꝛ seculares visitatiōi nisi valde necesse sit oīno nō debēt interesse</Initial>

in [unclear] against disorderly monks or those forgetful of their profession, etc. Likewise, chapter 6, section decretum, says as follows: Where they do not find disciplines effective for reform, let him institute new ceremonies according to canonical sanctions and the statutes of the provincial chapter, which those visited are bound to observe without any contradiction. If it seems necessary to the visitors, they may bind those to be visited by a bodily oath to tell the truth, as in the constitution of lord Nicholas [unclear], chapter 3; and these matters must be discussed in their own place. In chapter 15 all those to be visited are instructed to receive their visitors with all reverence and humility and to treat them charitably, and diligently to heed and observe their admonitions and ordinances. The visitors themselves also have authority to impose greater penalties than are expressed in the constitutions, and to compel rebels, by ecclesiastical censure, to obedience to their commands.

But sometimes many impediments occur concerning the visitations of monasteries. For sometimes the monks themselves and abbots maliciously obstruct these by themselves; sometimes through the ordinary bishops; sometimes through princes; and often through their blood-relations, friends, and supporters. What must be done in these cases, if they occur, I shall try to make clear from the statutes of the fathers. In chapter 15, which was celebrated second at Seligenstadt, we read the statute.

That no one may obstruct the so salutary office of visitation by any contrived device or pretext: we will that each and all abbots, provosts, priors, and their professed members who refuse or contradict their visitors, and those same rebels, disobedient persons, and those who obstruct the office of visitation by nod, word, deed, or writing, or who arrange, procure, or by any device, by themselves or through another or others, directly or indirectly cause or attempt that it be obstructed by their friends, noble or ignoble, or by any subordinates whatsoever, so that the visitors cannot freely and quietly exercise this office of theirs, incur sentence of excommunication by the very fact. The visitors themselves are also bound to publish this same sentence of excommunication against them and to hand it over for due execution. But if the visitors cannot execute the aforesaid things, in chapter 21, celebrated fourth at Nuremberg, it was thus decreed: that the disobedient and contumacious persons visited should be denounced to the nearest of the presidents, who shall proceed against them by appropriate remedies of law on apostolic authority. And in chapter 23 this statute follows: We also strictly forbid anyone henceforth, by himself or through others, in any way to make arrangements with diocesans, princes, or any other temporal lords whatsoever, so that visitors are not admitted; nor let him attempt in any way that those visitors, who do not need the permission of the ordinaries of the place, since they are directed by apostolic authority, are not to be admitted, under penalty of thirty Rhenish florins, to be paid irremissibly to the chapter as often as any of the abbots and other rectors shall do the contrary. Moreover, this penalty seems to be imposed on the rectors of monasteries, without removing the aforesaid provision that they are to be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to obedience.

If a Bishop Wishes to Visit with Us. Chapter 9.

It is sometimes accustomed to happen that the ordinary bishops of the places wish to visit monasteries with us; whether they should be admitted in this way or not is often doubted. To settle this scruple, it must be considered that the bishops’ impulse to visit monasteries with the visitors of the order has two causes from which it arises. Either they do this from zeal for discipline, or from the contrivance of malice. If for the first reason, if their zeal is known and the necessity of visiting the monastery is so great, they may be admitted, but only in their own person, because laymen ought not at all to be present at a visitation unless it is very necessary.

[unclear] are to visit, even if the bishops have not been negligent.

How visitors are to be received and treated in the monasteries. The time for visiting. Chapter 11.

The time for visiting is to be fixed by the presiding visitors themselves, as is stated in Const. Bene., XII, chapter 2. Yet we find in the older statutes of the fathers the command that, within a year from the time of the chapter that has been held, they should fulfill the office of their visitation. It belongs to bishops, however, to visit every year, 10 q. 1, Relata, and c. Decrevimus.

Concerning the time of visitation, in chapter 7 held at Bamberg, it was laid down thus: "Let the visitors faithfully complete within the year the office of visitation enjoined upon them." Thus there.

And how often ought visitation to be made? It seems that every year, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in the Clementines. On this Franciscus de Zabarella poses the following question formally: "I ask," he says, "with respect to its saying that visitation is to be made every year, whether it is enough that it be made at the end of the first year and at the beginning of the second." The gloss on whether it suffices refers to the note in the same title, In singulis, where it is concluded that it does not, because in this way it could, in the case of chapter In singulis, be deferred up to six years, to the prejudice of the monastery; nor would that satisfy the law, which wishes it to be done from three-year period to three-year period.

Stephen says the same, because visitation is made for correcting things committed, not for things to be committed. Therefore, if the first was sufficient, the second will have nothing to correct. Paulus says the same, because if this were done at the end of the first year and at the beginning of the second, there would not be a year between the first and the second, but a two-year period. Hence it seems that they ought to be equally spaced; argument from De consanguinitate, Quod dilectio, as Paulus thinks. This is precisely true with respect to chapter In singulis, because the text there says "from three-year period to three-year period." Thus Franciscus Zabarella in the said chapter.

From these things it seems one should say that visitation ought to correspond to the chapter: as often as the chapter is held, so often also visitation should be held. We also have this in custom, that regularly we visit from three-year period to three-year period. This, however,

...in chapter Attendentes, namely, appears to concern nuns only; bishops are no less ordered to visit them.

Whether a visitation can be repeated? The answer is that it can, if there is a reasonable cause. On this matter, in chapter 17, in the third chapter celebrated at Nuremberg, the fathers decreed as follows: We ordain that after the visitors have once visited some monastery and have received procuration from it, if they judge it expedient for the more abundant observance of regular discipline, they may, by the authority of the chapter, exercise the office of visitation again as often as it seems useful to them; and they are also to be received as true visitors, yet without the exaction of procuration. Francis Zabarella says the same thing in the said chapter Attendentes, question 10: that visitation is to be made as often as there is need. From all these things I conclude that the visitation in the first year must be completed from the time of the chapter celebrated, and afterward can be repeated as often as there is need; but procuration ought not to be received except within a three-year period.

How visitors are to be received and treated in monasteries. Chapter 12.

When, therefore, visitors come to some monastery for the purpose of visitation, let them be received and led to prayer; if they are not neighbors and frequently received, let their feet be washed, and let them be treated charitably. In conventual places let the abbot of the house give way and recognize them; let him not take it amiss if he has others set over him. 2, question 6, Quis scit. Yet the abbot himself, according to his custom, should give the blessing to the people in every place, not the visitors. For this has been decreed in several chapters: that visitors be received with honor and reverence and be treated charitably, as is fitting, in all things.

With how many horses visitors ought to come. Chapter 13.

In the first two chapters it was decreed that none of the visitors should dare to bring with him more than twelve mounts, under the penalty contained in the same chapters; therefore at that time it was permitted for visitors, and also for those coming to the chapter, to bring twelve mounts with them. Then in the third chapter, which was celebrated at Fulda, it was decreed that a visitor should not bring with him more than six mounts. But Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, in his form of visitation, which he handed over to the visitors, commands that each visitor should be content with a chaplain and a servant, with three horses. Nevertheless, in the same constitutions of lord Nicholas the cardinal, he commands the visitors themselves to conduct themselves decently and to have honorable servants, so that they may not be burdensome to those visited. In chapter 15, celebrated at Seligenstadt for the second time, there is such a statute: The visitors themselves too shall have an honorable household and company, and each of them shall be content with the number four, unless a reasonable cause demands more.

How long visitors ought to remain in one monastery.

Therefore, lest the visitors become burdensome by the expenses of visitation, they shall strive to dispatch themselves as quickly as they can; and, as the fathers decreed, they shall not make a stay beyond three or four days in one place visited by them, without evident necessity. But if such things occur as demand delays of a longer time, they shall strive to dispatch themselves in such a way that they prove in all things that they seek not themselves but God and the peace of the visitors. Let the visitors also advise their servants to conduct themselves honorably and without murmuring in all things.

Chapter 14.

Those visited are bound diligently to guard the goods and horses of the visitors. Chapter 15.

Since sometimes, especially among those who hate being corrected, frauds and deceits are wont to occur against the visitors themselves, with malicious or wicked persons lying in ambush at the gate for those under them, lest the malicious should gain advantage from their own wickedness, the fathers in chapter 5, at Würzburg, first...

having been celebrated, they thus established. This sacred chapter decreed and established that, when visitors come to any monastery for the purpose of visitation, the abbot and convent of that monastery shall have the horses and belongings of the visitors guarded with the greatest diligence. But if anything of their goods or belongings should happen to be lost or taken away, before all else the abbot and convent of that monastery shall without any contradiction pay at once to those visitors the value of the goods or belongings lost. And nevertheless such negligence shall be punished in chapter at the discretion of the presidents. This was also often established afterward in other chapters.

Of the penalty for visitors who neglect to visit at the due time. Chapter 16.

Since the increase of holy religion and regular observance arises in no small measure from frequent and diligently performed visitations, lest so wholesome an institution of the fathers be brought to nothing through the torpor of negligent visitors (for where the governance of discipline is despised, what remains is that religion suffer shipwreck: De statu monachorum, Attendentes, in Clem.), the fathers in almost all chapters celebrated up to now have imposed penalties on visitors if they neglected their office. And first, indeed, in the constitution of Benedict XII, chapter 3, concerning visitors, it is said thus: But if the visitors themselves have neglected to carry out their office, we will that they incur automatically the penalties incurred by those who do not come to the provincial chapter without having a canonical impediment. And in chapters 4 and 5 and certain others it was established thus: This sacred chapter further decreed that those appointed to visit, if they have neglected the time appointed for them, namely within the year, shall pay the penalty like those who neglect to come to chapter, that is, thirty Rhenish florins, with moderation and just assessment reserved to the discretion of the presidents in the provincial chapter. And in chapter 19, celebrated at Bamberg for the second time, it was established that all visitors who have not completed their visitations as enjoined on them shall be bound, for each monastery not visited, to pay three florins to the chapter as a penalty, especially in the case of monasteries of men, unless they have a legitimate cause excusing them. This same thing was likewise established in chapters 20 and 21. Besides these things, however, the presidents, whenever it seems necessary to them, can also impose other penalties. Concerning these matters also the constitution of Honorius III, Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter Eaque, speaks thus: Let the following visitors diligently investigate the traces of the earlier visitors, and let them report their negligences and excesses to the following general chapter, so that according to their fault they may publicly receive the penalty due.

If it should happen that visitors are robbed on the way in the course of their office. Chapter 17.

Finally, if (which God forbid) [unclear] robbed in the course of their office [unclear].

When the visitors first come to any monastery to be visited. Chapter 18. How they should begin.

Therefore, when the visitors have gone to visit some monastery, if it can be done, on that same evening they shall summon the abbot and convent, the monks and professed lay brothers, to the chapter place, or on the following morning at an hour that they have decided is suitable; when these have been gathered, they too shall enter. And when all have sat down, one of the visitors shall say: Benedicite.

When they have answered, Dominus, let him add these or similar words.

Venerable father and beloved brothers, religious in Christ. If you have read the record of the last chapter, celebrated at N., you have certainly understood that we, although insufficient, have been appointed as visitors for you; but if you have not read the record, nevertheless we are ready to fulfill the office enjoined on us. And let him add:

We also do not doubt that you know that, in the order of visitation, three things are chiefly to be done. First, the visitors themselves ought to present themselves to those to be visited in the chapter-house, and to make known their authority to visit, and to put first a prayer according to the custom of the order, and an exhortation according to the character of the time and of the persons; on the state of monks, Attendentes, in the Clementines, and in the constitutions, chapter [unclear], and in [unclear]. Secondly, there ought to be a diligent examination of those to be visited, and an inquiry into their morals and the state of each; 10, question 1, Episcopum, and question 3, Cavendum; on the state of monks, chapter Eaque. Thirdly, the final conclusion and the due correction of offenders, chapter In singulis.

Since, therefore, even in the least matters divine aid must always be implored, and, as blessed Dionysius says in the fourth chapter of On the Divine Names, in spiritual matters one must above all begin from prayer, it is fitting that we also observe the commands of such teaching and not pass over the praiseworthy custom of the order. Let us therefore pray.

And, rising, let them read alternately the psalm:

To you have I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes on the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us. Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, for we are greatly filled with contempt. For our soul is greatly filled: reproach for those who abound, and contempt for the proud. Glory be to the Father. After this let the visitor make an exhortation.

Note that the visitation ought not to begin from examination or correction, but from exhortation. Chapter 19.

This is also contained in the statutes of the chapter in this way: Then one of the visitors should make to those to be visited an exhortatory address on discipline, on brotherly charity, on peace, on spiritual progress, on perseverance, and on other virtues according to the requirement of the persons or of the time.

How necessary matters are to be deposed. Chapter 20.

When the exhortation has been finished, let the visitor next admonish those to be visited how and in what manner they ought to conduct themselves in their depositions, and let him say thus in order:

Beloved brothers, although, having often been visited, you are not ignorant of the form of the visitation itself, nevertheless, on account of those who have more rarely been present at visitation, I shall briefly touch upon the manner and form in which you ought to conduct yourselves in depositions. First, we exhort you all and each one of you that, just as visitation was instituted for this purpose, that vices may be rooted out and virtues implanted, so also each one in making proclamations should direct his intention to the proper end. Likewise, each one should make deposition out of charity, if he has seen anything that must necessarily be amended, and not out of hatred, which God forbid, nor out of aversion, because this would be a grave sin. Likewise, each one should take care to observe what is due and honorable in depositions of this kind. Likewise, let no one withdraw those things which worthily

Likewise, let no one, making much of those small things that are corrected daily, set them down as though reserved by us for greater confusion, unless they were such things as seemed worthy of correction. Likewise, let each one of you keep before his eyes zeal for God and for souls, and conceal none of those things that ought to be brought to light. And when notice has been given in this manner, let a place suitable for examination be assigned to them; to it let the brothers come in order, beginning with the prior down to the last one established in sacred orders.

On Whether an Oath Is to Be Required or Not Required from Those Being Visited. Chapter 21.

But it is rightly asked whether those who are to be visited ought to be bound to speak by oath and to answer the truth about the matters asked. To know this: as I found in the ancient statutes, also of other provinces of the order, where it seemed necessary an oath was required from those being visited. This also now seems to me sufficiently reasonable, especially if the monks have conspired, or made a pact, or maliciously concealed the truth. And I think that this statute, which I approve, should be strengthened.

Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, writes as follows, among other things, to the visitors of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg: But because among very many people words of exhortation profit little unless a coercive penal censure is also added, therefore in the monasteries or places which you shall visit for the time being, after the act of salutary exhortation, when a bodily oath has been received from all concerning speaking the truth in their examination, you shall proceed according to the tenor of the commission delivered to you by our other letters.

Likewise, in the statutes of the chapter I found the contrary. For in the sixth chapter, held at Erfurt, the statute is read thus: It also pleased the fathers that, without demanding an oath, after first setting forth the word of God, the visitors themselves should complete their act. This same thing was established in the following chapter, held at Bamberg, [unclear]. Similarly also in certain others. What then? If he requires an oath, does he commit an offense against obedience, contrary to the statutes of the fathers? If it is not to be required, why did the cardinal legate of the apostolic see and magnificent doctor order it to be required? Can it never be required, and can it not be required? Plainly, I think it is so. Where it is necessary and useful, it can be required; but it ought not lightly to be required. And he took care to insert here such a form of the oath at hand, just as he also found it in the more ancient institutions of the fathers, so that if at any time it should be necessary, there should be no need of long inquiry.

The Form of the Oath and the Manner of Swearing, with the Hand Placed upon the Text of the Gospel, [unclear]. Chapter 22.

O brother M., I swear by these holy Gospels of God that concerning all matters about which I shall be questioned by you or by any one of you, generally or specially, I will speak the truth; and also all things that I know to require your reformation, and that are necessary for the reforming of the monastery entrusted to you to know, I will faithfully disclose to you. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God. Saying this, let him place his hands upon the Gospel according to Luke.

At that time, as Jesus was speaking to the crowds, a certain woman, lifting up her voice, said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked. But he said: Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Amen.

On Examination. Chapter 23.

Concerning examination and inquiry: when the visitors have been prepared and are seated at the assigned place, let them have great diligence in inquiries of this kind, in asking all necessary matters one by one. And if anything worthy of correction has been deposed, let one of the visitors mark it on a sheet, which he should also guard diligently, lest it ever come into the hands of anyone. XIII

First, let them inquire whether perhaps the abbot has presumed any such thing against the visitation. And if they find any such things, let them release them, as in Extra, De accusationibus, c. Olim.

Concerning general matters, the things written below, or at least some of them, may be inquired into.

First let them ask about general matters as seems good to them.

Whether the abbot extorted an oath from the monks about keeping silent the truth, or otherwise forbade them to report anything.

Likewise, whether all are professed, and how.

Likewise, whether any have been received simoniacally. And if so, what has been done with the simoniacal goods.

Likewise, whether they observe true obedience to the abbot and to his superiors according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Likewise, whether any or all are proprietors.

Likewise, whether any are fornicators, and who.

Likewise, whether they are chaste, as befits religious.

Likewise, whether, when healthy, they eat meat; whether all do so or some; where, when, and how often.

Likewise, whether they observe silence in the four forbidden places, and whether they do the same at night-time or not.

Likewise, whether they observe the fasts of the Church and of the Rule as they are bound to do.

Likewise, whether there is always reading at table for those eating.

Likewise, whether all eat together in one refectory.

Likewise, whether all sleep together in one place, and whether they are clothed and girded according to the Rule.

Likewise, whether they use linen garments or linen sheets.

Likewise, whether they sleep on feathers or mats.

Likewise, inquiry can be made and questions asked about their habit and tonsure.

Likewise, whether they continually wear the monastic habit.

Likewise, whether they run about outside the enclosures of the monastery without permission of their superiors.

Likewise, let inquiry be made about the state of temporal goods, what it is like, and how each item is spent.

These and similar matters may be inquired into in general, as shall seem expedient to discreet visitors.

Inquiries about the divine office should also be made thus or similarly.

Likewise, first, at what time they rise for matins.

Likewise, whether they sing matins and all the other hours, or some.

Likewise, at what time they rise for prime.

Likewise, at what time they perform the other hours.

Likewise, whether they discharge the hours slowly and religiously, as is fitting.

Likewise, how often the chapter of faults is held in the week.

Likewise, how faults are examined there.

Likewise, whether all diligently come together for the work of God.

Likewise, whether consecrated vestments and ecclesiastical ornaments, books, chalices, and other things are handled cleanly.

Likewise, how many masses are celebrated daily.

Likewise, whether they sing high mass every day.

Likewise, how often the brothers celebrate in the week.

Likewise, whether they always confess before mass.

Likewise, whether the Rule is read to them and expounded according to the statutes of the fathers.

And many other things in this manner.

if they are the supreme rulers of monasteries. An nimis anxius sit circa temporalia? Ite si regulã observat diligẽter in ieiunii vigilijs etcͣ? De ceteris aũt fratibus visitatores ẜm qđ eis visum fuerit opportunuʒ inquiret in charitate mu- tua/ de pace/ obediẽtia/ de continentia de peculio etcͣ. Ubi v̾o abbas in corrigẽdo diligẽs est/ minor de sim- plicibus fratribus fiet insinitio. Quissime postqͣꝫ oes fuerint examinati/ exani- net et ipse abbas/ si aliquid forte voluerit dice- re. Et pponant̉ sibi maiores articuli de ispo y fratres depositi: auiset̉ qʒ seriosi vt emẽdet. Qđ si tale qđ fu erit ꝙ sine correctõe nõ debeat transire/ et ipse negaue rit deponentiũ melius erunt examinãda testimonia/ donec veritas lucidius patescat. Caucãtur tñ tumul- tus et scandala. XIV

Likewise, whether he presides in person over the chapter of faults, and how often.

Likewise, whether he corrects offenders without respect of persons.

Likewise, whether he shows himself to the brothers as exemplary and imitable in all good things.

Likewise, whether he frequently and without reasonable cause wanders outside the monastery.

Likewise, whether he takes superfluous mounts with him.

Likewise, whether he has suspect familiars, or ones harmful to the monastery.

Likewise, whether he has any suspect intimacies with women.

Likewise, whether he has in any way been marked by incontinence.

Likewise, whether he admits women into the monastery, and what sort.

Likewise, whether he diligently preserves temporal goods.

Likewise, whether he is excessively intent upon cares for temporal goods.

Likewise, whether he provides necessities for the brothers according to the Rule.

Likewise, whether he burdens the monastery with debts.

Likewise, whether he alienates the immovable goods of the monastery.

Likewise, whether in matters to be done he acts according to the Rule with the counsel of the convent, or not.

Likewise, whether he has subject monasteries; whether he visits them.

Likewise, whether he has had the recesses of the chapter published in the convent.

Likewise, whether he has observed the charter of the last visitation.

Likewise, whether he duly observes the Rule in all things, as is fitting.

And many things similar to these may be inquired into, according as there shall be need; it would be tedious to set them all out here.

Likewise, questions concerning the other officials and brothers.

Concerning the other officials, however, questions are to be framed according to the need, namely:

Whether there is a prior; who he is, of what sort, and how great.

Likewise, whether he is useful to the convent in procuring necessities.

Likewise, whether he is zealous for discipline according to the statutes of the fathers.

Likewise, whether he gives the brothers an example of good conduct.

Likewise, whether he corrects offenders according to the Rule.

Likewise, whether he diligently sees that the other regular statutes are observed.

Likewise, whether he is diligent in the office committed to him.

Concerning the cellarer: who he is and of what sort. Of what sort.

Whether he diligently fulfills his office.

Whether he duly attends the divine offices and conventual services when he is otherwise free.

Whether he diligently provides necessities for the brothers according to the Rule.

Whether he is humble, good, and exemplary before outsiders.

How often he renders account to the abbots concerning receipts and expenditures.

Likewise, whether he reverently obeys the abbot’s commands in all things.

Likewise, whether he is wasteful and a squanderer of the monastery’s property.

Whether he is too anxious about temporal affairs.

Likewise, whether he diligently observes the Rule in fasts, vigils, etc.

Concerning the other brothers, however, the visitors shall inquire, according as seems opportune to them, about mutual charity, peace, obedience, continence, private property, etc.

But where the abbot is diligent in correcting, there will be less inquiry concerning the simple brothers.

Finally, after all have been examined, let the abbot himself also be examined, in case perhaps he wishes to say anything. And let the greater articles concerning him, which the brothers have deposed, be set before him; let him be advised seriously, that he may amend. But if there is anything of such a kind that it ought not to pass without correction, and he denies it, the testimonies of those deposing must be examined more carefully, until the truth becomes more clearly evident. Nevertheless, tumults and scandals are to be guarded against.

Concerning the last proclamation of each one. After the examination has been begun according to custom in the chapter. Chapter 24.

When it seems opportune to the visitors, let all be summoned to the chapter-place to continue the act of visitation. When they are seated, let one of the visitors say: Bless ye. And when the response has been made: The Lord. Let him add:

Dearest brothers, there now remains, as you know, the final execution of our visitation, which, for bringing it to completion, to God

with [God] assisting, we have come together; and we exhort Your Charities that you also charitably receive our admonitions, which we make in charity, since we intend only to accomplish what accords with our salvation and yours.

And he may add general matters reported or observed, for admonition and correction. Then the lay brothers, novices, and sub-priests, that is, those not yet constituted in sacred orders, are to be called to the mat, one after another, or two by two; or certainly any concerning whom such a matter has been reported that they deservedly ought to be accused. When the one called comes to the mat, let him bow moderately; and let the visitor tell him his faults; and he shall at once lie prostrate on the ground until he is ordered to rise.

When those who do not belong to chapter have been dealt with and have gone out, first the abbot is to be called to the mat, then the prior and the others according to order. But while the abbot stands in judgment before the visitors, all the other brothers ought, out of reverence, to stand uncovered, until he is ordered to sit again. And note that here the abbot’s faults are to be told briefly and the lesser ones, lest occasion for contempt be given to the weak. But in private, or before a few of the seniors, all things necessary are to be told him, great along with small, etc.

Penances are to be imposed at the visitors’ discretion, with discernment, according to the manner of daily accusation. But if anyone there comes to be punished more severely, let the visitors have this done through the abbot, as in Extra, De statu monachorum, Ea quae.

On the final exhortation to be made. Chapter 25.

After all who are to be accused have been accused, and penance has been enjoined on each, let the visitor make a brief exhortation concerning regular observance, rebuking the general negligences of the brothers; and let him explain how such things are contrary to the Rule and harmful to the soul, etc., and the other things in this manner, as shall seem expedient to them. At this exhortation, moreover, the other professed monks and lay brothers not belonging to chapter, who had gone out, may be recalled and be present, unless something else prevents it.

On the customary absolution. Chapter 26.

When these things have been completed according to custom, let all humble themselves for absolution, bending their knees, and say the Confiteor, concluding: Pray for me. Let the visitor, standing, say:

May almighty God have mercy on you, through the intercession of blessed Mary and all the saints, and forgive you all your sins, and bring you to eternal life. Amen.

By the authority of almighty God, and of the ecclesiastical keys granted in this matter to our order, we absolve you from ecclesiastical censures, and restore you to the communion of the Church and to participation; and we dispense with you and rehabilitate you for the execution of the things to be done. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. And let some psalms to be said be enjoined on each; on the lay brothers, the Lord’s Prayer twice or three times.

When these things have been completed, the visitors may excuse their insufficiency before those visited, and commend themselves to their prayers, as is often done in these or similar words:

Dearest brothers, we ask that the things we have said or done here to all, or also in private to individuals, you receive charitably, and that you think nothing else of us than that we have done everything in charity. Also, I ask you to forgive me for the things said above by me; and if I have offended anyone by words, or if I did not speak as I ought, or otherwise than I ought, impute it to my lack of skill, not to my will, etc.; such things. And let him add, if there is time: Our help is in the name of the Lord. Who made heaven and earth.

On the charter of visitation to be made. Chapter 27.

According to the statutes of the fathers, once the visitation has been completed, the condition of the monks visited will have to be set in order in a charter, in which the necessary articles are to be inserted in which each one ought to amend himself: first concerning the abbot, then concerning the prior—

concerning the cellarer and the other officials, and lastly concerning all matters in general. And he shall also enjoin, under penalties and censures if need be, in part or in whole, the observance of the matters set down below. At the end of the charter he shall state how often in the year it must be read in chapter, and shall enter the condition of the monasteries in respect of the number of persons and the amount of revenues, or also of debts. Let him seal the charter with the two seals of the said visitors, as testimony for each point. And it should be noted that the abbot is bound to render to his visitors an account of all revenues, according to the statutes of the fathers, as was established in chapters 1 and 2 and in many other places. The visitors shall have a copy of the charter transcribed by themselves or by the monks visited, not by a secular person, who ought not to know the defects of the monks. And they shall carry this copy with them, to be sent on to the chapter. Let the visitors take diligent care not to hand over to the abbot the schedules of the deponents, lest occasion be given for acting maliciously, however zealous he may be; but let them take them with them to disclose them to the lord presidents, or certainly, if they have no need of them, let them burn them in the fire.

What is to be received from those visited for the expenses of journeys. Chapter 28.

Every abbot and convent visited is bound, according to the decrees of the fathers, to pay three Rhenish florins without any contradiction, as in chapter 11 and in the three immediately following. Hence in the same place it is said thus: The whole community of the fathers decreed that every abbot visited is bound to pay the visitors three Rhenish florins for their travelling expenses, unless the visitors themselves, for some good consideration, wish to act more moderately. Thus there. But let the visitors see to it that they require necessary things in such a way that they do not hide avarice under the appearance of need. For a procuration of this kind ought not to be burdensome, but moderate: 10, question 3, Cavendum, and [unclear].

If visitors or their servants should dare to accept any gift or any money, offered in any way by those visited. Chapter 29.

Because gifts make the giver and the receiver turn aside from justice: 11, question 3, Pauper, and chapter Qui rector. It is strictly forbidden to all visitors to accept any gift from those visited, or any money offered in any way or by anyone, either by themselves or through their servants, as is said in [unclear], chapter 15, concerning visitors, where it has as follows: Visitors and their servants shall receive no money on such an occasion or in any other manner; nor shall they, or any of their people, presume to receive any gift, of whatever kind or quality it may be, offered by anyone, so that they may not seem to seek the things that are their own, but those that are Jesus Christ’s. Therefore we establish and ordain that all and each of the visitors of this kind, or their servants, who, besides the expenses to be furnished to them only in victuals, shall presume to demand or receive money even from one willing to give it, or if they themselves, or any of their household servants, shall presume in any way to receive gifts, they shall be bound within a month to restore double what they have received to the church or monastery or other place of the same order or religion from which, or from whom, it was received; otherwise, from that time forward, let visitors of this kind who delay restoring that double amount to them beyond the aforesaid time know themselves to be suspended from office and benefice until they make full satisfaction for this double amount to the churches or monasteries or places thus burdened, no remission, liberality, or favor of the givers being of any force for them in this matter. And nevertheless, if it is expedient, the visitors thus suspended shall be compelled by the presidents to restore the aforesaid double amount, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and through other suitable remedies, with the obstacle of appeal removed. Thus there. Therefore let the visitors forbid their chaplains and servants to accept anything from anyone on account of visiting during the time of visitation,

their customary expenses, under penalty; but if they do not do so, and those men receive anything, they will not be immune from the guilt of prevarication.

That those visited provide safe-conduct for their visitors. Chapter 30.

If need be, the abbots and convents visited shall provide, at their own expense, safe-conduct for their visitors from one monastery visited to another, to be visited at the appointed visitation, as has been established in many provincial chapters.

That visitors reveal the secrets of those visited to no one. Chapter 31.

But let the visitors beware that they presume not to reveal to anyone, especially to secular persons, things entrusted to them or even discovered by them in visitations; nor indeed to their own brethren, nor to any familiars whatever. For what each does not wish to be done to himself, let him not do to another. For he is fraudulent who reveals secrets, 6, question 5, Qui ambulat. And in the constitution of Pope Benedict XII, chapter [unclear], it is said: And because it proceeds from the virtue of prudence if the way is barred to scandals, we forbid the aforesaid visitors to presume to reveal to others those persons, or their names, who have revealed any secrets to them in visitations, except only when, on account of such things revealed, it will be necessary to proceed to someone’s punishment or penalty. But otherwise let them punish those revealing, more or less as the character of the deed shall require, according to the judgment of the presidents. Thus there.

This brief form of visitation, drawn from the writings and statutes of the fathers for the direction of myself and those like me, when there shall be need, as best I could, I, brother Johannes, abbot in Sponheim of the diocese of Mainz, have copied out and humbly offer to the lords president of the provincial chapter to be examined and corrected. If they approve it to be observed in visitations, I shall not be deprived of the fruit of my labor; but if they reject it, by humbly submitting myself I shall be endowed with the reward of humility. In the year of the Lord 1490. [unclear]

From the constitutions of Pope Benedict XII, concerning visitors. Chapter 3.

Furthermore, the visitors who, according to the aforesaid constitution of that general council, shall have been deputed in provincial chapters of this kind, are to be suitable, diligent, and discreet in carrying out their office of visitation; and they shall observe all things that are known to have been established in the aforesaid constitutions of the same council and in the other constitutions of the said Honorius, our predecessor.

But if the visitors themselves negligently omit to carry this out, we will that they incur by the very fact those penalties which are incurred by those who do not come to the provincial chapter without having a canonical impediment.

And because we desire that the conduct of the aforesaid visitors of this kind proceed with all sincerity, we prohibit any visitor from being able to be visitor in the same year of the visitor deputed to him. And the aforesaid visitors, or their familiars, in a cathedral church, monastic church, monastery, or other place of that order or religion to which they have had to turn aside for the purpose of visitation, shall by no means remain more than two days, unless evident necessity or the great advantage of such a church, monastery, or place required a longer stay there by those visitors or their familiars. But then they shall do this with the counsel of the elders of the aforesaid church, monastery, or place.

Nor shall the visitors or their familiars be burdensome and oppressive to the same churches, monasteries, and places visited; they shall not seek sumptuous banquets, but with thanksgiving shall receive what has been honestly and fittingly served to them.

And the said visitors and their familiars shall receive no money on this occasion or in any other way; nor shall they themselves, or any of their people, presume to ask for any gift whatever it may be, or however it may be offered, so that they may seem to seek not the things that are their own, but the things of Christ.

we decree and ordain: that all and each of visitors of this kind, or their attendants, who, beyond the expenses to be supplied to them only in victuals, shall presume to demand or receive money, even from one willing to give it, or if they themselves or any of their attendants shall likewise presume in any way to receive gifts, shall be bound within a month to restore double what they have received to the church or monastery or other place of that order or of the same religion from which it was received. Otherwise, from that time onward, visitors of this kind who put off restoring that double amount beyond this time shall know themselves to be suspended from office and benefice until they render full satisfaction for this double amount to the churches or monasteries or places thus burdened, no remission, liberality, or favor on the part of those who gave it being of any force for them in this matter. And nevertheless, if it is expedient, those visitors so suspended are to be compelled by the presiders over the said chapters, and by each of them, to restitution of the aforesaid double amount, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and other suitable remedies, the obstacle of appeal being removed.

And because it proceeds from the virtue of prudence if the way is closed to scandals, we forbid the aforesaid visitors to presume to reveal to others those persons, or the names of those persons, who have disclosed to them any secrets in visitations, except only when, on account of disclosures of this kind, proceedings must be taken for someone’s punishment or penalty. Otherwise, persons making such disclosures are to be punished more or less, as the nature of the deed shall require, according to the judgment of the same presiders.

There follow from the decrees various rubrics on the state of monks, which it is useful for some to have at hand in visitations.

The conduct of monks ought to be set apart from all persons, according to the etymology of the name, because he is called “singular.” 16, q. 1, c. 1.

Monks ought not to be among a throng of people, for they are therefore called singular because they ought to avoid the multitude of human beings. 16, q. 1, Si cupis.

A monk, according to the etymology of the name, should lead a solitary life; he should be content with his cloister, because just as a fish lacks life without water, so a monk without a monastery. Therefore let him sit alone and keep silence, because he is dead to the world, but lives to God. Let him recognize his name: for monos in Greek is in Latin “one”; achos in Greek is in Latin “sad.” Hence “monk” is said, that is, one and sad. Therefore let him sit sad and attend to his duty. 16, q. 1, Placuit communi.

Apart from illness, permission neither to taste nor to take meat is granted to a monk. But if anyone shall presume against the rule, let him be subject for a space of six months to confinement and penance. De cons., dist. 5, Carnem.

Monks ought to be subject to their abbots in all obedience and devotion. 18, q. 2, Abbates.

No one ought to become a monk in hope of an abbacy. 16, q. 7, Per laicos. See, however, the fine distinction in the gloss in the same place.

A monk cannot make a testament. 19, q. 3, Quia.

When someone has become a monk, all things that he had are to be transferred to the monastery, nor can he thereafter hand them over to anyone. 19, q. 3, Prelatum.

It is not lawful for a monk to vow vows without the consent of the abbot; but if he has vowed, it must be broken. 20, q. 4, Monacho.

No one should receive or ordain a monk without the permission of his abbot. 20, q. 4, Monachum.

A monk ought never to be idle, because every idle person is among desires; but he should always be engaged either in prayers or in manual labor that befits his state. Let him love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and he will not love the vices of the flesh. Let body and soul strive toward the Lord. Let his sense keep watch; and, not lying open to wandering thoughts, let him do some work, so that the devil may always find him occupied, and many other fine things Jerome says to Rusticus. De conse., dist. 5, Nunquam.

Monks may neither make spiritual co-parents for themselves nor have familiarity with women. 18, q. 2, pervenit ad nos.

Monks are not permitted to live with nuns or to dine with them. 18, q. 2, diffinivimus, and in the two following chapters.

Monks are not permitted at their own pleasure to expel abbots or appoint others. 18, q. 2, nullam.

Women are forbidden to enter the monasteries of monks. 18, q. 2, c. pervenit ad nos.

A monk is not permitted to possess anything of his own. 12, q. 1, non dicatis, and c. quia tua; but all things ought to be common to them, c. scimus.

Incontinent monks are to be confined in work-prisons for severe penance. 27, q. 1, impudicas. 12, q. 1, non dicatis.

A monk is not permitted to receive anything without the license of his prelate.

A congregation of monks, however holy it may seem, is rarely found without an admixture of wicked men. 47, dist., quantumlibet. And this is a saying of Augustine to Vincent the Donatist, where he also says: “As I have found it difficult to find better men than those who have advanced in a monastery, so I have not found worse men than those who have fallen away in a monastery.” Hence I think it was said in the last chapter of the Apocalypse: “Let the just man be justified still, and let him who is in filth be filthy still.” Thus there.

A monk who seeks to live delicately in religion, though he was poor in the world, is to be detested. 12, q. 2, gloria.

A monk has the office not of teaching but of lamenting, that he may mourn either himself or the world, and wait fearfully for the coming of the Lord. 16, q. 1, monachus.

Monks who fail in religion are the worst, and those who make progress are the best. 47, dist., quantumlibet.

True and religious monks, if good, are to be honored before the rest. 16, q. 1, qui vere.

Monks are not to be received into a monastery for a price, nor are they to be allowed to have private property. De statu monachorum, c. monachi.

A monk who has private property is to be removed from communion of the altar; and if such a man is found at the point of death, he is not to receive burial among the brothers. Ibid., and c. super quodam, and c. cum ad monasterium.

Monks are bound to keep continual silence in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister. Same chapter, cum ad monasterium.

Healthy monks are not to eat meat. Ibid., § in refectorio.

From the Summa of Brother Angelus, on religious persons.

Whether religious are bound to be perfect. It is answered that they are not, except with that perfection to which they have bound themselves; but they are bound to tend toward perfection, according to Thomas, Second Part of the Second Part, question 186. Contempt of perfection is contrary to this. Hence they are not liars, although outwardly they bear the state of perfection, because they do not assume it as though professing themselves to be perfect, but as professing that they are tending toward perfection. Hence they would indeed be liars if they turned their mind away from the intention of perfection, according to Astesanus, book 6, title 47.

On obedience, collected from the Decrees.

Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith and is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because by sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, but by obedience one’s own will is slain. 8, q. 1, sciendum.

Obedience ought to be promised in writing, which is by custom and by the precept of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Likewise, he who knows that he has been set over others should not take it hard that someone has been made prelate over him; but let him himself also render the obedience that he demands.

It is often not expedient to obey commands. 11, q. 3, non semper. It is not always evil not to obey commands: when a lord orders those things that are contrary to God, then indeed one must not obey. And the following chapter, and c. Iulianus, c. si is.

One must obey superiors promptly. 93, dist., si inimicus.

God must be obeyed chiefly. 8, dist., quae contra.

11 q. 3, Imperatores.

A monk ought to obey his abbot more than the bishop in those matters that pertain to the Rule. 18 q. 2, Quod sit, § Nullus, and c. Abbates, 9 q. 3, Conquestus.

The commands of superiors must be obeyed even if they themselves act otherwise, unless they have erred in the faith. 2 q. 7, Sacerdotes.

Never should evil be done through obedience; but sometimes, rather, a good may be omitted because of obedience: [unclear]. 11 q. 3, [unclear].

Likewise, collected from the Decrees concerning the correction of sinners.

Correction ought to be made out of charity, according to the diversity of faults. 24 q. 3, Corripiantur.

Correction ought to be made with the intention of healing, not of raging. 86 dist., Odio; 23 q. 4, Ita plane circa me.

Correction ought to be mixed with kindness and severity. 45 dist., Disciplina; 12 q. 2, Fraternitas; 45 dist., Omnis.

For excessive severity on the part of one who rebukes receives neither correction nor salvation. 45 dist., Cum beatus.

Many things on these matters are found scattered above in the formula of visitation.

Before God he curses who consents to sins. 11 q. 3.

He who consents to sinners and defends another who offends will be accursed before God and before men, and will be corrected with the severest rebuke. Hence also a certain most holy father says: If anyone defends a sinner, let him be restrained more sharply than the one who sinned. These things are said there by Isidore, and c. Ita corporis, and in the two following chapters.

He who does not resist errors consents. 83 dist. Error which is not resisted is approved; and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed. Indeed, to neglect to disturb the perverse when you can is nothing other than to foster them; nor is he free from the scruple of hidden fellowship who ceases to oppose manifest crime. It is a saying of Innocent, and c. [unclear], Pope Pius.

For what does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error, who [unclear] stands in agreement with error? And in the same chapter Gregory says:

You see that he consents to error who does not hasten to cut away the things that ought to be corrected.

The faults of inferiors are imputed to the negligence of rulers. 86 dist.

The faults of those under orders are to be referred to none more than to idle and negligent rulers, who often nurture many pestilences while they pretend not to apply the more austere medicine.

Men are to be loved, sins to be hated, [unclear]. Let them hate sins, not men. Let the proud be corrected; let the weak be borne with; and those whom it is necessary to chastise more severely are to be punished not with the spirit of one raging, but of one healing.

Everyone is to be pitied; the sinner is to be angered at. 23 q. 4. These two names, when we say “man” and “sinner,” move us; in vain do they say: because he is a sinner, correct him; because he is a man, pity him. Nor will you wholly free the man unless you have persecuted the sinner. These things are Augustine’s, on the Psalter.

XXI

The manner and form of celebrating the provincial chapter of the fathers of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz.

Since, in celebrating provincial chapters, many occupations are accustomed to confront the lord presidents, lest, when those well-worn and experienced have departed or are absent, those less experienced and not accustomed to celebrating chapters of this sort should happen to be distracted by those very many occupations, I have taken care to commit the present form in writing for the knowledge of those who follow. I saw and heard it in those very chapters at which I was often present when they were being celebrated. Although in it we do not have all the things that are to be done in chapters, nevertheless many things, and the more necessary ones, will be found. For I judge that this is useful both for those present, in the exercise of discipline, and for those to come, by the example and regard of their predecessors.

That the presiding officers, visitors, and treasurers should arrive before the day of the chapter.

Therefore the presidents, past and future, together with the visitors or treasurers, should arrive some days before the appointed day for celebrating the chapter, being meanwhile also supported at the expense of the chapter, in order to discuss and mutually advise one another on the things that arise to be done, as was ordained in the fifteenth chapter, celebrated for the second time at Seligenstadt in the year of the Lord 1454.

On the Saturday preceding the day of the chapter, let one citation be made of those absent and of those who have not yet made satisfaction concerning the imposition of the contribution. The promoter of the order, by mandate of the lord presidents, shall have this citation affixed by the notary of the chapter to the doors of the monastery under vespers or compline. And he shall have it similarly done in two other churches, if need be. The citation may be made under this form.

By mandate of the reverend [unclear] of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, all and each of the abbots, provosts, and priors of the order of the province are here cited
