De monialibus. Articus.15. A ꝟo que dicta funt de monasterijs virorũ vo¬ lumus in monasterijs monialiũ qͦ ad articulos sibi cõ¬ petẽtes sil̃r obseruari.Volentes nihilominus et ordi¬

according to the disposition of the abbot; and let them not use feather mattresses.

If, however, chambers are found in the dormitory, we command that they be destroyed by the visitors or by their mandate, or suitably barred off.

On silence in four places. Article 12. Silence is to be observed in the oratory, the dormitory, the refectory, and the cloister. And after Compline let no one be permitted to say anything, except as is contained in the Rule. And before the said Compline let the Conference of the Fathers be read, or something else edifying.

On the porter of the monastery. Article 13. At the gate of each monastery let one prudent and discreet porter or doorkeeper be appointed, so that without the permission of the abbot or of another presiding officer no freedom of leaving it may be granted to anyone. For if anyone shall go out without permission of this kind, let him be subjected to fitting and due penalties, as is provided in the constitutions of Benedict XII concerning the permission ordained for going outside the monastery. Let him also be attentive that he in no way permit women to enter the monastery.

That no one from the order of mendicants be received into our order. Article 14. Moreover, since we have heard that certain abbots and other presiding officers in monasteries have received mendicant religious as monks without the permission of their superiors, and afterwards, what is worse, permit them to wander, to the detriment of their souls and the scandal of religion, we forbid them to presume such things hereafter. And those whom they have already received, unless by authority and mandate of the Apostolic See or with sufficient permission, they shall recall to the monastery as soon as they can, and others wandering outside the monastery, or at least within a year; otherwise let them be punished by the visitors of the provincial chapter with grave penalties.

On nuns. Article 15. But the things that have been said concerning monasteries of men we wish similarly to be observed in monasteries of nuns with respect to the articles suited to them. Nevertheless wishing and ordaining that they be kept under due and perpetual enclosure, as is contained in the constitution of Boniface which begins Periculoso, concerning the status of nuns, and is commanded to be observed by this sacred Council of Basel, we enjoin the visitors of the chapter, in virtue of holy obedience, to apply diligence in this matter.

On the master of novices. Article 16. Likewise we ordain that abbots and other presiding officers have in their monasteries suitable and sufficient masters, who may introduce their novices to the elementary studies, and then, when they have been instructed, send them suitably, according to the form of the statutes of the aforesaid Benedict XII, to the general studies, assigning them a pension.

On the number of monks. Article 17. We will and ordain that in every monastery where resources and revenues suffice, the number of monks instituted from the foundation be maintained; or, if they do not suffice, that as many be maintained as can conveniently be sustained. And so no one is to be excused on the pretext of any privilege, pact, transaction, or custom, which is called a corruption, especially since we reprove that corruption by which some say that they can receive no one unless he is noble. For even if nobles, other things being equal, are preferred in reception, nevertheless others are not excluded on account of this, nor ought they to be excluded.

That the goods of monasteries not be divided, but that provision be made for all in common. Article 18. Since all the goods of the monastery are ordained for the sustenance of the monks and for bearing other necessities, from which provision ought to be made for individuals according to the need of all, as is provided in the Rule, chapter 33, it is most absurd that abbots and officers belch forth from the revenues of the monastery into superfluity, while poor cloistered monks lack clothing, food, or other necessities, and especially in bodily illness, so that they are often compelled to return to the support of their parents. We will and ordain that, notwithstanding the divisions of burdens among the abbot and the officers, all

provide the necessities to the monks from the goods of the monastery as a whole. And for this to be done, let a reduction be made extending even to the revenues of any officials whatsoever, and likewise of the abbot. Nor may that division, nor any other custom whatever, avail in opposition for that abbot or for any officials whatever. On this matter we wish the visitors of the chapter especially to be attentive.

Concerning places not to be leased out. Article 19.

Let places of the order not be leased out, except with observance of the Benedictine constitution concerning places not to be leased out; and we wish this to be firmly observed, both with respect to the persons to whom they are leased and also with respect to the other circumstances.

Concerning loans. Article 20.

We also wish that, when loans have to be made, provision likewise be made according to the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII concerning loans and sales; and we most strictly command that this likewise be observed, under the penalties added there and under others to be imposed by the aforesaid visitors of the chapter.

Concerning inventories of monasteries. Article 21.

So that the squanderers of the goods of a monastery, or their restorers, may be more plainly seen [unclear] and known, we wish that, at the assumption of any abbot or other presiding officer, inventories be made, as is contained in the constitutions of the aforesaid Pope Benedict [XII?] concerning inventories.

Concerning monks who own property. Article 23.

Against the vice of private ownership, let what is contained on this matter in [unclear], in the same title, in the constitution of the lord pope [XII?], be observed, and according to the form of common law.

Concerning the resignation of officials. Article 25.

We wish that all benefices or offices which are assigned for the support of burdens, both in the food and in the clothing of the monks, if, at the command of the abbot, they refuse after three warnings to pay or furnish to the religious the things that they owe, the said abbot may and must, with the counsel of three or four seniors of the monastery, remove them from the said offices or benefices, and establish others in their place, whatever appeal

Articulus.31. <Initial type="decorated-drop">U</Initial>Olumꝰ ꝙ pꝛioꝛ monachoꝛū studentiuꝫ dicti oꝛdinis de.xv.in.xv.dies habeat tenere suū capl̓m.et ibi coꝛrigere et punire ẜm foꝛmā regule quoscunqꝫ mo nachos studētes/dū exorbitauerint scādalose.in vitas seu vestitu ac desuꝑ debeat inquirere diligenter/et in

presiding, so that they make their accustomed residence and dwelling within the precincts of the monastery, and do not stay in remote castles, except rarely and sometimes only for the sake of modest recreation or of pursuing some public utility.

That abbots and presidents of monasteries are to celebrate there on solemnities. Article 28.

We also will that the said abbots, on the principal solemnities and on others according to the manner and custom hitherto laudably observed in the said monasteries, celebrate there.

That monks are not to live with their parents. Article 29.

We forbid abbots to permit their religious to make a long stay and dwelling with their parents or with other laypeople, or to be entangled in the services of such persons. Rather, if one prior with at least one religious cannot live honorably and fittingly in his priory, let him be brought back to the monastery, according to the constitution of Pope Benedict XII and of the Council of Vienne, which begins Ne in agro.

Concerning beneficed monks to be sent to general studies.

But if any priors or beneficed men wish to go to study, let the greatest care be taken lest, under the appearance and shadow of study, they wish to wander about in cities. For this reason, when they are seen to be useless and neglectful of study, let them be sent back to the cloister, or to their benefice if, as has been said, they are able to live there. And the prior general of the monks in the study is to take diligent care over this; we will that such priors be diligently visited and corrected by the provincial chapter within whose bounds such a study shall be.

Concerning the chapter of faults of monks who are studying. Article 31.

We will that the prior of the student monks of the said order hold his chapter every fifteen days, and there correct and punish, according to the form of the rule, any student monks whenever they have scandalously gone beyond bounds in life or dress; and furthermore he must inquire diligently and appoint upright investigators from that order in the same study.

According to the form of the constitution of lord Pope Benedict XII, no prior general is to remain in the study except for one year. And we will and decree that the same prior be a formed bachelor in theology, or licensed in decrees, or a man of advanced and approved religious life. This prior is also to have authority to punish the contumacious and rebellious by bodily imprisonment, yet with the assent of four or five notable religious men living in the study, to be chosen by the religious of the said order studying there; and further, with the consent of the aforesaid men, when he sees any to be incorrigible and excessively scandalous, he may send them back to the cloister or to their priory.

Likewise we will and ordain that all religious coming to the study present themselves to the said prior within five days, and that he have them all recorded in one book; nor are they to leave the study unless the cause of their return has first been made known to the said prior. If that prior sees that the cause is unjust on the part of the abbot, then let him take care diligently to notify the visitors of the provincial chapter, so that they may provide for this as above.

We forbid that monks go on pilgrimage. Article 32.

And that abbots not permit their monks, under pretext of some devotion to some saint, or of indulgences to be sought in some place, to go out from their places, especially beyond the limits of their diocese, unless perhaps to visit certain regions by whose example they may be edified, or to edify them; but this rarely and with great caution. And no prior or beneficed man is to remain outside his diocese for five days unless permission has been obtained from his abbot; otherwise let the visitors of the provincial chapter punish the guilty most sharply.

Concerning the increase of penalties. Article 33.

The aforesaid visitors [unclear] the heavier penalties of the constitution Ne in agro against any religious thus disordered or forgetful of their profession

that they are not ashamed to carry hunting birds on the fist, according to the custom of secular nobles, or have them carried before them by their attendants.

That foodstuffs are not to be given in money. Article 34.

We forbid foodstuffs, clothing, and other necessities to be supplied to monks in money or revenues in any way, notwithstanding any constitution or ordinance whatsoever. And in this matter the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Boniface XII is to be observed. We also will that the aforesaid clothing and foodstuffs be fittingly supplied at the appointed times to the religious of the Benedictine order.

Concerning the vice of incontinence. Article 35.

The visitors of the chapter also, with exact diligence, are to make inquiry whether anywhere there are persons marked by incontinence; and wherever they find that this is so, especially superiors, or those who connive at the incontinence of others, they are to take care with all zeal to purge out that vice with due punishment. And if, perhaps because of favor shown to persons, they cannot do this, let them report it to the provincial chapter. The said visitors are to inquire whether abbots are excessively carnal in distributing the offices and benefices of their monastery, so that they have more regard to the advancement of their blood-relatives, and because of them the monastery suffers ruin or harm in spiritual matters and is damaged in temporal matters; and they are to rebuke the guilty very severely and report them to the provincial chapter. They are also to inquire whether the abbot, in pride of heart, treats his monks harshly and not in brotherhood, as though he were not one of them; and whether he does not permit them to say anything, even charitably, for the good of the monastery and of morals, if he himself by his own fury is overturning his house; and all whom they find guilty they are to take care diligently to correct, or to denounce them to the provincial chapter.

Concerning the obligation of these [constitutions].

By these things we do not understand that the aforesaid matters bind more to guilt than they formerly bound, but only to penalty.

Concerning the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs. Article 37.

We also will that the declarations of the Roman pontiffs issued concerning the aforesaid Benedictine constitutions shall have place in the foregoing matters.

That visitors are to be diligent in all things. Article 38.

In all the foregoing articles it is entrusted to the visitation of the visitors that they be solicitous for the gain of souls, and according to the condition of persons and likewise of places they are to act prudently in all things.

That secular persons are not to be appointed over the necessities of the monastery.

Secular persons are not to be appointed over offices, Article 39, nor monks to receive and collect the goods of the monastery and to distribute them, except insofar as they are subject and servants of the officials themselves of the monasteries, and are bound to render account to them concerning what has been received and distributed. Given at Basel, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year from the Lord’s nativity 1439. Here ends the bull of the Council of Basel for the reformation of the order, transmitted to the chapter.

Here begins the constitution of lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter ad Vincula, legate, concerning visitation.

Nicholas, by divine mercy cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter ad Vincula of the holy Roman Church, legate of the apostolic see throughout Germany, to the visitors of the province, etc.

Concerning the life and morals of the visitors, especially while they visit.

Since formerly and below. Therefore, first of all, we will and, under attestation of the promise made to us and of the strict examination of the Last Judgment, enjoin upon you that at all times, and especially in the time of your visitation, in all conduct, life, morals, and discipline, you study to bear and conduct yourselves so religiously, sacredly, and honorably that to the others to be visited by you, not only by word but also by example, you may present the form of all perfection; proceeding in the time of visitation in fitting habit, with household and mounts appropriate and honorable, not excessive, so that each of you be content with a chaplain and servant, with three horses. let refreshment suffice for you without murmuring. The eating of meat, except in the case of illness according to the permission of the Rule, or even the acceptance of any offered gift, even one not suspect, shall in no way be permitted to you.

The Form of Visitation and the Method of Proceeding.

With gentleness preserve the censure of discipline, correcting crimes and excesses without any respect of persons; strive to extend to all the offices of charity and kindness. Take care to recall those at discord to concord, diligently exhorting prelates to solicitude and vigilance concerning the souls committed to them, and to reflect how much more perfect than others they ought to be, since they have pledged themselves to teach others the way of perfection; and what grave danger hangs over them, because in the strict examination of the Last Judgment they will be bound to render an exact account for their own deeds and for all those individually committed to them; and that all, both prelates and subjects, [unclear] of their profession, how they may fulfill them; likewise how sweet is the yoke of the Lord and light the burden to all of good will.

But because among very many the conversations of exhortation profit little unless the censure of coercion also be added, therefore in the monasteries or places which you shall visit for the time being, after the customary conference of salutary exhortation has first been given, for the carrying out of the act of visitation, once a bodily oath has been received from all concerning the truth to be spoken in their examination, proceed according to the tenor of the commission delivered to you through our other letters, even by the coercion of the censures and penalties there expressed, establishing, ordering, and executing what shall be necessary there for introducing and continuing regular observance and discipline.

Take especial care that the prelates of the monasteries which you shall visit be so instructed and imbued by the ministry of this visitation of yours that, with decent habit and tonsure, with honorable life, gravity of morals, the word of doctrine, and the example of holiness, they may preside over their subjects laudably and fruitfully, and correct the excesses of their subjects according to canonical and regular institutions. Let them recall all their fugitive and absent monks, except only those absent persons who are bound to the parochial cares of annexed churches, as soon as they can, within a suitable term fixed for them by us for this purpose, to their monastery, to live there under discipline and regular observance.

[Let them obey?] abbots, priors, and provosts, and indeed one another in fraternal charity.

That Monks Are Not to Have Private Property.

Let no one be permitted to use the damnable private ownership of things or goods acquired in whatever manner; rather, let all things be reduced to common use.

Concerning the Vice of Incontinence.

Against the incontinent, both prelates and subjects, let the stricter severity of censure proceed, so that not only public vices of incontinence be punished or restrained by vengeance, but also every material or occasion be removed from the midst from which suspicion of incontinence could arise.

Concerning the Three Essentials of Religious Life to Be Observed.

Let the three principal essentials of religious life be most fully observed by all, so that no dispensation or contrary custom may avail anyone against them.

That Monks Preserve Silence in These Places.

Let silence be observed in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and in the cloister, and in the other customary places and times.

How the Monks Are to Take Refreshment.

Let the brothers take refreshment together under table reading, to be continued until the end of the meal. The eating of meat shall be most strictly forbidden to all at every time and place, except only in a case permitted by the Rule.

How the Brothers Are to Sleep.

Let all sleep together in one dormitory, so far as possibility permits, girded with cords or [girdles?]

[unclear] on mats or mattresses, or on blankets, by no means using linen sheets and linen shirts. Monks shall not sleep in private places.

Concerning the enclosure of monasteries.

With regard to the enclosure of those monasteries, careful and diligent attention is to be applied; nor shall it be lawful for any religious, except certain officials, to pass beyond the bounds of the immunity of his cloister without the superior’s special permission to go out. Let all observe the fasts instituted both by the Church and by the Rule.

Concerning the divine office.

Monks shall reverently, as is fitting, and distinctly perform the divine office, both by day and by night, at suitable hours. When this has been completed, they shall devote themselves to readings or to the works of their hands, according to the demand of the time and of their duties, and according to the direction of the Rule of blessed Benedict. Let books be distributed to the brothers at the appointed time. Let the brothers’ beds be inspected from time to time on account of private property.

Concerning the daily celebration of the chapter of faults.

Let the chapter of faults be held daily; in it, after the readings of the martyrology and of the Rule have first been said, let them proceed to the exposition of the Rule and to the examination and correction of faults.

Concerning the celebration of masses, confession, and communion of monks.

Let the abbot celebrate or hear mass every day. Monks who are priests and reside in monasteries shall prepare themselves to celebrate at least once a week. Those who are not priests shall confess at least once a week, and shall receive communion on the first Sunday of each month.

That sick brothers and guests be provided for.

Let monks be suitably provided with food, drink, clothing, and other necessities, according to the determination of the Rule. Also, suitable places shall be assigned in those monasteries themselves both for the sick and for guests arriving for a time; toward them care and kindness shall be shown according to the provision of the same Rule. Let them lead guests to prayer; let a sacred reading be read to them for edification; and let them wash their feet.

That monasteries not be burdened with debts.

Let it be ensured with the greatest foresight that monasteries not be burdened with unbearable loads of debts; that their goods not be dispersed or alienated uselessly and without cause; and that, if any have been alienated, they be diligently recovered.

Concerning the preservation of property and privileges.

Abbots presiding, or rectors, shall diligently defend and guard the rights of their monasteries. They shall turn the fruits, revenues, and proceeds of the same monasteries to common uses and benefits. Books, vestments, crosses, chalices, and other vessels and ornaments, treasures, privileges, rights, letters, and the common seals of the convent shall be kept under locks and in safe places.

The rectors of monasteries are also ordered to render an account to their visitors every year. Prelates or rectors shall fully inform the visitors by whom they have been visited concerning the state of their temporal affairs. And the prelates themselves, and each of their officials, shall each year make a lawful account to the communities concerning their administrations.

Abbots shall entirely abstain from excessive mounts, dogs, and birds, and from unnecessary and unbecoming hunting dogs and birds and other animals and beasts, by which the inner man is defiled; so too shall the religious and their household.

Monks may not have weapons within the precincts of the monastery. Let none of the religious presume in any way to have weapons within the precincts of the monastery, or to contract spiritual co-fatherhood or co-motherhood.

Concerning nuns and their enclosure.

Nevertheless, insofar as the foregoing can concern abbesses and nuns, we wish it to be extended to their monasteries situated within the limits of your visitation, with perpetual enclosure to be confirmed by you by apostolic authority, according to the decretal Periculoso, Book 6.

Concerning those who wish to pass from unreformed monasteries to the reform.

To you moreover, the visitors and presidents of the provincial chapter, and to each of you, by the tenor of the present letters we grant the faculty of transferring persons of either sex who desire this from monasteries not yet reformed to reformed monasteries of the same order of yours, even when the permission of their prelates has been sought but not obtained.

Nicholas, by divine mercy cardinal of the holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, legate. To all the faithful of Christ throughout the province of Mainz, etc. On the enclosures of nuns.

Since [unclear]. We strictly enjoin and command that no man, of whatever estate, dignity, and preeminence, even if he be exempt, under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae, which we pronounce in these writings, unless he has license according to the disposition of common law from the ordinary or from him whom it concerns, and otherwise in cases permitted by law, shall hereafter and after the execution of the present mandate presume in any way to enter any monastery of nuns of the city and province of Mainz. If anyone attempts to do the contrary, then we will that he, by that very fact and without further declaration, be avoided by all as excommunicate, in divine services and outside them; and wherever he shall be, for as long as he remains there, the strictest interdict shall be observed in that place.

Likewise, nuns are forbidden under penalty of excommunication to go out from the monasteries.

Under penalty of latae sententiae and interdict, we enjoin all and each of the nuns of the aforesaid monasteries that, after notice of the present letters, they shall in no way, even when license has been given by the abbess and prioress or by any other woman whatsoever, unless as common law permits, dare to leave their monastery, nor shall any of them dare to do so. Rather, we will that a woman doing the contrary be excommunicate, and the place wherever she shall be be under interdict, without further declaration.

Commanding, under a like penalty of latae sententiae, all chaplains and priests who have certain knowledge of this, that they publish that nun as excommunicate and that place where she shall be as under interdict.

XLV

Constitutions of the provincial chapters of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg.

Preface.

Since, for one who wishes to know the individual statutes of the order, namely what statutes and of what kind have been issued by our most devout predecessors, the fathers, in provincial chapters, it would be laborious to go through all the acts and recesses of the same because of their length; yet lest so pious a desire of knowing be hindered by so great a labor, since it is also full of tedium for anyone to carry with him the larger volumes of the aforesaid recesses in celebrating chapters according to custom, I undertake to bring together the same statutes, abbreviated into one. And this is the order of this labor: I shall pass over the sanctions of the supreme pontiffs and also the decrees of general councils made for the celebration of chapters of this kind, so that what is to be done or thought in the remaining statutes may be recognized more easily. Then I shall summarize, with whatever brevity and diligence I can, the times, places, and statutes of the individual provincial chapters celebrated in our province from the time of the Council of Constance. And I believe that this labor will be sufficiently useful to posterity, if they should decide to add to these things what ought to be established. But if it should please no one, which I fear more, I nevertheless pray that I be forgiven, since I have satisfied, would that I had done so, not my own will, but that of the fathers who desired and requested it.

Innocent III, in the general council. That a provincial chapter be observed every three years.

In individual kingdoms or provinces, every three years, saving the right of diocesan pontiffs, let there be held a common chapter of abbots and priors not having their own abbots, who have not been accustomed to celebrate such a chapter; to which all who do not have a canonical impediment shall come together at one [unclear].

But at the beginnings of this kind of new arrangement they shall summon two neighboring abbots of the Cistercian order, to provide them suitable counsel and assistance, since from long custom they are more fully informed in holding chapters of this kind; and these, without contradiction, shall associate with themselves two from among them whom they shall see to be expedient. But these four shall preside over the whole chapter, so that none of them thereby assumes for himself the authority of prelacy; whence, when it is expedient, it can be changed by prudent deliberation. Let a chapter of this kind be held continuously for some fixed days, according to the custom of the Cistercian order; and in it let there be diligent discussion concerning the reform of the order and regular observance. And what shall have been decreed with the approval of those four is to be observed inviolably, all excuse, contradiction, and appeal being removed; provision nevertheless having been made where the chapter ought to be held at the next term.

And those who have assembled shall live a common life and shall all meet the expenses together proportionately, so that, if not all can lodge in the same house, at least several may lodge together in different houses. Also in the same chapter let religious and circumspect persons be appointed, who, according to the form prescribed to them, shall take care in our stead to visit each abbey of the same kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, correcting and reforming what they shall see to need the office of correction and reform; in such a way that, if they know that the ruler of a place should be removed altogether from administration, they shall notify his own bishop so that he may take care to remove him. But if he does not do so, let the visitors refer this to the examination of the apostolic see. We wish and command this same thing to be observed by regular canons according to their own order. But if, in this new arrangement, any difficulty whatever should arise which cannot be settled by the aforesaid persons, let it be referred without scandal to the judgment of the apostolic see, while the other things that have been provided by concordant deliberation are to be observed without opposition.

Moreover, diocesan bishops shall take care to reform the monasteries subject to them in such a way that, when the aforesaid visitors come to them, they may find in them more that is worthy of commendation than of correction; taking the utmost care that through them the said monasteries are not burdened with undue charges, for we wish the rights of superiors to be observed in such a way that we do not wish the injuries of inferiors to be endured. To this end we strictly command both diocesan bishops and the persons who will preside over the chapters to be held that, by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal removed, they restrain advocates, patrons, vice-lords, rectors and consuls, magnates and knights, or any others whatever, from presuming to injure monasteries in persons or property. And if perchance they have injured them, let them not fail to compel them to make satisfaction, so that they may be able to serve God more freely and peacefully.

Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, De statu monachorum, Ne in agro, in the Clementines, final section. The same text is found in the Clementines, Frequens, De excessibus praelatorum, at the end. Constitutions also confirm the same.

Again we decree that all and each who come to the same chapters shall not lead, or cause or permit to be led, mounts or household attendants excessive in number or in any way excessive; but, with the number of mounts and attendants suited to the condition of each of them, we will and command that they be content.

But those attendants themselves, and others whom they shall lead or cause to be led or keep, shall be humble and respectable, such that it cannot in any way be presumed of them that, by themselves or through other secular or regular persons, they would inflict upon any abbot, prior, administrator, office-holder, monk, or anyone else coming with them or otherwise to the said chapters, or staying in them, or returning from them, or upon churches, monasteries, priories, or other places of theirs,

of whatever dignity, status, or condition, who by himself or through another has maliciously impeded, or knowingly and deliberately caused to be impeded, the free holding of the aforesaid chapters; and whoever has presumed to seize, or cause to be seized, those going to them, staying in them, or returning from them, or to detain them once seized, or to impede them, or, on account of this matter, to inflict damages, injuries, or offenses upon them or their households, in their persons or goods, namely so that the celebration of any of these chapters may be disturbed or impeded; and also whoever of the said order or religion, under pretext of visitation, has maliciously and deliberately committed the aforesaid things, or any of them, by himself or through another, against the persons of abbots, priors, or greater prelates visiting their own subjects, or against the persons of those visited in provincial chapters, or against the persons of abbots or other prelates to be deputed by principals or priors of monks, or of their households, or against their goods; and whoever of the aforesaid order, in such visitations or corrections or executions of their process, has maliciously impeded them, or has stubbornly and insolently opposed them, or has consented to those doing the aforesaid things, by himself or through another, by maliciously procuring prayers, threats, letters, the aid of secular powers or laymen, or any other impediments whatsoever; and whoever impedes the same order or religion itself in contributions lawfully to be made.

But those presiding over the aforesaid provincial and annual chapters, and each of them, when it shall be evident to them simply and plainly that someone has incurred the aforesaid sentence of excommunication, shall solemnly publish him throughout all neighboring places of the same order or religion as shall seem good to them, and shall cause him to be published by others by apostolic authority, compelling by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside, those who do not obey them in this matter, until he has rendered fitting satisfaction and has been absolved by those presidents alone, or by at least two of them, by the aforesaid authority.

XLVIII. From the Council of Constance. When and why the provincial chapter was re-erected, and at what time.

Ancient authority teaches, and experience shows, that it is of little use to establish laws, however celebrated, unless they are duly entrusted to execution. Formerly, at various times, both a general council and Honorius, and also Benedict XII, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, are read to have issued, with much mature deliberation, salutary statutes concerning provincial chapters to be celebrated every three years in this religion and order, and concerning their general chapters to be held each year. These provincial as well as general chapters, in very many regions, are said rarely to have been put into execution for a long time. From their omission many inconveniences and almost irrecoverable losses in spiritual and temporal matters have come upon this religion.

Therefore, since from the celebration of such chapters there are undoubtedly wont to come about the correction of the depraved, the reformation of morals, the avoidance of many evils, and the promotion of manifold good, we, who bear in the bowels of charity the reformation of this sacred religion and order, whose uprightness and venerable character the testimonies of the fathers show, have resolved to restore what has been omitted in this matter, and especially to ordain new executors of the said constitutions in the regions where the old ones do not govern according to their tenor, before the sacred council is dissolved. And now, beginning in the province of Mainz, in which at present we are staying, we will and ordain that a provincial chapter of abbots and priors, or provosts not having abbots of their own, dwelling in the said province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, joined to that province in the aforementioned constitutions of Benedict XII, be celebrated in this city of Constance, or in its suburb, namely in the monastery called Petershausen, of the said order of Saint Benedict, beyond the bridge of this city, where

a sacred general council is sitting; in that council, indeed, there are many abbots and professed members of this order from various regions, who in the aforesaid chapters of the province of Mainz will be able to provide timely counsel and assistance in these matters, and to direct them, since they have been more fully informed by long custom in holding chapters of this kind.

In the same bull of the aforesaid council all the abbots and prelates of the whole province of Mainz and of the dioceses of Bamberg of this order were summoned, so that on the day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1417, in the city of Constance, in the monastery of Petershausen, they should appear in person to hold such a provincial chapter. This was also done in that manner. And from this time down to the present, in the aforesaid province, a chapter has been held every three years in accordance with the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs.

The first provincial chapter was held at Constance in the year of the Lord 1417.

In the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred and seventeen, on the last day of February, in the tenth indiction, while the apostolic see was vacant, in the third year of the Council of Constance, the first provincial chapter of our order of the province of Mainz and of the dioceses [unclear] was held; the abbots were Thomas of the monastery of Eboracum of this and the diocese, Sifridus of Elwangen of the diocese of Augsburg, and Johannes of St George of the dioceses of Constance.

Concerning the statutes issued in the same chapter.

In this provincial chapter many fathers were present, having been summoned by the general Council of Constance; and those who could not attend in person sent mandates through their proctors. And indeed in the same chapter several statutes for regular observance were issued, which, divided under individual rubrics, I have inserted below.

With what reverence and discipline the work of God is to be performed.

Directing the eyes of our mind toward the reform of the order, we ordain that the day office and likewise the night office be celebrated devoutly, deliberately, with pauses, not hurried through, not syncopated, and at suitable hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most learned father Benedict. To this, as soon as the signal has been heard, all things that are in their hands being left behind, they are to hasten together with the greatest speed, yet with dignity, lest levity find fuel; and so nothing is to be put before the work of God. And lest they be able to excuse themselves on the pretext of ignorance, saying that the signal was not heard, we will that the tract of Matins, which we wish to begin in the middle of the night, and that of Prime and Vespers, last at least beyond a fourth part of an hour. But anyone who does not come to the aforesaid divine office is to be punished without remission, as is contained in the Rule.

We further will and ordain that every day, in places where there are six monks, and in other places where it is customary, after Prime only one Mass is to be said; but if there are two, after the early Mass the other members of the aforesaid order are to celebrate, consecrate, and communicate, as is contained in constitution 12 concerning the celebration of Masses.

Concerning the chapter of faults.

We further will and ordain that whatever pertains to divine worship be clean.

The ornaments pertaining to divine worship are clean.

We will that each one, when he comes to his monastery, take care within a month concerning the judgments and firm leases [unclear] and the place where the Eucharist is kept there. And the books, with the other ornaments concerning the divine office of the monastery, are to be preserved with diligent custody.

Concerning the form and propriety of garments and tonsures.

Because through the propriety of outward habit and of tonsure [unclear].

[unclear] the professed and novices of the said order ought to display uprightness of conduct. We have decreed and ordain that all should wear large and broad tonsures, so that the circle of them does not exceed a space or thickness of two transverse fingers; and that they should comport themselves decently in clothing, habits, and footwear, according to the Clementine Ne in agro and the constitution of Benedict XII, De forma et honestate vitae: namely, that they should wear tunics and garments closest to their outer habit, of black, brown, or white color, according to the custom usually observed among them, round and reaching to the ankles, not slit and not marked by any other deformity, having wide sleeves extending to the fist, in no way buttoned or tied, yet not so wide that their width above the fist can be stretched out with the thumb raised. Nor should it extend around the mouth of the sleeve at the elbow, as the abuse of certain persons has it, beyond what would allow the arm to be turned and introduced easily.

They shall be content with almuces of fur in place of hoods. Yet in proper places where they are accustomed to wear them, they may, with the abbot’s permission, use decent hoods slit over the shoulders to a length of at least four transverse fingers.

For linings in their garments they shall not wear sendal, or miniver, or other costly materials, but for the said linings they shall use only skins of lambs or young lambs, or at least other cloths that are not costly. No linings shall appear in any way above the neck or at the edges of garments or sleeves. On the Habit of Those Travelling.

Furthermore, when it happens that they travel outside the monastery, they shall wear a frock, cowl, or cloak, and under the cloak, if they have worn it, a cowl or scapular.

Novices, however, shall use a cowl inside the monastery and outside, fitted on both sides. On the Habit of Novices. And lay brothers shall use a scapular with a hood attached to it, closed, inside and outside the monastery. On the Length of Garments, and on the Use of the Hood of Frocks. We ordain that its width shall not reach the mouth of the elbow by the thickness of two transverse fingers, nor may it be narrower or so short that it does not extend as far as the middle of the elbow and of the upper bone near the shoulder. The said hood, however, shall extend at the back at least as far as the belt, and may not extend beyond it by four fingers. The length of the sleeves shall extend one cubit beyond the hand and no more. And their width shall not exceed another cubit and a half. Yet below it shall be so wide that steps can easily be taken within it. And what has been said of the frock we wish to be understood of the cowl, setting aside sleeves, since it has none.

Within the monastery, however, in places where there are twelve, all shall use the frock, except only the presiding officer in the monastery and the first after him, whom we wish always to wear the frock. Yet in work and in the divine office beneath the alb, and when riding beneath the cloak, they may wear only the scapular, which we wish to comprise a space of at least half a cubit in width.

Likewise they shall not use linen or hemp shirts, but shall wear a woolen undergarment or woolen garment in place of the said shirts. And they shall wear boots or high laced shoes, so that the width comprises a space of four fingers on the shin above the [unclear].

Monks Living in Common Shall Abstain from Eating Meat When Healthy.

The brothers shall live in common and eat in the refectory, in which no one at all shall eat meat. And the visitors shall be diligent to cause the constitution of Pope Benedict XII concerning the eating of and abstinence from meats to be observed inviolably. At the Tables of the Brothers Eating sacred reading shall not be lacking; and he who is to read throughout the whole week shall enter on Sunday with a blessing, as is contained in Rule chapter 38. All shall sleep in one dormitory, in partitioned cells

Let each one sleep clothed in a separate bed, in the same place, if it can be done, or at least in groups of ten or twenty.

But not in chambers, especially if they have not been suitably latticed, so that the bedding in them can properly and clearly be seen; bedding according to the manner of life, at the abbot’s disposition. And those who have feather mattresses are not to use them.

If, however, chambers are found in the dormitory, we command that they be destroyed by the visitors or by their order, or at least suitably latticed. In these places and at these times silence is to be commanded to be kept according to the Rule. We further will that silence be observed at all times in the oratory, dormitory, refectory, and cloister, and that after Compline no one be allowed to say anything, except as is contained in the Rule. Before the said Compline, however, let the Collations of the Fathers, or another edifying work, be read.

On the collation.

On the porter of the monastery.

At the gate of each monastery one prudent and discreet porter or doorkeeper is to be appointed, so that without the permission of the abbot or of another presiding officer in the monastery no freedom of going out from it may be granted. But if anyone goes out without such permission, let him be subjected to the penalties of the constitution of Benedict XII, On Permission Not To Be Given for Going Outside the Monastery Without Reasonable Cause. The porter is also to be attentive that he permit women in no way to enter.

That a sufficient master of novices be had in the monastery.

We ordain that abbots place in their monasteries sufficient masters who will introduce their novices to the elementary sciences and, once they have been introduced, send them on to the general studies, assigning them a pension according to the form of the statutes of the often-mentioned Pope Benedict XII.

An inventory is to be made at the assumption of each abbey.

Let an inventory be made at the assumption of each abbot, as is contained in the Benedictine constitution. And so that the condition of the aforesaid monasteries may be known, we command, by virtue of holy obedience and under penalty of excommunication to be imposed by the visitors, that each abbot be bound to deliver distinctly to the visitors, in writing, the ancient and modern condition of his monastery.

On grants and leases at farm, and on sales and loans.

Let them not give places of the aforesaid order at farm unless the Benedictine constitution has first been consulted concerning places not to be given at farm; this we will to be firmly observed. We also will that when [unclear] loans are to be made, the constitution concerning loans and sales likewise provide for it, and that it likewise be observed.

As many monks are to be maintained in the monasteries as can be conveniently supported.

We will and ordain that the ancient established number of monks be maintained, if the resources suffice for this; but if not, let them maintain as many as can conveniently be supported. Nor may anyone defend himself in any way under pretext of a privilege or custom, which should rather be called a corruption, by which they say that they ought to receive no one unless he is noble, especially if they have no nobles whom they may receive or who wish to enter the aforesaid monasteries; yet if such are found, other things being equal, they are to be preferred.

Necessary things are not to be supplied to monks in money.

Victuals and other necessary things to be supplied to monks are in no way to be supplied in money or revenues, notwithstanding any constitution or ordinance whatsoever. And in this let the constitution of the aforesaid Benedict be observed, chapter [unclear], That Victuals Are Not To Be Supplied in Money. We will, however, that the said victuals and garments be supplied to the aforesaid religious persons at the [unclear] appointed in the Benedictine constitution, On Censuses and Revenues To Be Paid, chapter 21.

On nuns.

The things that have been said concerning monasteries of men we will likewise to be observed in monasteries also of nuns, as to the articles applicable to them; nevertheless willing and ordaining that they be kept under perpetual enclosure, as is contained in the constitution of Boniface that begins Periculoso, On the Status of Nuns, in Book Six; commanding the visitors, by virtue of holy obedience, that concerning this, as above,

when [unclear] has been exacted, they shall make and append it. The visitors and those coming to the provincial chapter shall not have more than twelve mounts. We further will that none of the visitors shall dare to bring with him more than twelve mounts; and we will that the same be observed concerning those coming to the chapter. But if they do the contrary, beyond the amount that they have spent, they shall be bound to pay it, to be placed in the common chest for the use of the aforesaid chapter within a month; but if they do not do so, they shall be condemned in double, as determined by the presidents, in the next chapter, no remission in this matter being of any benefit to them.

Concerning the appointment of the presidents, if it should happen that any one of them dies before [the chapter?] to be celebrated. We therefore keep silent about the names of the presidents for the chapter to be celebrated in the future, so that, if it should happen that any one or more of them should close his last day, the successor in the dignity of the abbacy shall likewise succeed in the presidency. We will that the same be understood concerning the preacher and the one who is to celebrate the Mass, and concerning each of the visitors of the whole aforesaid province and diocese.

That mendicants are not to be received into our order without apostolic authority or sufficient license. It has come to our hearing that certain abbots, or others presiding in monasteries of the said order, have received and incorporated mendicants as monks, even without the license of their superiors; and, what is worse, that they afterwards permit them to wander, to the detriment of their souls and to the scandal of very many. We forbid them to presume such things henceforth; and those whom they have already received by apostolic authority or sufficient license they shall be bound to keep as much as they can, and others wandering outside the monasteries they shall be bound, at least within a year, to recall to the monastery; otherwise, if they have not exercised diligence in this matter, they shall incur sentences of suspension.

That these statutes be published to all subject to the provincial chapter, and twice in the year, together with the constitutions of blessed Pope [Benedict XII?]. That the aforesaid may be read publicly through all places of the order of the aforesaid province and diocese, and may be better observed, we ordain that within a year, or at least one month before the future chapter, every abbot shall be bound to hold and complete a general chapter, if he has any subjects outside his monastery, in which the aforesaid statutes shall be published. We nevertheless will that they be read distinctly twice in the year, in the daily chapter, so that no one may be able to plead the cause of ignorance, together with the constitution of Benedict.

The second chapter was celebrated at Mainz among the Augustinians, in the year of the Lord 1418.

In the year of the Lord 1418, in the eleventh indiction, on the first day of the month of September, in the pontificate of the lord Pope Martin V, the second provincial chapter was celebrated at Mainz in the monastery of the Brothers Hermits of Saint Augustine, since it could not be celebrated at Saint Alban’s, where it had been placed in the preceding year, because of the transfer from the order that was then being conducted. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of Fulda, Kempten, Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, and Reinhardsbrunn.

Concerning the statutes.

In this second provincial chapter few statutes were newly issued; rather, all and each of the old statutes of the preceding chapter were approved and repeated word for word. It is not necessary to set them down here again, since they have once been set down above. Yet I shall briefly make mention after them of those things which above were not marked or established. For I judge that the new things should precede in this place.

We further ordain. Concerning the spoils of benefices.

That abbots and others to whom by custom, statute, or privilege it belongs to receive the spoils of benefices subject to them, when receiving them, shall observe constitution 11. But if they have gravely exceeded in this, they shall be punished by the visitors, even beyond the penalties contained in it, which they may have power to impose.

Concerning the statutes of the preceding chapter, here repeated.

Finally, as I said before, all the statutes issued in the preceding chapter were here renewed and repeated word for word, namely: [unclear] discipline [unclear].

how the divine office is to be performed, and that at their proper times the monks confess, celebrate, and receive communion. Likewise, that the chapter of faults be observed daily. Likewise, that sacred relics and ornaments and vessels pertaining to divine worship be kept clean. Concerning the form and propriety of garments, and concerning the habit of those travelling and of novices. Concerning the common life of monks, and that they eat together in the refectory, with sacred reading never lacking to them as they eat. How monks are to sleep: each one in a separate bed, as above. Concerning silence to be observed in the four regular places. Likewise concerning the porter. Concerning the collation before compline. Concerning having a sufficient master of novices in every monastery. And concerning places of the order not to be given out at farm. Likewise concerning inventories to be made at the installation of a new abbot of any monastery. And that the due number of monks be maintained in every monastery. That provisions not be furnished to monks in money. Concerning nuns, as to the articles that concern them. Likewise, that visitors coming to the chapter not bring more than twelve mounts with them. That mendicants not be received into our order without apostolic authority or sufficient licence. And that the statutes of the present chapter be published and read in every manner expressed.

And all the other statutes above were inserted in this recess word for word. How prelates are to correct their subjects.

Finally, we exhort and beseech, in the bowels of Jesus Christ, under the attestation of his strict and final judgement, all and each of the abbots, provosts, deans, conventual and cloister priors of the said order, that each should so correct, amend, and reform his subjects and monasteries, and compose their conduct in regular discipline, that when the visitors come to their monasteries for the purpose of visitation, they may find rather what edifies them than what exists as worthy of correction.

The third provincial chapter was celebrated at Fulda, in the diocese of Würzburg, in the year 1420.

In the year of the Lord 1420, in the thirteenth indiction, in the third year of the pontificate of lord Martin, pope the fifth, on the fifth day of the month of May, the third provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Boniface at Fulda. In it the venerable fathers Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Michelsberg near Bamberg, Frederick, abbot of Hirsau, and Heinrich, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gotthard at Hildesheim, presided.

Concerning its statutes.

In this chapter also many of the statutes which had been issued in the first chapter celebrated at Constance were repeated and inserted word for word, as they are given above. In it it was ordained that visitors ought not to have more than six mounts, unless necessity should require otherwise; and whatever they have beyond that ought to fall to the benefit of the chapter.

Concerning the discipline of praying.

For the reform of the order, first, we ordain and decree that the divine office, by day and by night, be celebrated devoutly, drawn out, with pauses, not run through, not syncopated, nor one anticipating another, and at the proper hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most blessed father Benedict. For this, as soon as the signal has been heard, all are to leave everything that was in their hands and hasten together with the greatest speed, yet with gravity, lest frivolity find occasion. And lest under pretext of ignorance, etc., as is contained above in the first chapter. Therefore let nothing be preferred to the work of God, for cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently. But lest anyone, on account of a lack of persons, be able to excuse himself from celebrating divine offices of this kind according to the institution of monks, we will that in each monastery as many monks be maintained and received as can conveniently be supported from their goods and revenues without want.

That monks not be received for a price or simoniacally.

Itaqꝫ opi dei nihil p̄ponant̉/ qr maledictus hōqͥ facit opus dei negli¬ gente aūt quisqͣꝫ ꝓ De institutōe monachoru (genter pter defectū ꝑsonarū ab hmōi diuinis officijs celebrā¬ dis valeat se excusare. volumus vt in singulis mona¬ sterijs tot monachi teneāt̉ et recipiant̉/ qt cōmode de¬ ipsoꝛū bonis atqꝫ ꝓuentibus poterūt sine penuria su¬ stentari. Ne monachi p̄cio recipiant̉ seu simoniace.

We most strictly forbid that anyone wishing henceforth to transfer to that religious order should promise any money for his reception, either by himself or through others, or otherwise that he will give anything, except those things which his parents, of their free will and without any agreement with the boy, offer at the altar. And those received in this way, when the year of probation has passed, shall promise to live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, and to fulfill and observe it according as the vow of profession and promise sounds.

Concerning the celebration of masses.

Concerning the daily chapter of faults.

Moreover we will that, in accordance with the constitution of Pope Benedict XII, the daily chapter be observed, in which regular discipline and correction shall be treated; and there also all things shall be carried out just as the aforesaid Pope Benedict established.

That conventual places which have collapsed are to be restored.

We also will, and most strictly command in virtue of holy obedience, that in monasteries in which perhaps refectories, infirmaries, or dormitories have collapsed, or have otherwise been destroyed, they be restored; and the negligent persons to whom such restoration belongs shall be gravely punished by the visitors.

That entrance to the monasteries of monks is not open to women.

We wholly forbid the female sex entrance into the monasteries, choirs, and cloisters, commanding that all doors of the same monasteries of the said order be closed as the visitors shall have arranged.

Likewise concerning the same.

We decree that in monasteries, or within their enclosures, in houses in which monks dwell, no one shall presume to keep women, even if they are mothers or sisters. Those doing the contrary shall be duly punished according to the fault.

That beggars are not to be received into our order, and that those already received who wander are to be recalled to their monasteries.

We forbid that beggars henceforth be received into our order; but those already received shall be recalled to their cloisters, and shall be instructed and reformed according to the Rule and the statutes of our order.

Concerning the claustral prior.

We will, and in virtue of holy obedience strictly command, that in each monastery there be appointed a provident and discreet prior, as the more suitable one can be found in the congregation of the monastery; and let him be such a one as is powerful in work and useful in speech, who is able to exercise care of the cloister and governance in spiritual matters; who shall diligently observe all the aforesaid articles insofar as they concern him, and shall cause them to be observed by all; and who, concerning the discipline of the choir, dormitory, refectory, and other things as they have previously been described, shall have watchful and faithful care in spiritual matters. And if any difficulty arises in any matter, he shall refer it to the abbot, who shall discuss and judge these things.

Concerning baths.

Because indeed the use of baths is sometimes necessary for monks, we will that every abbot, or the person to whom it belongs by office, shall make and build a bathing-room in his monastery, so that the way of wandering about may be closed to the monks.

Concerning conspiracies, games of dice, and betrayals of the secrets of the chapter.

Moreover we forbid all conspiracies against abbots, as well as private defamations of persons and of brothers, and every betrayal of the secret of the chapter or council; and let every game of dice, knucklebones, chess, and other games and disorders, by whatever name they are reckoned, cease.

That monks are not to become co-fathers.

Moreover we decree, prohibiting according to the ancient decrees of the holy fathers, that monks are not to become co-fathers, as in De consecratione, distinction 4, Non licet abbati, and Causa 16, question 1, Placuit communi.

That the ornaments and books of divine worship are to be kept clean.

Furthermore it has been decreed and established, with this holy chapter approving, that churches, oratories, altars, vessels, corporals, vestments, and other ecclesiastical ornaments be kept clean and neat. And that full provision be made for breviaries, missals, and other books, vestments, chalices, and any ornaments necessary for divine worship.

Concerning the quality of vestments.

Ut diuini cul Oecretū insuꝑ tis ornamēta et libri mūde seruent̉. est hoc sacro approbāte capl̓o et statutū/ vt ecclesie ora¬ toria altaria vasa corꝑalia vestimēta et alia ornamēta ecclesiastica/ mūda et nitida conseruent̉. Et vt de bre¬ uiarijs missalibus aliijsqꝫ libris. vestimētis. calicibus ac ornamētis qͥbuslibet necessarijs diuino cultui oīno ꝓuideatur. De qualitate vestimentorum.

We will that those things that have been written and defined concerning the quality and quantity of habits, garments, and footwear in the chapters held at Constance and Mainz be observed inviolably by all.

That monks live in common. That they sleep in one place.

We will that the brothers live in common according to the Rule, and likewise eat in one refectory, in which no one at all is to eat meat. They are to maintain an infirmary according to the Rule and the disposition of the abbot. All private little houses also are to be destroyed at the abbot’s command, or assigned to some offices for the benefit of the monastery. But all are to sleep in one dormitory, in partitioned chambers, each in his own bed, according to the disposition of the abbot. Concerning the other statutes of the preceding chapters, repeated here.

Furthermore, the constitutions and statutes decreed in past chapters were repeated precisely, word for word, in this one, just as they are contained above: namely, concerning the divine office; concerning the ringing for matins, prime, and vespers; likewise, that monasteries and conventual places that have fallen into ruin and been destroyed are to be reformed; and that a prudent old man is to be placed at the gate of each monastery; likewise, that abbots and the other officials of monasteries, after debts and expenses have been set out, are to render to the visitors a full and faithful account; that silence also is to be kept most strictly in its four conventual places; and that, concerning loans, leases, spoils, fiefs, those to be sent to studies, and also concerning the preservation of the Eucharist and relics, the Benedictina is to be observed.

Concerning nuns.

Those things that have been said and are contained in the [unclear] chapter concerning monasteries of men, we will to be understood also in monasteries of nuns, as regards the articles relevant to them; and we also command them to remain under perpetual enclosure.

Concerning the observance of the commands.

All these our aforesaid commands, however, we will, ordain, and command to be observed inviolably by all subject to our chapter, as each is concerned. Nor by this do we restrict the statutes of our order or of preceding chapters, but we will that those likewise be diligently and firmly fulfilled and observed by all, without any contradiction. Let the visitors therefore provide that all and each of the things mentioned above be diligently observed, as they are bound to render account on the day of their death and of the Last Judgment.

The fourth provincial chapter was held in Seligenstadt in the year of the Lord 1422.

In the year of the Lord 1422, in the fifteenth indiction, on the third day of the month of May, in the fifth year of Pope Martin V, the fourth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs, in Seligenstadt. In it these venerable fathers presided: Albert of Hersfeld, George of [Kastl?], and Theoderic of Amorbach, abbots of monasteries.

Concerning the statutes of this chapter.

Before I recount the statutes of this chapter, and before those that were published and ratified in this sacred chapter, it is pleasing to set forth briefly those things that, having been decreed in past chapters, were inserted word for word here into the record. For the repeated insertion of statutes so often serves this purpose: that the more often something has been decreed in several chapters, the greater authority it may possess.

First, this sacred assembly of fathers repeated the statute of the first chapter concerning deceased presidents: that one succeeding someone in an abbacy also succeeds in the presidency.

Likewise, that visitors are not to bring with them more than six mounts, under the penalty contained above.

Likewise, concerning the ringing for matins, prime, and vespers, to be done for the space of one quarter of an hour, as above, chapter 1.

And that the chapter of faults is to be observed daily, as in the same place.

Likewise, that the brothers live in common and eat in one refectory, in which no one is to eat meat.

in one locked dormitory, with enclosed chambers at each bed. Private little houses are to be destroyed; also the conventual places that have fallen into ruin are to be restored. Likewise, provisions are not to be supplied to monks in money. And concerning a prudent elderly porter. Likewise, monks are not to be received for a price. Women are not to enter the cloister of men. And abbots and each of the officials are to render an account to their visitors. And silence is to be observed at its proper times by all and in all places. And concerning nuns, as above. And the other things that were issued in the preceding chapters were also here enacted as though newly decreed.

Concerning the claustral prior, what sort he ought to be. This sacred chapter has decreed that a prudent and discreet prior be appointed in every monastery, as the more suitable one can be found in the congregation, who is able in deed and speech and diligent regarding regular discipline, and observes the articles of the order concerning him or the brothers. But if he is found to be a transgressor or blameworthy in any respect, let him be admonished once and again. If he does not amend, let him be removed by the abbot from the office of the priorate, and let another who is suitable be substituted in his place. This is to be understood not only of the prior, but also of all officials of the monastery.

The lord presidents, visitors, and treasurers are to come before the day of the chapter. We further enact and ordain that the presidents, both past and future, of the chapter shall henceforth come before the appointed day together with the treasurers and visitors, so that the treasurers are there on the penultimate Saturday before the Sunday on which the chapter is to be celebrated, and the presidents and visitors on the following Tuesday, so that they may report opportunely to the presidents concerning their visitations. Therefore these same presidents and treasurers are also ordered, as has been said, to come before the day of the chapter to be celebrated, so that they may inform one another about each particular matter, and render account to the new presidents and to the chapter concerning receipts and expenditures. This statute had also been issued in the earlier chapters, namely in the first and following.

LVI

Concerning visitors. We further decree and ordain that the visitors appointed in chapter shall, immediately after the chapter has been celebrated, if it can conveniently be done, or as soon as possible, begin and complete the act of their visitation, having God alone before their eyes. We also wish that these appointed visitors, and those to be appointed, not omit to visit also the monasteries of nuns in the dioceses in which they are to visit.

Concerning the penalty of visitors who neglect to visit at the proper time. If the visitors neglect to visit within the time appointed for them, namely within the year, they shall pay the penalty, like those who come to the chapter neither in person nor through suitable proctors, namely thirty Rhenish florins, saving moderation and just assessment at the discretion of the presidents in the provincial chapter.

Concerning the procurations of the visitors. Commanding also, we wish that every abbot and convent, when their visitors have come to them for the sake of visitation, shall satisfy them within three days with the sum of three Rhenish florins.

Concerning the confessions of monks. We prohibit and forbid all monks, conversi, and brothers subject to us that anyone henceforth should dare to confess to anyone inside or outside the monastery without the permission of his superior.

Concerning the celebration of masses. Concerning celebrations, let them observe those things that are contained in the constitutions of lord Pope Benedict XII and in the statutes of the preceding chapters; and we perpetually forbid them all games and unseemly exercises, lest they become [unclear].

Concerning habit, clothing, and footwear; concerning inventories and accounts to be made to the visitors. We wish and ordain that, concerning habit, clothing, footwear, inventories, and accounts to be made, those things be observed inviolably which are found decreed on these matters in the preceding chapters, see in c. i, 2, 2. De ha¬

Concerning the habit of those travelling, whether riding or walking.

... we have decreed that it is to be ordered in this way: namely, that the outer habit shall be a mantle hanging to the middle of the calves, cut on each side with one opening, and beneath it a scapular, which shall exceed the mantle by the length of three transverse fingers, whose appendage shall appear outwardly, because of fear of the excommunication issued against such persons as conceal or alter the habit without reasonable cause.

Privileges of monasteries. Concerning the custody of privileges.

And other jewels, relics, and treasures we command to be kept under faithful custody and secure enclosure.

Concerning conspiracy and defamation.

We forbid abbots and the other prelates and rectors, as well as private persons, [unclear] and defamation of abbots and brethren, and every betrayal of the secret chapter, commanding that transgressors be corrected by their superiors in such a way that the rest may take warning.

That mendicants are not henceforth to be received into our order.

We also forbid, by virtue of holy obedience, all prelates subject to our chapter to receive mendicants into our order hereafter. But those who have already been received and wander about here and there are to be recalled as quickly as possible to their monasteries.

Mercy alone is companion to all things. Concerning deceased brethren.

Concerning the state of the deceased, we establish and ordain that individual abbots, or their curators, shall henceforth bring and present in each chapter brief notices of the names of the deceased brethren and of the days of death of those who have died within the chapter celebrated and to be celebrated, so that prayers and suffrages may be made for them. And this is the form of the briefs: that such-and-such a priest or Levite, etc., died on such-and-such a day in such-and-such a place, etc.

Concerning nuns.

What has been said about monasteries of men we also wish to be observed inviolably in monasteries of nuns, as to the articles that apply to them.

Concerning the general chapter and the publication of statutes [unclear]

The statute also concerning the publication of all the proceedings of the present chapter and of the statutes of this chapter, set down several times above, and concerning the general chapter to be held within the year, is here again set down and renewed throughout, as [unclear] c. i at the end; let it be read there.

Conclusion.

Many other matters were here enacted, ordained, and treated, which are contained partly above; partly, as less necessary, I have passed over. All, however, are contained in the book of recesses.

The fifth provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Stephen’s in Würzburg, in the year of the Lord 1424.

In the year of the Lord 1424, in the second indiction, on the fourteenth day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, in the seventh year of the pontificate of lord Martin, pope, the fifth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Stephen at Würzburg. In it the venerable fathers presided: Baldwin in Lüneburg, Theoderic in Northeim, Appello in Suijsheym, and Helfric of Saint John’s in Rheingau, abbots of monasteries.

Concerning the old statutes.

In this chapter almost all the statutes of the preceding chapters were approved and inserted into the recess word for word, with only a few additions; some of these, because of their greater authority, I have taken care to note here briefly.

First, the ordinances concerning the divine office; concerning the ringing of bells; concerning the chapter of faults to be observed daily; concerning the creation of monks; that monks are not to be received for a price; concerning the celebration of masses; concerning the common life of all the brethren; that victuals are not to be given in money; concerning the dormitory; concerning silence; concerning reforming ruined places; concerning the accounting to be made to the visitors; concerning the aged porter; concerning propriety in clothing; concerning conspiracies; concerning [unclear]; concerning mendicants not to be received into the order; concerning the publication of statutes; concerning nuns; concerning visitors. h

that he not take more than six mounts with him. On the penalty for visitors who neglect to visit within the year. And many other things which are set out above and are contained in the book of capitular recesses. Now let us append the particular statutes of this chapter.

Those being visited are to guard carefully the goods and horses of the visitors.

Furthermore, when visitors have come to some monastery for the purpose of visiting, the abbot and convent of that monastery shall cause the horses, property, and goods of the visitors to be guarded with the utmost diligence. But if anything of their property, goods, or horses should happen to be lost or taken away, before all else the abbot and convent of that place itself, without any objection, shall pay the value of the lost goods or property to those visitors without delay; and nevertheless they shall be punished in chapter, at the discretion of the presidents, for such negligence.

But if, which God forbid, the visitors have been robbed or harmed in any respect on the road while they are going to make a visitation, the provincial chapter shall make satisfaction to them for such loss, as is fitting. On the safe-conduct of visitors.

for the use of the chapter shall be kept at Nuremberg in the monastery of St. Giles, of the order of St. Benedict. And from there the designated treasurers [unclear].

Concerning the brief of the dead. We further decree that each abbot, or their procurators, whenever in all future time they come to the provincial chapter to be held, shall bring with them briefs containing the names of the deceased brothers of their monasteries who have died between the chapter held and the chapter to be held, so that they may be commended to the prayers of the fathers. This concludes this fifth chapter. Many other things also were decreed and repeated in the present chapter, which are not here expressed one by one, because they have once been set down above in the same words, and it would be tedious to repeat the same things so often in writing.

The sixth provincial chapter was held at St. Peter’s in Erfurt in the year of the Lord 1426.

In the year of the Lord 1426, in the fourth indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Martin V, on the twenty-first day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the sixth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of St. Peter in Erfurt. At it the venerable fathers and lord abbots presided: Johannes in Vrauwe, Henricus of St. Giles in Brunswick, Georgius of St. Giles in Nuremberg, and Nicolaus in Bretzenhausen.

First of all the old statutes are praised. With the common consent of all, first of all we approve, ratify, and renew all and singular the statutes issued in previous chapters, and we wish them to be considered expressly confirmed, as if inserted here.

Here the sentence of excommunication and the censure are removed. It pleased the lord presidents and all those residing in chapter to remove and relax the sentences of excommunication and censures pronounced in past chapters, lest they should beget a snare for souls. Whereupon they said: The penalties and sentences of excommunication, suspension, and interdict issued by the presidents in past chapters, lest they should bring forth a snare for souls, are, in the name of God, removed.
