we relax and revoke, and those constrained or bound by the same, insofar as lies within us, by apostolic authority, in the name of God, we absolve by these presents; all statutes nevertheless remaining safe and continuing in their force.

Concerning also the proctors of absentees

Furthermore, we moderate and mitigate the statute of the fifth chapter, in which it is provided that no one may be proctor for more than three, decreeing that some religious man otherwise suitable may be proctor for four or even five abbots in great necessities.

Let the visitors first reform themselves and their own, and only then visit others.

Those appointed by the provincial chapter shall, first and before all else, visit and reform themselves and their own monasteries and those subject to them, lest, when they direct their eyes to the reform of others, the weak should murmur and say, “Physician, heal thyself.” Therefore let them begin first with themselves, and so confidently visit and reform the monasteries committed to them, of monks as well as of nuns.

Concerning the report of the visitors to the presidents

Moreover it has been decreed that, when the visitors have completed the duty of their visitation, they shall make a faithful report in chapter to the lord presidents concerning the state of all the monasteries visited by them, both in spiritual and in temporal matters.

An oath concerning the telling of the truth is not to be extorted from those to be visited.

It also pleased us that, without the exaction of an oath, after first setting forth the word of God, the visitors themselves shall begin and complete their action according to the form prescribed for them in the sacred canons.

Likewise concerning the form of visitation.

We also will and ordain that the visitors shall effectively reform, as far as they are able, all and several monasteries of either sex that are to be visited by them before they depart from the place to be visited, according to the Rule of our most blessed father Benedict, especially in the three essentials, which are obedience, continence, and poverty, without which no religious life subsists. And where they do not find valid disciplines and ceremonies, new

canonical sanctions and the statutes of the fathers and of the chapters: which those visited shall be bound to observe without any prior announcement.

We command all and each of the prelates of our province and those subject to the chapter, that each of them, immediately after notification of the present letters, in his monastery, should strive, as far as he can, to correct and reform himself and his monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the canonical sanctions, and the statutes of the provincial chapter and of the order, especially in the three substantial matters: obedience, continence, and poverty; in the eating and abstaining from meats; in divine worship and the other monastic disciplines, trembling at that terrible but truthful sentence of our blessed father: “Let the abbot know that whatever the master of the household shall find less useful in the sheep lies as the fault of the shepherd.”

The seventh provincial chapter was held on the Monks’ Mountain near Bamberg, in the year of the Lord 1429.

In the year of the Lord 1429, in the seventh indiction, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of lord Martin, pope the fifth, on the tenth day of the month of April, which was the Sunday Misericordia Domini, our seventh provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Saint Michael of the Monks’ Mountain near Bamberg. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Georgius in the castle of Saint Peter of Erfurt, Heinrich of Saint Giles of Nuremberg, Hugo in Alpersbach.

On the statutes of the ancients approved.

First of all we approve and renew the ancient statutes, and we will that all of them, just as they were duly and lawfully issued, be inviolably observed by those subject to our chapter.

That those coming to the chapter should live communally during those three days.

The provincial sacred chapter further decreed that those coming to celebrate the provincial chapter in future times, according to the constitution of Innocent, pope the third, of happy memory, Extra, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, should lead a common life and be refreshed together during those three days. And only two dishes of fish should be served, one of eggs or of fried things, and two good pottages, with cheese added, and some fruits if they can be had.

On the [unclear] of the lords.

We establish and ordain, by the authority of the presidents, with all the fathers consenting, that each of the presidents shall have full power and authority jointly and severally to carry out execution and to proceed, according to the tenor of the Benedictine letters, against all and each persons of either sex who oppose those visiting them, or do not admit them, or hinder them, or obstruct them in any other way whatsoever; and against those who offend monasteries in persons or in goods in any way whatsoever. And that they should compel the visitors to exact, for the chapter, according to the Benedictine letter, from the monasteries the visitation or the penalties for contumacy from abbots who neglect to come to the chapter.

Visitors. On fulfilling the time of visitation.

Within the year they shall faithfully complete the office of visitation entrusted to them, and as quickly as they can they shall make a report of it to the lord presidents. Those rebellious against the visitors shall be denounced to one of the presidents, the nearer one, so that he may proceed against such rebels, and also against those who do not obey the visitors, by apostolic authority through ecclesiastical censure according to the measure of the faults and of the rebellion.

On certain statutes placed in the preceding chapter and repeated in this one word for word.

In the immediately preceding chapter certain statutes were issued, which in this one also were precisely repeated and inserted word for word in the recess, namely: that the visitors should first strive to reform themselves and their own; likewise that, after the word of God has been set forth, they should proceed without the exaction of an oath; and concerning the full reform to be introduced by them; likewise the mandate made to the prelates concerning the reform of themselves and their own, all of which are contained in the preceding chapter.

The eighth provincial chapter was celebrated at St. Ulrich's in Augsburg in the year of the Lord 1432.

In the year of the Lord 1432, in the tenth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Eugene IV, on the eleventh day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, the eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra in the city of Augsburg. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Ortwin of St. Peter's at Erfurt, Johannes in Stein of the diocese of Constance, and Heinrich in Amorbach, of Mainz, presided. In it provision was made concerning persons to be sent to study.

The old statutes are renewed and approved.

First, by common consent, we approve, ratify, and renew each and every statute issued in the preceding chapters, and we will that they be inviolably observed by all those subject to our chapter, so far as each one is concerned. These statutes, set out above, were set down here again.

Finally, in this chapter almost all the statutes were repeated and inserted in the recess; but, to avoid tedium, it will suffice to note them briefly. First, the statute that the fathers coming together to the chapter should live in common in the refectory during those three days, and concerning the number of dishes, as above, chapter 7. Likewise the statute concerning the visitors, that they should first reform themselves and their own. And, beginning with the word of God, they should fulfill their office without exacting an oath, as above, chapters 6 and 7. A mandate was also given to the abbots that they should be diligent in reforming themselves and their own in the three especially substantial matters, concerning abstinence from meat and the other things that were issued above, chapters 6 and 7; they are similarly set down here. Furthermore, the statute concerning the authority of the lord presidents, as above, chapters 6 and 7, is likewise set down here in the same words.

Concerning the time of visitation.

We moreover command these visitors, and under penalty of excommunication to be imposed we enjoin

so that within a year they faithfully and effectively carry out the office of visitor enjoined upon them, and make a report as quickly as they can to the nearer president.

That they should not receive mendicants into the order

We forbid all abbots and prelates of our chapter, under penalty of excommunication, to receive anyone from the order of mendicants into obedience; and they are to bring back to their monasteries as soon as possible those already received who are now wandering. See c. 2 and c. 3; and this has often been decreed in many other places.

Concerning fugitive monks

Under the same penalty of excommunication we command all abbots and prelates subject to our provincial chapter to gather back their fugitive monks, and not henceforth to give anyone permission to dwell in parishes or to govern them, unless they are annexed to monasteries.

What sort abbots ought to be

Since the madness of wolves must be deterred by the barking of dogs and the staff of the shepherds toward their subjects, we command all abbots of our province subject to the chapter that, after the example of the good shepherd Jesus Christ, whose place they appear to hold in monasteries, they should kindly cherish and prudently defend their monks and subjects, not lording it over the clergy, but being made an example to the flock.

LXI

In the year of the Lord 1435, in the tenth indiction, in the fifth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius IV, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of June, which was the Sunday after the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist, the ninth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of the Friars Preachers at Basel, while the general council was being held there at the same time. At it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Ortwin of Saint Peter at Erfurt, Frideric of Saint Mark in Reichenau, John of Saint George in Stein, and Heinrich in Faucibus, of the dioceses of Mainz, Constance, and Augsburg.

Concerning the statutes of the former chapters.

Moreover, first of all we approve and commend the statutes, and we will that they be observed by all as though expressed here.

The statutes of the preceding chapters repeated here.

In this chapter of the fathers almost all the statutes issued in the preceding three chapters were again repeated word for word. First, namely, the statute concerning the common life of those coming to the chapter, and concerning the number of dishes at the same, as is set forth precisely above, chapters 6, 7, and 8. And there it was ordained that the treasurers themselves should provide for the refreshment during the three days of the provincial chapter. Likewise concerning the power of the lord presidents, namely that each of them individually should have authority to proceed against rebels. Concerning the visitors also, who were compelled under penalty of excommunication to fulfill their office faithfully within the year, and to make a report of the whole matter to one of the nearest presidents; and that they should first visit and reform themselves and their own, and only then proceed to the reformation of others. Likewise that mendicants should henceforth not be received into our order, under penalty of excommunication, as above. Under the same penalty it is decreed, as above, that abbots should seek out their fugitives and should not give anyone permission to reside or govern in parishes except as is permitted above, chapters 7 and 8. Likewise the statute concerning fugitive monks not to be received to obedience without letters of recommendation is repeated as above. All these things which I have briefly reviewed, just as they are contained above in form word for word, were again issued and made as though anew.

Decree concerning the penalty for those in contumacy.

It was further decreed that the presidents, and each one of them, should compel by ecclesiastical censures, with appeal removed, according to constitution 12, the abbots and others who did not come to the chapter in person nor send lawful proctors with sufficient mandate for paying the double amount, and also for paying the contributions imposed by the chapter.

Concerning the observance of the precepts.

We also command all visitors appointed and to be appointed that in each monastery which they visit they leave a recess or visitation charter. We command that all and singular the statutes and mandates written above be observed inviolably by all, reserving, however, what is to be added, decreed, or changed in the sacred Council of Basel for the reformation of our said order. For the cause of this reformation, in the said sacred council twelve prelates of the aforesaid order from the said province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg have already been appointed and elected.

The tenth provincial chapter was held at Nuremberg, in which the bull of the Council of Basel was accepted, in the year of the Lord 1439.

In the year of the Lord 1439, in the second indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Eugenius IV, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the tenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Saint Giles at Nuremberg, of the same order. At it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Hartung of Saint Peter at Erfurt, George of Saint Giles at Nuremberg, Nicholas of Saint Blaise, and Heinrich in Amerbach. In this chapter the bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reformation of our order throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg was presented and accepted. For its dispatch twelve prelates in the same

were appointed by the council concerning the order and province aforesaid, as above.

Concerning the old statutes. C. 9, at the end. With the consent of all the fathers residing in chapter, we approve and renew all and every one of the decrees and statutes issued in the provincial chapters held hitherto, insofar as they do not run counter to the reform.

Concerning the power of the presidents. We will that each of the presidents, jointly and severally, have full and complete power and authority to carry out execution and to proceed, according to the form and tenor of the constitutions of lord Pope Benedict XII and the provision of the common law, against all and each persons of either sex who shall have presumed to oppose the visitors, or shall not have admitted them for visitation, or shall have impeded them in any way, or shall have been found opposed to the reform agreed upon, and who shall have harmed those monasteries in goods or in persons. The presidents shall personally visit the royal monasteries, taking the visitors with them.

The sacred chapter decreed that each one of the presidents ought personally to visit the exempt and royal monasteries assigned to him, together with the visitors of those monasteries, or one of them. Let the same be done in the other monasteries where and as often as it shall be necessary. Concerning the visitors, as above. The statutes issued in the preceding four chapters were again set down in this form and inserted in the recess: concerning the visitors, that within the year they begin their office with the word of God and report as soon as possible to the nearest president the condition of those monasteries visited by them; all of which matters are contained more fully above, chapters 6, 7, and following.

Concerning the bull of the Council of Basel. To the fathers residing in the sacred chapter there was exhibited and read the lead-sealed bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reform of our order throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg. Because of its length I did not wish to place it here, but it is set down separately, fol. 34. Given on 20 February, in the year of the Lord 1439. The fathers unanimously accept this bull.

By harmonious and unanimous vote, [no one?] dissenting, and with mature deliberation, we accept and, so far as lies in us, approve the bull of the sacred general Council of Basel; and concerning the reform of our monasteries subject to the chapter, we will and command that it be observed in all our monasteries not yet more strictly reformed, nevertheless enjoining all and each prelates throughout the aforesaid province of our order that they apply themselves to reforming those subject to them who have not yet been more strictly reformed according to the same form.

That the bull of the aforesaid reform be read publicly in each monastery and once in every quarter in community. We also will and command that the form of the aforesaid reform, carefully copied word for word, be kept in every monastery in good and legible writing, and that once in every quarter it be read publicly in daily chapter; and that it be explained in the vernacular to the brothers by the president, or by whomever he himself shall have ordered, lest anyone be able to excuse himself under pretext of ignorance.

Those coming to the provincial chapter shall live communally. Those coming to the chapter shall likewise take their meals during that three-day period in one refectory, and there shall be served to them two dishes of fish only, and one of eggs or fried dishes, and two good dishes of pottage, with cheese and some fruits added.

The eleventh provincial chapter was held at Nuremberg for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1441.

In the year of the Lord 1441, on the last day of the month of April, which was the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the eleventh provincial chapter was held at St. Giles in Nuremberg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the abbots of St. Giles there, of St. Peter of Erfurt, of St. Blaise, and at Amorbach.

We accept anew the bull of the Council of Basel for reform. With the common assent of all the fathers present and of the proctors of those absent, we receive and accept anew the bull of the Council of Basel for initiating the reform and

Ueniētes ad capitl̓m ꝓuinciale viuāt cõiter. Ad capitl̓m veniētes ꝑ illud triduū sil̓ reficiāt in vno refectorio et ministrabunt̉ eis duo fercu la de piscibꝰ dūtaxat et vnū de ouis aut frixis/ ac duo bona pulmētaria/ adiūcto caseo et aliqͥbus fructibus. Capitl̓m prouinciale .xj. celebratum fuit in Nurenberga secundo Anno dn̄ii 1441. Anno dn̄i 1441 ultima die mensis aprilis que erat dn̄ica Misdͦia dn̄i celebratū fuit capitl̓m ꝓuincipale vndecimū apud scitm̄ egi- diū in nurenberga In qͦ p̄sederūt venera- biles pres abbates sciti egidijs ibidē sciti petri erforden̄ sciti blasij et in amorbach Bulla cõcilij basilieñ ꝓ refor matōe denuo acceptamꝰ De cõi oīm patrū pn̄tium et matōe denuo acceptat̉ ꝓcuratorū absentiū assensu suscipimus et acceptamꝰ denuo bullā ꝯcilijs basilieñ ꝑ inchoāda reformatōe et

we will that every abbot have a copy of it in his monastery, and that superiors take effective care to reform the monasteries subject to them according to it, lest those already more strictly reformed should wish, under pretext of this form, to relax themselves to a laxer life. We nevertheless admonish and exhort in the Lord Jesus those who up to now have made a beginning in holy religion in the observance of a stricter life, that they persist in their good beginnings and advance more and more from day to day, and that, not turning aside from their purpose under pretext of this norm, they turn themselves to laxer things; for the constitution of this bull was issued as a beginning of regular life for those who hitherto have been more negligent, until the best God grant them greater gifts.

The aforesaid bull also here commands that an authentic copy be kept in every monastery, in good and legible writing, and be read publicly once in each quarter in convent, as above in the preceding chapter.

On the procurators of the visitors.

It has further pleased us, and we decree, that the appointed procurators of the absent shall see whether the visitors have fulfilled their visitations, and shall report the negligent to the nearer presidents, who shall compel them, by ecclesiastical censure and other penalties if need be, to fulfill their office.

That no one be procurator for more than three.

We also forbid anyone henceforth to dare to be procurator for more than three, except because of evident necessity, under a penalty to be imposed by the lord presidents.

On the viaticum of three florins to be paid to the visitors.

The whole community of the fathers has also decreed that every visited abbot shall pay his visitors three Rhenish florins for viaticum, unless the visitors themselves, for good reason, wish to receive less; in this matter we burden their consciences.

That prelates not absent themselves from the chapter.

We also strictly forbid, under the penalties contained in the Benedictina, that prelates who are bound to come to the provincial chapter should henceforth presume to absent themselves from such a chapter.

On the accounting to be made by the former presidents to the new ones concerning receipts and expenditures.

We further will and ordain that, when their office has expired, the presidents shall render to the new presidents a full and clear account of each and every item received and expended on behalf of the chapter.

The twelfth provincial chapter, celebrated at Erfurt at St. Peter’s for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1444.

In the year of the Lord 1444, on the tenth day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the twelfth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of St. Peter at Erfurt. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of St. Peter there, of St. Gall, of St. Giles of Nuremberg, and of St. Stephen of Würzburg. In it procurators were appointed who were to accuse the negligence of the visitors before the presidents.

On the old statutes here renewed and repeated.

In this sacred chapter, as also in the two immediately preceding, the bull of the Council of Basel concerning reform was accepted in the same words as above. And that it should be kept in every monastery and read four times in the year, as above in the preceding chapter. And that the brothers of a stricter life should not wish, under pretext of this bull, to descend to laxer things, but should persevere by advancing toward the better, as in the same place. Likewise the statute concerning the authority of the presidents over the rebellious, and concerning the investigating of the negligence of the visitors by procurators, is set down here in precisely the same words in which it is contained above in the same chapter 10, together with certain other matters.

Royal monasteries are to be visited by the presidents.

Royal monasteries shall henceforth be visited by one of the presidents, with the visitors of that diocese taken along with him, as above in chapter 10.

On the monasteries of nuns to be visited.

But also the monasteries of nuns in each diocese shall be visited by the visitors of that diocese; and every visited monastery shall pay its visitors, when they depart, three Rhenish florins for viaticum.

On the briefs of the dead.

The names of the brothers, sisters, and confraters of all the monasteries throughout our province

of the deceased, within the chapter held and to be held, shall henceforth be brought to that same chapter, so that the debt of fraternity may be paid for them there. This statute is often repeated in the preceding and following chapters.

The thirteenth provincial chapter, held for the second time in the monastery of Petershausen at Constance. In the year 1447.

In the year of the Lord 1447, on the seventh day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the thirteenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of Petershausen at Constance. Presiding at it were the venerable fathers, the lords abbots of Petershausen there, of Saint Giles at Nuremberg, of Saint Stephen at Würzburg, and of Saint Gotthard at Hildesheim. Concerning the old statutes here renewed and repeated.

First, it receives the often-mentioned bull of the Council of Basel, and orders it to be kept and read in every monastery, as above, in the same words and form. Several other statutes also are set down here in the recess, which nevertheless had often been previously defined in the preceding chapters: namely, concerning the authority of the lord presidents over rebels; and that the visitors of each diocese should visit the monasteries of nuns; and concerning the negligence of visitors to be reported by the curators to the presidents; with many others which are set out fully above in various places.

That only reformed men are to be deputed to the offices of the provincial chapter.

As the Lord says in the Gospel: if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the ditch. We decree that, so far as can be done, this regulation be observed in the election of presidents and visitors: that reformed men be deputed to such offices, because he who has neglected first to reform himself can never properly instruct others.

Concerning the negligence of visitors.

And because we have learned by experience that some visitors have hitherto shown themselves negligent in the tradition and have not taken care to fulfill the office enjoined upon them, therefore we will and command all visitors to strive to fulfill the office of their visitation with all diligence as quickly as possible; otherwise, according to the tenor of the Benedictine [statute?], we will and declare that they and each of them incur by that very fact the penalties which those incur who did not come to the provincial chapter without having a canonical impediment.

Who are to be excused from the chapter.

It pleased the fathers that henceforth no one should put forward any excuse for not coming to the chapter except bodily infirmity, enmities, or evident and plainly established poverty. And concerning these only, the proxies of absent abbots are to be admitted in chapter.

Concerning wandering monks, not to be received.

Wandering monks without letters commendatory from their abbot are not to be kept, nor received as conventuals, nor lodged in any monastery beyond three days.

Concerning a monk who has laid violent hands on an abbot.

If any monk, at the devil’s prompting, should break out into such audacity that he lays violent hands on an abbot or another brother, such a man is not to be accepted or kept in the province.

Concerning one who wishes to transfer from an unreformed monastery.

If anyone with pious intention wishes to transfer from an unreformed monastery to a monastery, let him seek permission from his superior; but if he refuses, let him seek it from one of the presidents, who will give him permission to remain there for a time, or even to establish himself there, but with the consent of those receiving him.

Concerning the safe-conduct and travelling expenses of the visitors.

Each abbot or prelate visited, with the help of his convent, shall conduct his visitors as far as another monastery to be visited by them; and, when they wish to depart, he shall not refuse to give them three Rhenish florins for the contribution or collection imposed by the chapter for relieving burdens, unless the visitors themselves, for a pious reason, have decided that less should be received.

The fourteenth provincial chapter, held for the second time at Würzburg, in the presence of the lord cardinal, in the year of the Lord 1451 [unclear].

In the year of the Lord 1451, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the fourteenth provincial chapter was held at St Stephen’s in Würzburg, the most reverend father lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal priest of the title of St Peter ad Vincula and legate, being present and presiding over that chapter. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots of St Egidius in Nuremberg, St Burkhard in Würzburg, St Peter in Erfurt, and St Godehard in Hildesheim, presided.

Of the old statutes repeated.

Besides those statutes which the aforesaid lord cardinal Nicholas issued, the present holy chapter enacted certain things, and repeated word for word many things issued in previous chapters, namely:

Concerning safe-conduct and travelling expenses for visitors, as in the immediately preceding chapter.

Likewise, that the names of deceased brothers are to be announced in each chapter, as above, chapter 12. And many other things which it would seem superfluous to insert here in order.

Concerning collations and drinkings not to be held in the monasteries.

It has come to our hearing by truthful report that in some monasteries, even reformed ones, by a certain singular gracious permission of prelates, collations before compline have customarily been held; and now the brothers in certain monasteries contend that these are held daily as if by right, taking them up on their own authority, to no small prejudice and loss of the purity of reform and of the peace of the same, with detractions, frivolities, reports of secular affairs, and even sometimes extending to excessive contentions, and at times in the presence of laypeople. Therefore we prohibit those same collations from henceforth being held without the special favor of those same prelates; and we also will that the visitors be particularly admonished about them.

Besides these things nothing new was enacted in this chapter. But the lord cardinal issued certain constitutions for the visitors, some of which are contained here separately.

The fifteenth provincial chapter, held at Seligenstadt for the second time, was celebrated in the year of the Lord 1454.

In the year of the Lord 1454, on the twelfth day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, the fifteenth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt. In it the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Wolfram of Hirsau, Christian of St Peter in Erfurt, Ulrich in Wiblingen, and Berthold of St Stephen in Würzburg, presided.

They approve the statutes of the lord cardinal.

Following in the footsteps of the lord cardinal and legate, we command that all and each of the things enacted, issued, and ordained by him for the reform of our order in the provincial chapter most recently held at Würzburg, and then unanimously accepted by the lord presidents and the whole chapter, under the penalties and censures contained and expressed in the letters made concerning them by the said lord cardinal, be strictly observed by all, with the sacred chapter approving.

That the presidents, visitors, and treasurers come before the day of the chapter.

We further will and ordain that, for provincial chapters to be celebrated henceforth in the future, the lord presidents, visitors, and treasurers come together on certain preceding days, meanwhile being supported also at the chapter’s expense, to treat those matters which shall arise as necessary and opportune for the more useful and speedier celebration and dispatch of that chapter.

How visitors are to be received and treated.

We also strictly command all prelates and convents that they, if required concerning this, provide for their visitors, at their own expense and to the best of their ability and knowledge, safe-conduct from the princes of the region and of that place or dominion, as far as another monastery to be visited. And they shall receive and treat those visitors with all reverence and humility, charitably, and shall diligently observe and obey their admonitions and ordinances. Also the things of those same visitors, horses and other goods, under

they shall keep with faithful security, under penalty of restitution and payment of all and each of the things deceitfully or fraudulently thus lost.

Concerning the household of the visitors. The visitors, moreover, shall have with them an honorable household and retinue, and each of them shall be content with four mounts, unless a reasonable cause requires more.

Those impeding visitation incur the sentence of excommunication. Lest anyone impede so salutary an office of visitation by any contrived device or pretext, we will that all and singular abbots, priors, provosts, and their monks who refuse to receive their visitors, or who forbid them, and who are rebellious and disobedient to them, and who impede the office of visitation by nod, deed, or writing, or who subordinate it to be impeded by their friends, noble or ignoble, or by any persons whatsoever, or who order or procure by any device, by themselves or through another, or who directly or indirectly do or attempt anything whereby the visitors cannot freely and quietly exercise this office of theirs, shall incur by that very fact the sentence of excommunication. The same visitors are also bound to publish that sentence of excommunication against them and to commit it to due execution. Likewise we will that all and singular abbots, provosts, priors, convents, and persons who have rejected from themselves this reform of the lord cardinal legate and of the chapter, previously received and continued up to the time, shall incur the same sentence of excommunication, unless they effectively resume it at least within the time to be fixed for them by their visitors and continue it.

The practice of begging is forbidden. It has come to our ears by reliable report that persons of both sexes of our order, driven not so much by poverty as by the sake of gain, go about procuring that such begging of theirs be announced from pulpits, and even begging door to door, to the disparagement of the order. We forbid this to be done or to happen henceforth, and we exhort the people of God not to extend helping hands to such persons. And the same persons to their own

they are to send them back to the monasteries; or, if the resources of those same monasteries do not suffice, the brothers themselves, or persons of the order, are to see to it that such petitions are published and that the alms collected are conveyed, not by themselves but through secular persons; and they are to seek the necessities of life from the nearer monasteries of the same order. If, after this our prohibition, they do not desist from the aforesaid matters, each presiding officer will be able, and ought, to proceed against them as disobedient, according to the character of their offenses.

That monks not be given license to wander.

We have also learned that some abbots of monasteries [and?] prelates do not hesitate to receive into obedience, without due proof, fugitive monks and others fleeing the restraints of discipline, and moreover sometimes wandering about after license has been extorted from their superiors; and that they give occasion for wandering to those who wish it, to the peril of their souls and the scandal of very many. We therefore, wishing to cure a deadly disease, strictly forbid such things to be done henceforth, under penalty of infamy and incapacity; after prior warning, the visitors are to impose this penalty on prelates who grant license to wander, and on monks who receive it, with heavier penalties nevertheless to be added if the fault requires it.

Concerning proctors of absent persons.

Let one not be proctor for more than three abbots, under penalty of suspension from divine services, to be imposed by the presiding officers for the time being, unless an evident cause stands in the way. Whether that cause is sufficient must be set forth before the presiding officers.

Concerning the old statutes here repeated anew.

Consequently, in this chapter very many statutes of past chapters are repeated in form, namely: that abbots are henceforth not to withdraw themselves from the chapter, as above, chapter 13; and that all are publicly and everywhere to wear a habit befitting religion, as above, chapter 1; and likewise that those visited are to pay their visitors three florins for travel expenses, as chapter 4; and certain other things, which are contained more fully above in their own places.

LXVII

The sixteenth provincial chapter, celebrated at Erfurt for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1456.

In the year of the Lord 1456, on Jubilate Sunday, the sixteenth chapter was celebrated at St. Peter’s in Erfurt. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Berthold of St. Stephen’s, Würzburg; Johannes of St. Michael’s, Hildesheim; Udalricus in Blaubeuren; Rubertus of St. James’s, Mainz.

The election of future presidents and visitors belongs to the presidents.

We decree and declare that the election of succeeding presidents and visitors belongs to the presidents for the time being, just as the constitution of Pope Benedict XII defines.

That secular persons may not attend capitular acts.

We will that henceforth no secular person be admitted to the deliberations and acts of chapters; but when some act must be reduced to public form, then notaries and honest, trustworthy witnesses are to be summoned.

Concerning conformity of habit and tonsure among those coming to the chapter.

We also will and ordain that henceforth the prelates coming to the chapter, and the proctors of absent prelates, should strive for conformity of manners, especially in habit and tonsure. And those who use birettas should not wear them bare and openly, with the hood of the cowl lowered, as some are accustomed to do, but should place the hood of the cowl itself under the biretta for the sake of conformity, since this too seems to be a sign of humility. And we will this to be firmly observed henceforth in every place, especially by the simple conventual brothers of our order, except in the divine offices.

That the names of the abbots and proctors present at the chapter be inserted individually in the recess.

We have also decreed that henceforth, in the recess of the chapter celebrated for the time being, the names of the fathers present and of the proctors of the absent be written down individually.

Concerning not requiring an oath in the act of visitation.

The visitors of the provincial chapter, in the act of their visitation, shall not constrain either prelates or subjects, by oath or otherwise indiscreetly, to disclose or publish hidden matters, especially criminal ones, unless the order of fraternal charity has been observed.

That provostships and priories be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter.

Certain abbots who have provostships, priories, and deaneries subject to themselves or to their monasteries have, as we have learned, hitherto been negligent in visiting them. Therefore we decree that the same provostships, priories, and deaneries are henceforth to be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter. The abbots to whom they are subject, however, may likewise attend such visitation if they wish. And such persons visited shall be bound for the time being to pay only half the levy.

Monks and nuns ought not to devote themselves to disorderly feasting.

It has become known to us that there is an abuse among certain persons of our order: that after dinner, and also after supper, they hold in turn disorderly and excessive feasts and drinkings, mixing vain and scurrilous talk with them. This abuse we remove by the present statute and forbid it to be done henceforth, ordering that those who shall be found transgressors in these matters be duly punished by the visitors with abstinence on bread and water, or otherwise according to the nature of the offense.

And because the aforesaid abuse is said to be fostered by a certain other abuse, altogether more detestable, namely that in certain monasteries they usurp special revenues and arrange for them to be dispensed not through the cellarer but through whomever they themselves wish: we likewise will that this abuse be abolished entirely, and that all things be brought into common use and the necessary things be supplied to all by the cellarer according to the Rule.

Concerning the visitation of monasteries of nuns.

The monasteries of nuns of our holy order are to be visited by the visitors of the provincial chapter. They also, among other things, taking counsel for the security of those same monasteries, shall strive to exclude from them secular girls who, not for the sake of conversion but at the request of their parents

With What Caution Nuns Are to Be Visited by Prelates. LXVIII

Since the sight of women is contagious to spiritual men, let him to whom the care of souls is committed take care never to conduct a visitation of nuns out of a desire to see them, but only for the sake of necessity; and when that has been completed, let him depart all the more quickly. Nor should he presume to enter the enclosures of the monastery unless great necessity or advantage demands it.

On Appointing a Confessor for Nuns

Let a confessor for nuns not be appointed without the consent of at least one president. But if anyone presumes to attempt otherwise, whether prelate or subject, let him be punished most severely by the visitors. Moreover, entry into the enclosures of nuns shall be wholly forbidden to the confessor.

[That Monks Are to Be Received Without Regard to Persons or Nobility]

Furthermore, it is reported that in our province there are certain monasteries of both sexes in which only knights and nobles have customarily been received to profession. From this proceeds every dissolution and abandonment of regular observance, and the total ruin of those same monasteries in spiritual and temporal matters. Let the visitors examine the reason for this custom; and if privileges are alleged, let them examine them diligently, so that, once the truth has been discovered, an abusive practice of this kind, being elated, may be abolished; and thereafter persons, otherwise suitable, may be professed there according to the Rule without regard to nobility.

Let No One from a Reformed Monastery Be Received Elsewhere Without Letters from His Abbot

We forbid anyone from among the monks, converts, or donors who has gone out from a reformed monastery to be received in another.

Let No Guest Monk Be Permitted to Govern a Parish Cure. Let a Guest Monk Not Govern. Incorrigibles Are to Be Brought Before the Presidents to Be Corrected.

If any monks or religious are found to be such that they cannot be restrained by their prelates and visitors, let such persons be reported to the presidents, so that [unclear] may make provision concerning them. iiij

On the Proclamation of the Fathers in Chapter

Because the fathers of the Order ought, among other things, rightly to come together for this purpose and be gathered in the Lord, namely to celebrate provincial chapters and to clear themselves before the presidents concerning their various negligences and faults, the lord presidents decree and establish that henceforth, in celebrating chapters of this kind, each of the fathers must proclaim himself concerning his faults, excesses, and negligences, with a faithful and humble mind, ready to accept punishment according to the judgment of the presidents.

On Supplying the Negligence of the Visitors

If any of the visitors, because of a legitimate impediment, is unable to fulfill the office assigned to him, let him signify this to the nearest president, who will supply his place, or else will appoint some other one of the prelates to supply it.

That the Presidents and Visitors [unclear] the Day for Celebrating the Chapter at Least Four Days [unclear]

We wish the visitors, together with the president, to hasten to arrive at least four days before the day for beginning the chapter, to report to the presidents the things discovered, done, and completed by them in their visitations, so that those presidents, once the fathers have gathered, may be ready to correct the excesses of the rebellious and disobedient, or also to punish the negligence of those same visitors if any has been found.

The Seventeenth Provincial Chapter, Celebrated at Nuremberg in the Third Year, A.D. 1459

In the year of the Lord 1459, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the seventeenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Giles at Nuremberg. In it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots George of Saint Giles in that same place, Berthold of Saint Giles in Brunswick, Eberhard of Saint James at Mainz, and Henry of Blessed Mary in Ettenmunster.

Here He Repeats the Ancient Statutes

In this chapter, as also in almost all the others, certain ancient statutes were repeated in form. Of these, first

[unclear] was that the presidents and visitors should arrive in advance on the Wednesday, the appointed day for beginning the chapter, together with the other things that are contained above. And there all who had privileges for receiving nobles alone renounced their rights. Then, by the common consent of all, those same privileges were completely abolished.

Concerning the preacher. The one who is to give the sermon should arrive somewhat before the aforesaid appointed day, and should in good time submit the sermon itself, in the form in which it is to be delivered, to the correction or alteration of the presidents.

If one of the presidents should happen to be absent. If at such an advance meeting any one of the presidents is absent for any reason, the rest shall discuss and arrange all things that are necessary, with power to call in one of the fathers present if need be, until the one arrives who ought to have attended this advance meeting.

Concerning the death of a president. Concerning the death of any president, or of another failing in any way, the bull of Pope Martin V, which is placed above at the beginning of this volume, is to be observed, with this declaration added in this chapter: that the authority of the former presidents lasts up to, but not including, the day for beginning the chapter, and on that day the authority of the new presidents begins.

That schoolboys not take part by singing in the choirs of monks. Since the association of schoolboys and secular clerics in the divine offices is recognized as a corruption of maturity in the minds of religious, the lord presidents decreed that those same schoolboys and clerics are to be sent away to their parishes. But if anywhere they could not be sent away without notable scandal, the visitors of those monasteries, after hearing the reasons, shall determine how far and in what manner they ought to be tolerated.

The eighteenth provincial chapter, celebrated at Wuerzburg for the third time, in the year of the Lord 1464.

In the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on Jubilate Sunday, the eighteenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of St. Stephen at Wuerzburg. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Berthold of St. Stephen in the same place, John of St. Michael's in Hildesheim, Melchior of St. Ulrich's in Augsburg, and Eberhard of Monks' Mount. In it it was ordained that serious resistance be made to those who wish to transfer themselves from the order to the secular state or to that of secular canons, and that procurators be appointed against them in the Roman curia.

In difficult and important cases the votes of the fathers are to be sought. We wish above all and ordain that in the great and difficult cases of the chapter and of the order, henceforth during the time of the chapter itself, the votes of the individual fathers present be canvassed in order; and each of them, according to God and his conscience, when asked, shall say with humility and reverence what he has judged better.

Concerning the multiplication of constitutions. Noting that, although in earlier chapters many useful things were decreed, from which as yet, alas, little fruit is found to have followed because of the negligence of very many, since it is superfluous to enact laws, however celebrated, if they are not duly committed to execution, and lest the multitude of statutes increase the material for transgression, we do not now wish to establish new ones, but command the observance of the old constitutions to be kept by each more diligently than hitherto.

The nineteenth provincial chapter, celebrated at Monks' Mount for the first time, in the year of the Lord 1467.

In the year of the Lord 1467, in the fifteenth indiction, on the nineteenth day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the nineteenth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Monks' Mount at Bamberg. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots John of Bursfelde, Melchior of Augsburg, Heinrich of St. Michael's in Hildesheim, and John in Werdea.

Concerning old statutes repeated again. Many old statutes were repeated again in this chapter; since they are contained above, they were not to be inserted here again. Let us insert only the new ones. Concerning [unclear]

It pleased us that, when any one of the presidents or visitors dies, the person who succeeds him in the abbacy should also succeed, without any new summons, in the presidency or visitation, both in the office and in the dignity of the presidency.

Concerning the feast of the commemoration of Saint Benedict.

We further will that, in accordance with the apostolic prohibitions, the feast of the translation of our most holy father Benedict shall henceforth not be observed; but in place of the translation, the feast of his commemoration shall be kept in the hours and divine offices with all the customary ceremonies.

It was also decreed: A new penalty for negligent visitors.

That all visitors who have not fulfilled the office of visitation enjoined upon them shall, for each monastery not visited, be bound to pay three Rhenish florins to the chapter as a penalty, unless a legitimate cause has intervened.

Concerning the form of the procuratory.

And because negligence often occurs in the procuratories of absent fathers, when they are not sent in proper form, ignorance, as we believe, being the cause of this: therefore, to obviate those errors, we unanimously receive and approve this form of a sufficient procuratory inserted here.

Form of the procuratory.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lords presidents of the sacred provincial chapter of the province of Mainz and of the diocese of Bamberg, of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, to be celebrated in the monastery of N., of the diocese of N., on the coming Sunday Jubilate: N., called abbot in N., of the same order, of the diocese of N., obedience, reverence, and honor.

Venerable fathers and lords, because according to the laudable statutes of the fathers a provincial chapter is to be celebrated, to which, as I ought and am bound, I cannot come in person, being prevented by such a cause. Let the cause be expressed. Hence it is that I appoint the venerable father lord N., abbot in N., or the religious brother N., professed of our monastery of N., as my undoubted procurator, in the better form, with full mandate to appear in my stead in the aforesaid chapter, to treat, vote, conclude, and do all and singular other things which I myself could and ought to do if I were present in person; with power to swear on my soul, if need be, that the cause of my absence alleged above is true. Further, if it should happen that a monetary collection be imposed by a chapter of this kind, he is to accept it in my person, which also I shall lawfully pay when I have been required. Promising, under the witness of these present letters, that I shall hold ratified and acceptable whatever shall have been established and ordained in the same chapter, and that, so far as I can, I shall observe it, both myself and those subject to me. In faith and witness of all these things, my abbatial seal is impressed below upon the presents. Given in my aforesaid monastery, in the year etc.

The twentieth provincial chapter, celebrated at Erfurt for the fourth time, in the year of the Lord 1470.

In the year of the Lord 1470, in the third indiction, on the fifteenth day of the month of May, which was Sunday Jubilate, the twentieth provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Peter’s in Erfurt for the fourth time, with the customary protestations, that the fathers do not intend to admit excommunicates, and that neither they themselves nor the procurators should depart before the end of the chapter, under penalty of excommunication, namely of a sentence to be issued. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Gunther, abbot there; Melchior of Saints Afra and Ulrich in Augsburg; Sebald of Saint Giles in Nuremberg; Paul of Saint Mary in Elchingen. In it it was ordained that the individual acts of the individual preceding chapters should be brought together into one summary compendium, as has here been attempted in the present compilation.

Concerning the old statutes which were here again renewed.

In the present chapter many statutes of the old chapters were renewed and inserted again in the recess as though anew. Among them are these. First, the form of the procuratory is inserted and confirmed word for word. Likewise, that the presidents of each chapter, together with the visitors, should come on the Wednesday before the appointed day for celebrating the chapter, as above, c. 17. And concerning the supplying of negligence [unclear].

[unclear] not arriving beforehand on that Wednesday itself, as in the same place. Also, that no one be made procurator for more than three, as above, chapter 15. And that negligent visitators shall pay three florins for each monastery not visited, as above, chapter 19. And likewise that provostships and priories be visited by the same visitators, with their own abbot present if he wishes, saving half the procuration, as chapter 16. The same concerning reformed nuns, and [unclear].

The statute formerly issued in chapters 8 and 9 concerning recalling fugitives and not giving anyone a general letter of license was again renewed word for word, as above, chapter 15.

That the procurators of absent persons may be able to be present at chapter discussions.

It pleased the lord presidents and the chapter that monks who are procurators of absent fathers and have sufficient procuratorial authority may be present at chapter discussions, just as they have hitherto been present.

Also concerning the procurators of absent persons.

The procurator of absent persons must be fully informed about the visitations of those who send him, if there have been any visitators, and must make a report about all these things to the lord presidents; he must take upon himself, in the place of those who send him, penalties and humiliations, and within the space of two months must send the recess of the chapter to those by whom he was sent. But if he has not done this and is found negligent in the aforesaid matters, if he is an abbot let him be punished by a penalty of two florins for each monastery; if he is a simple monk, by suspension from divine offices.

On the propriety and quality of clothing.

We also ordain and decree that abbots and religious, whoever they may be or to whatever offices they may have been deputed, both inside and outside the monastery shall wear their habit decently, or a pluvial garment over their scapulars, with cowls sewn on and birettas covered, and shall go about with a fitting household also, all affectation being set aside.

If an abbot, in excuse of himself, [sends] letters of princes to the chapter.

No abbot or prelate shall henceforth presume to obtain letters of princes to be sent to the chapter concerning his absence, under penalty of three Rhenish florins to be paid to the chapter without any remission. [unclear]

What sort of person ought to be elected as abbot, provost, or prior.

The lord presidents, together with the fathers, decreed that no one henceforth be elected or postulated as abbot, provost, or prior unless he has stood, without pretense, for at least the space of a year in observance and regular life, and has held and observed it. But if otherwise has been done, there shall be done concerning such a person what the lord cardinal legate ordered in such matters to be done by his letters.

Whether a general letter of license should be granted to monks by their prelates.

We most strictly forbid any prelate of our province or chapter henceforth to grant to his brothers, to be sent to whatever monastery, a general letter of license; nor shall he permit those already so granted to be used, but rather let him prudently revoke as soon as possible what he imprudently granted to the peril of souls.

Concerning surreptitious apostolic indults.

We have also salutarily decreed that apostolic indults already obtained, or perhaps to be obtained in future without the knowledge of the presidents, especially those which tend to the detriment of observance and regular discipline, are henceforth not to be used, as being useless and surreptitious.

The twenty-first provincial chapter, held at Nuremberg for the fourth time, in the year of the Lord 1473.

In the year of the Lord 1473, in the sixth indiction, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the twenty-first provincial chapter was held at Nuremberg, at Saint Giles, for the fourth time. At it presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Theodericus of Bursfelde, Guntherus of Saint Peter in Erfurt, Johannes of Saint Giles in Nuremberg, and Johannes of Holy Cross in Werdea. These statutes of the elders were repeated here.

First, the lord presidents and fathers enjoined all the statutes of the preceding chapters, as though they were inserted here word for word, inviolably upon all those subject to the chapter...

[unclear] to be observed. There were also some of the same statutes inserted anew in this recess, which are contained above word for word, namely: that the presiding visitors and the preacher are to arrive on Wednesday before the appointed day of the chapter. Likewise, that if one of the presidents is absent at this preliminary meeting, the others, having joined to themselves one of the priors if they wish, shall do everything with full power until he comes. Also the decree concerning apostolic indults not to be sought or used, as above in the preceding chapter. Similarly, that no one is to be procurator for more than three; and that the procurators of those visited are to be fully informed about each matter, under the penalty as above, and that they transmit the recess to them within two months. And this: that abbots and monks are to wear their habit decently in every place. Also that which forbids any abbot, in excuse of himself, to dare to obtain letters of princes for the chapter. Likewise, that prelates are to seek out their fugitives, and henceforth grant no general licence-letter to anyone. And that the visitors are to visit provostships, priories, and convents of nuns, the abbot of those places being able to be present if he wishes, as above. Also, that those visited are to pay their visitors three Rhenish florins for travel expenses. And concerning the penalty of three florins for each monastery not visited, imposed on negligent visitors. Likewise also this: that visitors are to denounce the rebellious and disobedient to the nearer president, to be punished. These and similar things, which are contained above word for word, were here again repeated, with the following, however, newly added, as it seemed.

A novice is not to be admitted to profession before the completion of the year of probation. To meet future dangers, relying as far as we can on regular and legal provision, we strictly forbid any prelate henceforth to receive a novice to profession before the completion of the year of his probation.

Concerning the habit of lay brothers. For pleasing uniformity in all respects, the lay brothers shall wear cowls open in the front, after the manner of the monks.

The twenty-second provincial chapter was celebrated at Monchsberg for the third time in the year of the Lord 1476.

In the year of the Lord 1476, in the ninth indiction, on Jubilate Sunday, the twenty-second provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Monchsberg near Bamberg for the third time. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Martin in Schwarzach, Hermann of St. James in Mainz, Heinrich in Blaubeuren, and Johannes of St. Egidius in Nuremberg.

The statutes of previous chapters are first approved.

[unclear] in chapters and recesses were statutes directing the mind. We confirm and approve all the constitutions and decrees of the same, and we wish them to be held as expressed and to be observed by all, as if they had been inserted here word for word.

Concerning surreptitious apostolic indults not to be used, under penalty of excommunication.

Under penalty of excommunication we command that no one presume to use apostolic indults obtained surreptitiously, tending to danger of souls and to the detriment of regular observance, whether already obtained or perhaps to be obtained in the future without the knowledge of the presidents, as is also contained above.

That absentees with a procuratory [unclear].

[unclear] for him whose procurator he is, under penalty of contumacy of the same, without contradiction, shall henceforth pay four Rhenish florins to the chapter.

Concerning other statutes placed here.

The statute also concerning procurators, that they transmit to those by whom they were sent the recess of the chapter within two months after the chapter has been celebrated, under penalty of two florins if the procurator is an abbot, and of suspension from divine offices if he is a monk, as chapter 20 contains word for word, was here again renewed.

The twenty-fourth provincial chapter was celebrated at Nuremberg for the fifth time in the year of the Lord 1479.

77

LXXIII

In the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the twenty-fourth provincial chapter was held at St. Giles in Nuremberg for the fifth time. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Martin in Schwarzach, Leonhard of St. Peter in Castell, Bernhard in Hirsau, and Hermann of St. James in Mainz.

Which statutes of the preceding chapters were here repeated again.

In this sacred provincial [chapter?] several statutes were repeated as though anew; yet these are known to have been ordained earlier in other chapters of preceding times, with few exceptions, in almost the same words. Among them are these. First, concerning not using surreptitious apostolic indults, as above, chapter 20 at the end, with this clause, however, added which follows: those matters which must be expedited or obtained in the Roman curia for the order or for the monasteries, jointly or separately, are to be expedited by all the prelates and monks of our province and order through the procurator of the order then present in the curia, or with his express consent.

Likewise the statute that the visitors are to be received and treated kindly, and that three Rhenish florins are to be paid to them for travel expenses, with the penalty of triple payment added, and that safe-conduct is to be provided for them, was similarly repeated. And certain other matters also; yet because of the penalties and certain particular points it has pleased us to set them out again. Of these, this is the first.

That no monk be received without letters commendatory from his abbot, under penalty of thirty florins.

We also very strictly forbid, under penalty of thirty Rhenish florins, all prelates and superiors of our order and province henceforth to receive any brother or monk in their monasteries without letters commendatory from his own abbot; and those already received otherwise they are to dismiss as quickly as possible, under the same penalty, to be paid to the chapter without contradiction as often as they do the contrary.

That no general licence be granted to anyone, under penalty of fifty florins.

We also forbid all the same prelates henceforth to grant to their monks and professed members a general letter of licence without the consent of those presiding over the provincial chapter, under penalty of fifty florins, to be paid to the same chapter as often as they transgress this our constitution.

Concerning visitors.

We also strictly forbid all those subject by law or custom to our chapter to arrange in any way, either by themselves or through others, with diocesan bishops or princes or nobles, that the visitors should be prevented from freely fulfilling their office. Nor are they to object that visitors are not to be admitted without the consent of the ordinaries, since they are sent by apostolic authority and visit, in place of the lord pope, the monasteries assigned to them, as in the Extravagants, De statu monachorum, chapter In singulis, section Ordinentur. Nor is anyone to impose conditions on the visitors with which they will admit them, or without which they will refuse to admit them, under penalty of thirty florins.

Concerning the records of visitations.

Under the same penalty we command all the aforesaid abbots, provosts, priors, deans, monks, and communities diligently to keep, read, preserve, and put into practice the records, ordinances, and statutes made or to be made for them by the visitors.

That an abbot not allow private property to a monk.

Since private property is always destructive to monks and the overthrow of all religion, we most strictly forbid all prelates to allow any of their monks private property; for what the supreme pontiff declares that he does not dare to do is judged very rash for an inferior to presume in any way, as we have clearly in the Extravagants, De statu monachorum, Cum ad monasterium, at the end.

The twenty-third provincial chapter was held at Blaubeuren in the year of the Lord 1482.

In the year of our Lord 1482, in the fifteenth indiction, on the Sunday Iubilate, the twenty-fourth provincial chapter was held in the monastery of St. John the Baptist in Blaubeuren, in the diocese of Constance. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Georg of St. Stephen in Würzburg

LXXIII

Item, Johannes in Wiblingen, Ulrich of [unclear], and Johannes of Saint Giles in Nuremberg.

That the recesses of the provincial chapters from the time of the Council of Constance be kept in all monasteries and publicly read in the convents.

Lest the statutes and ordinances of the provincial chapters held up to now become unknown to those who are bound to know them, we will and strictly command, under penalty of 20 florins, that all and each of the fathers cause to be written and have all the recesses of chapters of this kind from the time of the Council of Constance up to the present in one volume, which they are to bring with them at the time of holding a chapter; and that in their convents they see to it that the same recesses are publicly read every quarter. But this statute concerning the reading of each of the recesses would seem too harsh, as it appears to me. Concerning an abbreviation, therefore, I think it must be understood as will appear below.

Concerning fugitives.

And lest an occasion for wandering here and there should arise for monks if they were everywhere received with hospitality, we command all our abbots, under penalty of 30 Rhenish florins, that wherever they find a wandering monk of our province, immediately, if opportunity is present, they send him, at the expense of that same monastery, to the monastery from which he had gone out, to his own abbot; and that abbot is bound to receive him so sent, after paying the expenses to the sender, without contradiction.

And under the same penalty we forbid all our prelates to admit in any way, or lodge, any monks or conversi coming aside to their monasteries who have not first shown commendatory or credential letters, as they are commonly called, unless perhaps with the intention that, having detained them, they send them to their abbots.

Furthermore, because no small force of regular observance consists in visitations, Concerning visitations. To the abbots. therefore we forbid all those subject to us to presume in any way to impede the visitors in their offices; but let them receive and treat them honorably and reverently, and provide for safe-conduct and traveling expenses of three florins according to the statutes of the preceding chapters, under penalty of 20 florins.

Concerning the form of visitation.

But so that the visitors may be able to observe due order in their visitations, we will and strictly command, under penalty of 10 florins, that they take care to fulfill their office according to the tenor of the form of visitation contained in the bull of the lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal legate, which he gave to the visitors of our province at that time. And note that this form, contained in the constitutions of the same cardinal concerning visitation, was inserted here word for word in the recess; but since I have placed it separately with the others on folio 42, I judged it superfluous to repeat the same again in one present volume.

The twenty-fifth provincial chapter, held at Augsburg for the second time, in the year of the Lord 1485.

In the year of the Lord 1485, in the third indiction, on the Sunday Jubilate, the twenty-fifth provincial chapter was held at Saints Afra and Ulrich in Augsburg for the second time. In it there presided the venerable fathers, the lord abbots Johannes of Saint Giles in Nuremberg, Johannes of Saint Martin in Sponheim, Heinrich of Saints Peter and Paul in Weissenburg, and Paulus of Blessed Mary in Elchingen. There the following statutes were made.

That criminals and the incorrigible are not to be expelled but imprisoned.

Although our blessed father Benedict in the Rule orders incorrigible monks to be expelled from the monastery, nevertheless we, considering the manifest danger for many from this if it were put into practice, have judged that the statutes should be varied according to the change of times. Therefore we strictly forbid all our abbots and prelates to presume to expel or exclude from the monastery their monks, conversi, or donati, guilty of whatever crime, since such expulsion of the incorrigible offers them the opportunity to wander and to commit graver offenses. Let them thrust such persons, offending so enormously, into prisons, to be punished for a longer time according to the character of the crime committed.

And two offices are to be performed in the convents after chapters have been held.

We further decree and ordain that in every monastery of our province, immediately after the chapter has been celebrated, each prelate shall cause two offices to be celebrated conventually on suitable days: one for the living and the other for the dead, with the appropriate vigils, for the brothers and benefactors of the provincial chapter and of the order.

Concerning the sentence of excommunication.

We also will and decree that those excommunicated, and those henceforth to be excommunicated in provincial chapters for whatever cause, even for a contribution imposed by the presidents and not paid, shall be proclaimed in their dioceses and monasteries; and that executors shall be appointed for this by the chapter, so that they may not in any way be able to excuse themselves from such sentences and censures, or plead ignorance, until they learn to obey the commands of the presidents.

Visitors of a monastery shall make charters for the monasteries visited by them, and shall send these also to the presidents at the time of celebrating the chapter.

We further command the visitors that they leave the charters of their visitations in the monasteries visited by them, according to the ancient statutes and ordinances; and that they, or their proctors, send copies of these to the chapter itself at the proper time. In these they shall clearly inform the lord presidents concerning the state of those monasteries, in temporal and spiritual matters and in persons, so that the presidents themselves, once the defects are known, may be able to come as quickly as possible to the aid of such monasteries. But if the state and necessity of the monasteries shall demand it from the visitor, then, immediately after the visitation has been made, the visitors shall send copies of the charters to the presidents with the necessary notification.

Concerning the expenses of monasteries attempting to sever themselves from the order.

Further, we will and ordain that the expenses which the chapter has happened to incur for monasteries attempting to sever themselves from the order, or even for recovering those already transferred, shall be paid to the chapter by such restored monasteries, according to their own resources, which are to be taken into account.

Concerning the debts of dead men.

We will and ordain that in each future chapter the names of deceased brothers shall be sent by the abbots, or by their proctors, in slips to the chapter itself to be celebrated at the proper time, so that they may be commended to the prayers of the fathers.

The twenty-sixth provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint James in Mainz, in the year of the Lord 1487.

In the year of the Lord 1487, in the sixth indiction, on the Sunday Jubilate, the twenty-sixth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of Saint James near Mainz. In it there presided the venerable fathers and lords abbots: Heinrich in Wissembourg, Conrad in Wiblingen, Berthamus of Saint Gotthard in Hildesheim, and Johannes in Seligenstadt.

Concerning definitors to be chosen by the presidents.

It pleased all of us, gathered in chapter, that henceforth, in each chapter to be celebrated, definitors shall be chosen from the fathers by the presidents.

Concerning the age required in the person to be received for profession of the order.

We further forbid all abbots and prelates of our chapter henceforth to receive anyone to profession of the order unless he is established at the proper age: namely, a male at fourteen complete years, and a female at twelve complete years.

Concerning the age of brothers to be ordained.

We also forbid all the same prelates henceforth to promote their subjects to major orders while they are minors, contrary to the disposition of common law and the ordinance of the supreme pontiffs.

Concerning novices obliged to perform the canonical hours.

We decree that all professed members and novices of our order, even those established in no sacred order, are obliged to say the canonical hours every day according to the ordinance of the rule.

The twenty-seventh provincial chapter was celebrated in Nuremberg for the sixth time, in the year of the Lord 1490.

In the year of the Lord 1490, on the Sunday Misericordia Domini, the twenty-seventh provincial chapter was celebrated at Saint Giles in Nuremberg for the sixth time. In it there presided the venerable fathers and lords abbots: Georgius of Saint Stephen in Würzburg, Johannes of Saint Giles in Nuremberg, [unclear].

Bergen. Henry in Blaubeuren and Blasius in Hirsau.

Concerning those who do not admit the visitors

It has come to our ears by a certain and serious report that some abbots and monks not only refused to admit their visitors, but, what is more serious, even drove them shamefully from their places with reproach and indignation, to the manifest contempt of the chapter of the order and of the canons. Therefore we exhort all and each of the prelates and professed members established anywhere throughout our province in the order, that henceforth they not presume to attempt such things, under the penalty more fully expressed in the preceding statutes; and we wish that penalty to be extended without remission against rebels of this kind by the visitors themselves or by those presiding. But all who are to be visited should meet their visitors cheerfully and reverently, receive them humbly and gladly, and treat them humanely; and, if need be, they should also provide them, at their own expense, with safe conduct as far as another monastery to be visited by them.

Concerning the documents of visitations

It pleased the fathers that, unless contempt has intervened, in the documents of visitations henceforth words of command or threat under censures should not be inserted, but rather exhortatory or entreating words, by which the minds of subjects may be drawn to virtues from love; unless, as we have said, contempt has intervened, or where the matter concerns transgression of the three substantial vows, or otherwise an evident necessity somewhere compels it.

The twenty-eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the year of the Lord 1493

In the year of our Lord 1493, on Jubilate Sunday, the twenty-eighth provincial chapter was celebrated in the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul at Hirsau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer. In it presided the venerable fathers and lords Johannes in Sponheim, Conrad in Wiblingen, Bartholomew of Holy Cross in Werdea, and Andreas of the Mountain of the Monks near Bamberg, abbots of monasteries of the dioceses of Mainz, Constance, Augsburg, and Bamberg. In this same chapter the statutes of the earlier chapters were confirmed anew, with this one addition, which follows word for word.

Concerning the confession of monks

We will and ordain that every monk professed according to the rule of Saint Benedict, in accordance with the Clementine constitution Ne in agro, on the status of monks, must and is bound to make confession to his abbot at least once a month concerning matters that occur, and, concerning reserved cases, to the abbot as often as he knows himself to have offended in such matters, under the penalties contained in the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs, general councils, or provincial chapters. It was also decreed that, after this statute of the provincial chapters has been printed and presented to the individual monasteries, it must thereafter be read publicly at least once every three years.
