A brief and summary recapitulation, or epilogue, of all the foregoing. In what order and manner individuals must come together for the provincial chapter.

First rubric.

When some chapter is to be celebrated, those who are officials for the time being, namely the presidents, visitors, treasurers, and the one making the sermon there, according to the ordinance of the seventeenth chapter, and certain others, must arrive four days before the chapter itself, so that, namely, they may be present there on Wednesday and may more conveniently inform themselves, both concerning things done and concerning things to be done in their offices, and finally may be able to dispatch matters more quickly. This must be understood concerning the presidents of either chapter, namely [unclear], as appears above, chapter 20. As for the one making the sermon, this has been ordained: namely, that his sermon first be examined, so that, if there were need, it might be corrected and amended. The rest, whether abbots or proctors, must present themselves there, so that when the chapter is to be begun no one may be found to be absent. Nor is the excuse of anyone to be admitted, except either of one who is ill, or has mortal enmities, or certainly is so poor that he cannot at all conveniently present himself to the chapter without danger. Hence no proctor for any absent person without such true and manifest impediments should ever be admitted.

Likewise, no one ought to procure letters from princes or nobles concerning his absence, under penalty of three florins. If, however, any of the officials is absent, the rest will nevertheless be able to carry on the proceedings according to the ordinance of chapter 20. But in the case that none of the presidents is present, the others assembled for the celebration may, on that occasion, depute other suitable presidents by the indult of Pope Martin V, whose bull is found among the acts of the first chapter. By the same indult those presidents may also change the place of the chapter, with prorogation of the term, for causes. Likewise, no one there, whether he is an official or not, ought to depart from there before the end of the chapter without the permission of the presidents, under penalty, as above, chapters 3 and 4, and of excommunication to be imposed, as above, chapter 20. Also, no one coming together for the chapter ought to have more than six mounts; and if anyone does the contrary, he must put back into the chest, for the common use of the chapter, within a month, as much as he is proved to have spent on the rest, as above, chapter 2. And if he has not observed even this, at the next future chapter he must be fined double by the presidents, without any remission. Likewise, each must contribute there three Rhenish florins, which they must pay either then or within the three days during which the visitors happen to be with them, without further delay, under penalty of excommunication; the visitors are most strictly ordered to impose this on them immediately once the term has elapsed, according to [unclear], as above, chapter 1.

How the chapter is to be celebrated and how the [fathers?] ought to conduct themselves in it. Second rubric.

If, therefore, the time is at hand for the chapter to be celebrated, which has been established always to be celebrated every three years unless, for a certain and reasonable cause, it is prorogued longer by the presidents, first, after the mass and sermon have been held, and after the [fathers?] have been gathered together in one place in the chapter-room, and after the Benedicite has been said, following the reading of the martyrology and a passage from the text of the Rule recited by the reader, a declaration must be made concerning the non-admission of excommunicated persons, as above, chapter 20. [unclear] chapter is to be named and announced by the presidents; this place should not and cannot be changed except for a grave and reasonable cause, and this only by the presidents, as above, chapter 1. Then, according to the ordinance of the seventeenth chapter and of certain others, the presidents and the other officials of the future chapter are to be appointed, and also the visitors of the monasteries; likewise the one who is to deliver the sermon, and the other who is to celebrate the Mass, not indeed under their proper names but only under the names of their offices, so that, if anyone should resign or die or indeed be deposed, then the abbot of the same place would carry out the office enjoined on him; for although the person is changed, nevertheless the dignity, which does not die, always continues. Finally, action must be taken concerning those things which are to be corrected in the order, and which perhaps will have to be newly ordained and instituted for the advantage of the whole order; here the beginning must first be made with those who are present, each of whom must declare his fault in the matter and voluntarily offer himself for fitting amendment; their visitors are to accuse and proclaim them. Those, however, who at that time are proctors of the absent must undergo disciplines and other fitting penances not only for themselves but also for those who appointed them, such as the presidents themselves, according to the report of the visitors or any other certain and evident knowledge, have justly and reasonably decreed should be inflicted. Secondly, the absent are to be dealt with. And so, consequently, with the remaining business pressing upon the order. And last, each thing issued and handled is to be reduced into a certain form and inserted in the charter or recess. Nor should anyone from among secular men be present at these discussions or be admitted there, except only a public notary and honorable witnesses. But neither should these be admitted indiscriminately, but only then when the act itself is now to be reduced into public form. In that form the names of all the abbots present and of the proctors of the absent must also be written. All who are present must receive a copy of it; but their proctors must transmit it to the absent within two months, under the penalty expressed above, chapter 20.

Likewise, in the chapter itself, where great and difficult matters are discussed, the votes of each individual must be examined, and each must state his vote according to God and conscience, with humility and purity of intention, and assign the reason moving him. Moreover, how the fathers should conduct themselves there in their manner of life has been so ordained that all, both abbots and proctors of abbots, must strive after conformity of manners, especially in habit and tonsure; nor henceforth should anyone use a bare biretta, but should place the hood of the cowl over the biretta, as above, chapter 16. Likewise, during the three days for which the chapter continues, all must come together at one table, so that they may sit together and be refreshed together; there only two courses of fish, one of eggs or fried dishes, and two good pottages are to be served, with cheese or some fruits added, as above, chapter 7. The treasurers, however, must pay the expenses, which they in turn must collect from the contribution of each abbot, as above, chapter 9. Likewise, briefs must also be offered there by the abbots and the proctors of abbots, in which the names of those who have died since the next preceding chapter are contained, so that they may be absolved in the chapter, namely by way of prayer, and prayers may be made for them. The form of these briefs is as follows: Brother N., priest or Levite, died on such a day in that place, etc., as above, chapter 4. Concerning the presidents. Third rubric.

The presidents who are to preside in the future chapter must, according to the ordinance of the sixteenth chapter, which is drawn from the constitutions of Benedict XII, be chosen by the presidents of the preceding chapter; and, according to the ordinance of the thirteenth chapter, only from among the reformed. Furthermore, in that same future chapter over which they will preside, they are to choose, just as their predecessors did, all the officials of the chapter, the vice-presidents, visitors, etc., and to do the other things which are contained in the constitutions of the aforementioned Benedict XII. For they have the duty of presiding in the chapter, hearing faults, investigating and discussing them, and penalties and penances according to

to compel [them], under ecclesiastical censures, to carry out the office enjoined upon them; to determine in certain cases an increase of the subsidy or viaticum which is owed to the visitors by the monasteries visited by them, beyond three florins; to make ordinance concerning brothers to be sent for study; and to license brothers who, with pious intention, desire to pass from an unreformed monastery to a reformed one. Against those not appearing in chapter, and against all who hinder or oppose reform and visitations, or do not admit them, or are in any other way contrary; also against those who do not obey the visitors; and against those who injure monasteries in things, persons, etc., they have power to proceed jointly by censures, by apostolic authority. They also have and ought personally to visit, with the visitors, even exempt and royal monasteries. Likewise, from Martin V they have power, for certain reasons, to change the place appointed for holding the chapter, even with prorogation of the term. The same pope aforesaid also grants that if at any time someone elected as president is unwilling to accept the office, or cannot conveniently be present, then the other presidents, with the consent of the greater part of those making up the chapter, or, if none of the presidents should be present, the others assembling for the celebration of the chapter, may elect and appoint other suitable persons as presidents for those same occasions.

Concerning the chest and the guardians of the chest. Fourth rubric.

The common chest is always known to be necessary because of the usefulness of the chapter, so that in it may be received and placed both monetary contributions and penalties for contumacy or any other fault whatsoever of abbots, and also the other things which, either through the visitors or through the treasurers, pertain to the necessity or usefulness of the chapter. But it is also necessary that this be kept in a safe and suitable place under trustworthy guardians, who are called treasurers, having full power to exact penalties from those who are liable to penalties, under like censures, and to absolve if it should perhaps happen that any have been excommunicated on account of the aforesaid matters. Therefore in the fifth chapter the monastery of Saint Giles in Nuremberg was appointed as the place where today the chest is stored; and thence treasurers were designated, having the authority already expressed above. They must also provide for the meal during the three days in the provincial chapter, as above, chapter 9. And they must assemble at the chapter itself according to the ordinance expressed above in the first rubric.

Concerning proctors. Fifth rubric.

There are two kinds of proctors. Some are general, who belong to the whole chapter; and it falls to them to urge the visitors to carry out the office enjoined upon them vigorously and faithfully; indeed, also to compel them by censures, if there is need, and to report their negligence to the presidents, as above, chapter 13 and in certain following chapters. Others are special, who are substituted for certain abbots who cannot come to the chapter. Concerning these, and concerning the abbots substituting them, enough has been said above in chapter 20 and in very many other foregoing chapters, namely 4, 6, 11, 13, 17, and 18: how they are not to receive the causes of more than three abbots, excepting the causes expressed there; and that they are not to be admitted without a bodily oath effectively taken, and so concerning many other things which can be seen there. The form of the proxy, too, for the sake of the uninstructed, has been inserted in the recess of the nineteenth chapter. And it is as follows. To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents of the sacred provincial chapter of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, to be celebrated in the monastery N. of the diocese N. on the coming Sunday Jubilate, N., humble abbot of the monastery N. of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz: whatever reverence and honor he can. Reverend fathers and lords, because according to the praiseworthy statutes of the fathers the provincial chapter comes to be celebrated, to which I both ought and am bound to come in person; but because, by such a cause, I am so impeded that I cannot conveniently appear in person, hence it is that I constitute the reverend lord abbot N. as my legate and true proctor in the better form, with full mandate in my stead in the said provincial chapter

...of obeying, promising, concluding, and doing all things which I myself could and ought to do if I were personally present, with power to swear on my soul, if need be, that the cause alleged for my absence is true. Moreover, if it should happen that a monetary levy is imposed by the chapter, accepting it in my person, which I promise to pay lawfully if I am required; promising, under the testimony of the present letters, that whatever things shall have been duly and lawfully ordained in the same chapter I will hold as valid and pleasing, and, as far as I can, will observe them both for myself and for those committed to me. In testimony of all which my abbatial seal has been impressed on the present document. Given in the year of the Lord, etc.

Concerning visitors. Rubric 6.

Visitors of monasteries, and visitors of the visitors, must be chosen by the presidents in the provincial chapter, as in chapter 16; and only from among the reformed, as in chapter 13. They are obliged to know each single thing that has been transacted and ordained in each chapter, from the first to the last, so that they themselves, first observing most strictly in their own persons the law which they wish and are bound to impose on others, may at length more effectively require it of others and bind them to the same; and also may be able and have power to punish transgressors, as they ought, with due vengeance, under the strictest accounting to be rendered in the dreadful future judgment.

These visitors, after they have come from the chapter, must begin their visitations within a year, under penalty of thirty florins, as in chapter 4, or of three florins for each monastery to be visited, as in chapter 20, indeed also under penalty of excommunication with sentence to be pronounced, as in chapter 8, unless they are excused by reason of hostility, illness, or some other lawful cause, as in chapter 13; and they must faithfully complete them under the virtue of holy obedience, having God before their eyes, to whom they are to render a strict account. Thus, before they leave the monasteries, they are to reform effectively in them, so far as lies in them, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the canonical sanctions, and the statutes of the provincial chapter and of the order, and especially in the three substantial matters, which are obedience, continence, and poverty. And where they do not find disciplines and ceremonies [unclear]

valid, they must institute those disciplines and ceremonies which they have received as given to them by the chapter, as in chapter 6; and thereafter they must make a report of the whole matter as quickly as possible to the nearest president.

Likewise, in whatever diocese they have been deputed to visit monasteries of men, they must also visit in it the monasteries of nuns, just as do the others to whom the care of them has been committed. Nevertheless, let them see to it that they never visit them from a lust of seeing them, since the sight of them is contagious; but when they have finished, they must depart from there as quickly as possible, as in chapter 16. Similarly, they must visit provostships, priories, and deaneries which are subject to certain monasteries, while nevertheless admitting the abbots to whom they are subject, if they wish to be present. And those visited in such places shall pay half the levy.

They must complete the very act of visitation according to the form prescribed to them by the provincial chapter and the presidents, without demanding an oath, after first setting forth the word of God, as in chapter 6. Nor must they bind anyone by oath, or otherwise indiscreetly, to disclose and make public hidden crimes, unless the order of fraternal correction has been observed. They may also visit again a monastery previously [unclear] by them, and require purgation. Likewise they can and must impose penalties according to the requirement of the faults, and exact those previously imposed either by the provincial chapter or otherwise by anyone, both corporal and monetary. The money, however, which they receive, whether contributory or penal, they must transmit to the keepers of the chest, so that it may be placed in the chest by them.

Likewise, for contumacy or rebellion and disobedience, they can pronounce a sentence of excommunication, and absolve from one previously imposed, with fitting satisfaction first having been made. Likewise, rebels and resisters, if they find any whom they cannot correct, they must denounce to the nearest presidency, so that he may proceed against such persons by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure, according to the measure of their faults. For all those are also excommunicated by the fact itself who in any way either impede visitations from being held or abandon a reform already begun, unless within the time by a visita-

... they shall strive to begin again what is to be established by the [unclear]. Likewise, they must present the proceedings to each monastery visited by them. To these things, therefore, the visitors themselves are bound under obedience and the penalties noted above. If they have been negligent, whether in many matters or in few, they must be compelled by the presidents and procurators of the chapter, through ecclesiastical censure or some other penalty, not to neglect the office enjoined upon them. But lest they be compelled to do labor without reward and, according to the apostolic tradition, to serve as soldiers at their own expense, it has been ordained that each monastery visited by them must give them three Rhenish florins for travel expenses; and it has been entrusted to their consciences, from good consideration, even to increase those same florins for them. Likewise, that the visited monasteries should guard their horses and other goods with the greatest diligence. And if, which God forbid, anything of their goods should happen to be lost or stolen, before all else the abbot and convent of such a monastery must pay without delay, and without contradiction, the value of the goods or things lost; and nevertheless they are to be punished for negligence by a penalty to be moderated by the presidents. And the same abbot must also provide safe-conduct for the visitors [unclear] if they have been despoiled or harmed [unclear] he must also provide [unclear] six mounts, neither in the act of visitation nor in coming to the chapter.

On the act of visitation. Rubric seven.

In the act of visitation the eye of consideration of the fathers who are visiting must be directed to four principal things. First, namely, to the places of the monasteries, as to the more visible things. Second, to the persons living within the places of the monasteries. Third, to the conduct and discipline of the persons. Fourth and last, to the divine worship itself. If one considers the first of these diligently, it at once shows what is probably to be thought concerning the second; and again the second, what concerning the third; and so on in consequence.

On the places of monasteries. Rubric eight.

The Apostle says: “For what is spiritual is not first, but what is animal.” First, therefore, as has been said, one must consider exterior matters, that is, places as corporeal things. Places, however, fall under a threefold distinction. Some are necessary, such as the oratory, cloister, refectory, dormitory, infirmary, bath, pantry, cellar, place for guests together with the abbot’s house, kitchen, and porter’s cell, with the chapter-place. If any of these places is lacking, it must be built within a year, in virtue of holy obedience, or repaired if it has collapsed; and the negligent must actually be punished by the visitors, as above, chapter 3. Some places, however, are for well-being, such as the garden, bakery, mill, workshop for binding books, and [unclear]. Others, however, are superfluous and harmful and contrary to the regular norm: such are the wandering byways, secluded and suspicious dwellings of certain houses, which must either be destroyed from the foundations or converted to some other better use of the monastery, under the same obedience as above. The oratory, which is first among the necessary places, must be adorned with lights, altars, and ornaments that are neat, clean, and seemly. The choir must be furnished with seats, pulpits, and chant books. The sacristy must be furnished with chalices, corporals, missal books, sacred jewels, and sacred vestments and ornaments concerning the divine office and ministries, as is said in chapter 1, where these things also are added: “We will,” it says, “that provision be made within a month for a clean, seemly, and secure vessel and place in which and where the Eucharist is to be reserved.” And the same is laid down concerning the baptistery there and in the following statutes. Books, together with the other ornaments, are to be kept under diligent custody. These things concerning jewels and seals, and certain following chapters, wish to be understood and observed. Therefore the visitors must diligently attend to each of these things concerning the oratory.

and besides these things to consider what revenues, offerings, etc., have regard to the oratory and the sacristy; likewise in what way, whether simoniacally or not; likewise under what species of vice he possesses property, and so with the others. And likewise concerning the other officials it is similarly ordained, as concerning the abbot, cellarer, etc.: whether they render an account every year, and how.

For it is commanded in the aforesaid third chapter, and also in the first, by virtue of holy obedience and under penalty of excommunication to be imposed by the visitors, that every abbot hand over to the visitors in writing, distinctly, the former and present state of his monastery; and that all officials render to them a faithful account of what has been received and distributed. Likewise, that inventories be made; that places not be handed over on lease, except according to the Benedictine constitution, which must also be observed in receiving spoils from benefices and in making loans and sales. And transgressors must be severely punished, even beyond the penalties contained in the aforesaid constitutions. This concerning the oratory. Concerning the remaining places it will appear below, in connection with the discipline of persons.

Concerning the persons who dwell within monasteries. Rubric 9.

The persons who dwell within monasteries, if they are not professed, must be not only necessary and useful, but also honorable and without suspicion. Hence all superfluous, dishonorable, and suspicious persons must be removed far from the bounds of monasteries. But those who are already actually professed, or are soon to be professed, must be considered most diligently, both according to the quantity of their number and according to the quality of their condition. For everywhere the number of monks formerly established must, if resources suffice, be preserved complete; or at least there must be no fewer than can conveniently be maintained, as above, chapter 1 and certain following chapters, through whom divine worship can be perfectly and laudably discharged. From these, sufficient and necessary officials are to be appointed according to the disposition of the Rule, namely abbot, prior, deans, cellarer, porter, infirmarian, and so with the rest; and especially some suitable men who may sufficiently instruct the young in the rudimentary sciences, according to the form of the statutes of Benedict XII, as above, chapters 1 and 3. And some from reformed houses are to be brought from elsewhere, if the monastery itself has not previously been well reformed.

Likewise, not only nobles are to be received, nor only [Scots?], but according to the Rule, both the one and the other: both the freeborn and one converted from servitude; both the poor man who has nothing at all and the rich, powerful man who has great abundance, as above in the same chapter and consequently in many others, such as 16 and 17. Nor ought anything to be exacted from them, nor may any one of them promise anything for his reception, either by himself or through others, nor otherwise promise that he will give anything, except those things which, without agreement, he himself or his parents, of free will, wishes or has wished to offer at the altar or otherwise to the monastery or to God. And those so received, when the year of probation has elapsed, are to make profession and promise stability according to the Rule, as above, chapter 2. Without this probation, moreover, no one ought to be received as an obedientiary, neither one newly coming from the world nor one arriving from another monastery, with letters or without letters, as above, chapters 8, 13, and 15, etc.

Nor henceforth should brothers be received without the permission of their superiors, nor allowed to wander; if any have hitherto been received, even by authority of the apostolic see or otherwise with sufficient permission, they are to be recalled as quickly as possible, namely within two months, and instructed according to the statutes of our order, under penalty of excommunication and suspension, as above, chapters 1 and 2; or they are even to be sent back to their own monasteries, if they were received without sufficient permission and authority, under the same penalty, as above, chapter 8. Fugitive or wandering monks must not be received without letters of commendation from their abbots or from the nearer presiding superior. Nor may they even be given hospitality except for three days, as above, chapters 8 and 12, under a similar penalty. Likewise, if any have laid or should lay violent hands upon a monk or upon an abbot, he also must not be received nor permitted to remain in the province, as above, chapter 12, under the same penalty.

Likewise, still concerning persons, it must be considered whether all are present; whether any are sick or in prison; whether any are fugitives and have not been recalled, or have been sent out with general letters, which ought not to be done henceforth; whether any are in priories—

or provostships? whether any are in a place of study or in another unreformed monastery, even with a special mandate: for no one ought to be sent from a reformed monastery to an unreformed one except for the cause of reform. In all these matters likewise, and in the following as also in the preceding matters, the visitors, according to the mandate of the presidents, in virtue of holy obedience [unclear], ought both to show and to exercise exact diligence.

Concerning the Discipline of Persons within Monasteries

The discipline of monks, both those residing there. Rubric 10.

According to the Rule, and also according to the statutes of the fathers, it must be weighed and considered in many respects. First, however, concerning the outward aspects of a man’s life, namely tonsure and clothing. And by whom garments are supplied to the brothers: whether by a common keeper of clothing, or whether they have them through friends or from some private source. And whether provision is made for each equally, or differently without infirmity or another reasonable cause. Likewise, the garments should be necessary according to the stature prescribed by the fathers only, namely, and religious both in material and in form.

Second, concerning food and fasting. Whether all, except the sick, take refreshment in the refectory without eating meat. Whether there is a reader at table and ministers, who, according to the Rule, enter on Sunday with a blessing. For it ought not to be allowed that each person, or any from among the individuals, have special youths or servants as ministers, as it is known to be done in certain monasteries. Nor ought anyone to arrange anything for himself by himself, by his labors, through friends, or through any others whatsoever; or to receive anything, even not so arranged but offered freely, without permission, but to hope for all things from the father of the monastery. And if the eating of meat is at times granted to some for a reason, this ought to be done only on fixed days and in the infirmary alone, where no layperson ought to be admitted. But on the road, or outside the monastery, no healthy person ought to eat meat, just as not within the monastery. Likewise, whether alms are given from the surplus. And whether the ministers perform their washings on Saturday at the mandatum. Likewise concerning fasting: whether he duly observes the fast both ecclesiastical and regular; when and how and with whom dispensation is made concerning a later meal; when they use oil, and when eggs or butter; how in Advent, how in Lent.

Third, concerning nocturnal rest and silence. Namely, whether all sleep together in one dormitory, girded and clothed. Whether each one is in a separate bed, or two in one, which ought not to happen. Whether seniors are mixed with juniors. Whether the dormitory is locked, and when. Whether the prior has the keys to all the cells. Whether they sleep in woolen garments. Whether the cells are sufficiently barred, as they ought to be under penalty of a sentence of excommunication already incurred. Whether the beds are frequently inspected because of private property. Whether silence is observed in the dormitory, oratory, cloister, refectory after compline, and before chapter, and at other times and places, in the manner and form just as the Rule has concerning this.

Fourth, concerning subjects: whether they are obedient. Whether there are proprietaries, possessing anything at all from offerings, masses, labors, offices, or any other sources whatsoever. Whether there is a report concerning anyone in the matter of continence.

Fifth, concerning shaving and the bath: when and how, and with what discipline, they have them. And concerning the sick, how they are provided for. Whether they have an infirmarian and cellarer who are solicitous and fear God. Likewise also the rest in the community, how, namely, and whether they themselves are provided for. Whether they have suitable comforts at their proper time. And whether the young are instructed by sufficient masters in morals and ceremonies, and likewise in the first elements of knowledge; and by whom, whether by monks or seculars; and whether any are in a place of study.

Sixth, how they conduct themselves toward one another: whether humbly and charitably. And whether, after a disturbance has arisen, they seek reconciliation according to the Rule.

Seventh, how they conduct themselves toward others and outsiders: whether perhaps they are too familiar with them, or whether on account of them, or even on account of relatives, friends, or parents, it happens that they frequently leave the monastery. Likewise, on the contrary, whether they receive guests who come to them with all humanity into lodging and to table, with the mandatum, the washing of feet, and le-

... of the divine law? Eighth, how they conduct themselves in going out of the monastery: whether, namely, with permission, and whose permission; whether with a companion, and of what kind; with how many horses and servants, and of what sort; whether with a blessing, both when going out and when coming in; whether also in suitable habit and with books of hours, and so concerning the other matters of which [there is mention] above, chapter 1, and below in the following rubric. Ninth, concerning individual persons, a separate consideration and inquiry must be made.

First concerning the abbot: whether before his election he was reformed, or at least had remained for a year in the reform; whether afterward he continued the reform; whether he attended the chapter and paid the contribution; whether he renders an account every year, and handed over in writing the state of his monastery to the former visitors; and whether he obeyed them in all their ordinances. Whether he alienated, pawned, or handed over to friends the goods of the monastery. How he confers benefices. How he appoints offices: whether with counsel or according to his own opinion. Whether he has priories, provostships, or churches annexed to the monastery. How he confers them, and on whom. Likewise whether each year he receives an account from them and holds a chapter. Whether he frequents the choir or gives himself to hunting; and so concerning the other matters which are noted above in various places about the abbot, and which will still be touched on below in certain rubrics. And the same is also to be done likewise with the prior, cellarer, custodian, vestiarian, and the remaining officials, with each according to the requirement of his office. Likewise with the porter: whether he is old and mature, going with the others to the refectory, dormitory, etc.; likewise whether they allow women to enter or to live inside; whether the brothers frequently go out; and so concerning the other matters. Concerning all these things there is clearer treatment in the decrees of the first and third chapters, and also still of other chapters, and in the manner of visitation, folio 13, as well as in the bull of lord Nicholas, the legate often mentioned, whose points are given below in the last rubric.

Tenth, concerning the daily chapter: whether it is practiced daily, with exposition of the Rule and correction of faults.

On the propriety of external habit. From chapter 1. Rubric II.

We ordain and decree that all should wear large and broad tonsures, so that their circle does not exceed the space of two transverse fingers; and that they should conduct themselves fittingly in clothing, habits, and footwear, according to the Clementine Ne in agro and the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict, On the form and propriety of garments: namely, that they should wear tunics and garments next beneath the outer habit, of black, brown, or white color, according to the custom usual among them; round, reaching to the ankles, not slit, nor marked by any other deformity, having wide sleeves extended as far as the fist, not buttoned or knotted in any way, yet not so wide that their width above the fist can be stretched out with the thumb raised. Nor should they extend beyond the elbow, as the abuse of certain men has it, more than so far that the arm can easily be turned and drawn inside. Let them be content with almuces of skins in place of cowls. Yet in suitable places where they have been accustomed to wear them, they may, by permission of the abbot, use honorable cowls, slit above the shoulders to the length of at least four transverse fingers. In their garments they should not wear sendal for linings, or miniver, or other costly material, but only skins of lambs or young lambs for the said linings; nor should the linings appear in any way above the neck or at the edges of the garments or sleeves. Furthermore, when it happens that they travel outside the monastery, they should wear a frock, cuculla, or cloak open on either side; and the conversi should use a scapular with a cowl attached to it, inside and outside the monastery. But because some use the aforesaid habits broader and longer, and others less so, therefore the breadth and length

we have decided should be inserted in the present letters, and which we wish to be observed. And first, beginning with the hood of the frock, we ordain that its width shall not reach the bone of the elbow by the thickness of two fingers set crosswise; nor may it be narrower or so short that it does not extend as far as the middle between the elbow and the upper bone near the shoulder-blade. The said hood, moreover, at the back shall extend at least as far as the belt; nor may it extend beyond it by as much as four fingers. The length of the sleeves shall extend one cubit beyond the hand, and their width shall not exceed another cubit and a half. Yet below it shall be so wide that steps may easily be taken within it. And what has been said of the frock we wish to be understood also of the cowl, apart from sleeves, since it has none. Within the monastery, however, in places where there are twelve monks, all shall use the frock. But in other places where there is not so large a congregation, they may use cowls; if they wear them, no one shall use the frock, except only the president of the monastery and the first after him, whom we wish altogether to wear the frock. Yet in works, namely in the divine office under the alb, and when riding under the cloak, they shall wear a scapular, at least half a cubit wide. They shall not use linen and hempen shirts, but shall wear either a woollen undergarment or a woollen garment in place of the aforesaid shirts. And they shall wear high boots or buskins or laced shoes, so that their height takes in a space of four fingers of the leg above the ankle. If they are negligent in any of the foregoing, or within three months after they have come to their monasteries, as stated above, then, in addition to the penalties inflicted by law, we wish them to be punished by their superior in religion, or, if they have no superior, by the aforesaid visitors, in such a way that it may serve as an example to the rest.

Concerning Divine Worship. Rubric 12.

The office in divine worship, both by day and by night, must be celebrated at the proper hours according to the Rule, devoutly, deliberately, and with pauses, not by running through it or cutting it short. Nothing must be preferred to this work; but as soon as the signal has been heard, leaving everything that is in their hands, all must hasten to it with the greatest speed, yet with gravity, lest buffoonery find occasion, as above, chapters 1 and 3. For this reason also the signal for matins, which must be made at midnight, as above, chapter 1, and for prime likewise and for vespers, must be prolonged for at least a quarter of an hour, where above and in several following chapters. And lest, because of a shortage of persons, some could excuse themselves from carrying out that worship perfectly, it has been ordained above, chapter 3, that everywhere as many monks must be maintained and received as can conveniently be supported from the goods of the monastery; and those negligent in these matters must be punished very severely. Abbots and the others must also celebrate, confess, and communicate, as is contained in the constitutions of Benedict XII concerning the celebration of masses. And all who, according to the laws and Benedictine sanctions, ought to be established in orders must be promoted to orders within a year, as above, chapter 1, and in the following chapters. This also must be considered by the visitors: whether there are any churches annexed to the monastery; and whether any masses are to be performed inside or outside the monastery; how many there are; how they were founded and accepted; and how they are performed, and by whom. Likewise also concerning anniversaries and other foundations, or votive manual actions, and also meditations, whether they are regularly attended to.

Concerning Monasteries of Nuns. Rubric 13.

The things that have been said concerning monasteries of men must also be observed in monasteries of nuns, as to the articles appropriate to them, as above, chapter 1 and following. Nor should secular girls be permitted there who are not staying there for the sake of conversion, as above, chapter 16. They must be under perpetual enclosure, as above, chapter 1, as is contained in the constitution of Boniface that begins Periculoso, on the state of monks, book 6. they must visit, as has been touched on above in the rubric on visitors, and they must not enter their enclosures unless great necessity or utility demands it, as above, chapter 16. Entry of this sort is also wholly forbidden to their confessor, in the same chapter. Nor ought anyone to be appointed their confessor without the consent of at least one president.

On the manner and form of reforming monasteries, according to the tenor of the bull of lord Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal of the Roman Church of the title of St. Peter ad Vincula and legate de latere throughout Germany. Rubric 14.

Rubric 14.

First, that the prelates of the monasteries to be visited be so instructed that, by suitable habit and tonsure, by uprightness of life, by gravity of morals, by the word of doctrine, and by the example of holiness, they may laudably and fruitfully preside over their subjects. Let them correct and amend the excesses of individuals according to the rule and statutes of the order, without any dissimulation. Let them recall all their fugitive brethren and absent monks, with a term to be appointed for them by the visitors for this purpose, except those who preside over annexed parishes. And let no one be permitted to use the damnable practice of private property; rather, let all things be reduced to common use.

Against the incontinent, both prelates and subjects, let a heavier discipline and censures proceed, so that not only may the vices of public incontinence be punished as they deserve, but also every occasion be removed from their midst from which suspicion of incontinence could arise.

Let the three substantial elements of the rule especially be preserved most fully by all, so that no dispensation or contrary custom may ever avail anyone against them.

Let silence be observed in the oratory, refectory, and cloister, etc. Likewise, let the brethren take refreshment under table reading, which is to continue until the end of the meal. The eating of meat is to be most strictly forbidden to all healthy persons, in every place and time.

Let all likewise sleep in the dormitory, so far as possibility permits, girded with belts or cords, upon mats, mattresses, or blankets. Let them by no means use linen shirts and sheets.

Concerning the enclosure of monasteries, let due custody be applied, so that entry to the precincts of the monastery may not be open to women, even those not suspect; nor may it be lawful for any religious, except officials, to leave the precincts of his monastery without the special permission of his superior.

Let all healthy persons observe the fasts established both by the rule and by the Church.

Let the divine office, both by day and by night, be performed properly and distinctly, as is fitting, at the appropriate hours. When it has been completed, let them devote themselves to readings or to the works of their hands according to the requirement of time and business, and according to the direction of the aforesaid rule.

Let blankets be supplied to the brethren at the determined time. Likewise, let the beds of the brethren be [unclear] because of particular work.

Let the chapter of faults be observed daily; in it, after the readings of the martyrology and the rule have first been made, let them proceed, if need be, to the exposition of the rule and to the examination and correction of faults.

Let him also provide that the brethren do not neglect to confess, communicate, and celebrate at the appointed times.

Let him diligently provide for the monks concerning food and drink according to the disposition of the rule.

Let suitable places also be assigned in those monasteries, both for sick brethren and for guests arriving for a time; to all of them let care and humanity be shown according as the aforesaid rule requires. Let them lead guests to prayer; let reading be read to them for edification, and let him wash their feet.

Let him take the greatest care that monasteries not be burdened with unbearable loads of debts, and that their goods not be dispersed or alienated, according to the sanctions of Benedict XII and other apostolic sanctions, and according to the oaths sworn by abbots at their confirmation and blessing. Let alienated goods, if there are any, be carefully recovered.

Let abbots, provosts, priors, or rectors diligently preserve the rights of those monasteries. Let them render a lawful account of fruits, revenues, and proceeds, and of the condition of temporal goods.

Let them abstain from superfluous and unbecoming riding-horses, dogs, and hunting birds.

Nor let any religious within the precincts of the monastery

...that they presume in no way to have arms or to contract spiritual kinship. These and other things handed down by the holy fathers and by canonical and regular institutions, as the character of the time and the condition of persons require and as seems salutary to the visitors, they shall renew by establishing them in monasteries and places that have fallen away from regular observance, for the introduction of holy reform. And they shall take care to entrust them to due execution, causing each and all of them to be firmly observed by ecclesiastical censure, by our authority, which by these presents we commit to them.

To the present volume, divided and apportioned into a form for visiting the monasteries, both of nuns and of monks, of the order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg; into a manner of holding their provincial chapter every three years; into an abridgment of the recess of each provincial chapter held from the year of grace 1417 up to the present; into a summary of the privileges granted to the aforesaid order; into an epilogue expressing the foregoing matters in ordered brevity: at the request of the reverend father in Christ, the lord abbot of the monastery at Saint Giles in Nuremberg, a prelate of the said order, whose wish he greatly desires to accommodate, Georg Stuchs of Sulzbach, citizen of Nuremberg, with his art as guide and fortune as companion, gave the work its preconceived and intended end, in the year 1493 of the incarnation of the intelligible divine Word by the Holy Spirit from Mary ever virgin, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [20 September]. May [the merits?] of most blessed Benedict aid us in obtaining his clear intellectual and most blessed vision. Amen.
